papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) produces rich training experience, yet outcome rewards reduce each attempt to a single number and leave most of this information unused. Training-time scaffolds, such as strategies or hints added to the prompt during training, offer a natural way to turn this information into guidance, but their design and adaptation are largely left to humans and tailored to specific domains. We introduce AutoScaffold, a unified AI-for-AI framework that turns a student's training experience into adaptive scaffolds, with minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention during training. A frozen teacher periodically examines this experience, diagnoses bottlenecks, and designs scaffolds in two forms: (i) strategies shared across a class of tasks and (ii) hints for individual hard tasks, adjusting the content and amount of support as the student learns. The scaffolds are removed at evaluation. We apply the same framework to ALFWorld, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation. When evaluated without scaffolds, students trained with AutoScaffold outperform those trained with the corresponding RL baselines in all four domains, with gains of 7.2 points in ALFWorld success and 4.0 points in average QA exact match. On GPU kernel generation, AutoScaffold increases the fraction of tasks with a correct kernel that runs faster than the PyTorch reference by up to 5.0 points. On math, our student surpasses QuestA's reported accuracy using approximately one-third as many student training steps. Analyses show that the teacher identifies a different failure in each task class and shifts its scaffolds from step-by-step workflows to targeted fixes as the student improves, and that its revised scaffolds help the student learn more than keeping the previous scaffold or using no scaffold.
authors: Zijian Zhang, Rizhen Hu, Jiangweizhi Peng, Shiyang Li, Sujay Bhatt, Sihan Zeng, Mingyi Hong

Table 1: Positioning of AutoScaffold. Stage: whether the method changes how a model behaves at inference time or how it is trained. What it changes: the object that is designed or edited. Granularity: whether guidance is shared by a class of tasks, specific to one task, or both. Automatic: an AI system decides the changes, without hand-designed content or schedules (◦: content is generated by a model, but its use follows hand-designed rules). Adapts to student progress: whether guidance or training settings are revised in response to the student’s current performance and observed failures (◦: changes follow predefined rules or schedules). No extra runs: changes are decided and tested within a single training run, without training separate runs or branches (◦: branches are trained from checkpoints). papers.abstract: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. No harness-based method gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.
authors: Daniel Lenton

papers.abstract: Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace, which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent's reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On $79$ procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach $93.8\%$ completion, against $96.8\%$ for the agent, at $24\%$ lower cost per task. On $\tau^2$-Bench, they reach $75.8\%$ task success (agent: $80.6\%$) and run in $1.3$s instead of $170$s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift $k{=}2$ workflows from $66.7\%$ to $81.2\%$. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ($80.6\%$ vs. $83.6\%$), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to $87.8\%$ at $0.40$s per task, compared to $85.5\%$ in $46.6$s for the agent.
authors: Kaiyuan Hou, Yang Ping Kuo, Indranil Bhattacharya, Rohith Nama, Arushi Gupta, Carlos D. Castillo, Prathap Ramachandra, Xiaofan Jiang, Francesco Carbone

papers.selection_reason: Distills LLM agent runs into low-latency code workflows, reducing inference cost; relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows
papers.tldr: ReTrace distills a few LLM-agent executions into reusable, planner-free workflows that substantially reduce runtime and cost while retaining much of the agent’s task performance.

papers.abstract: Memory-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) policies are meant to remember what happened. Many of them, however, fill memory by time: they sample frames uniformly across the episode and stamp each frame with its time step. Because time passes even when nothing happens, such a memory may not tell waiting from working. We show that it does not. On the counting tasks of RoboMME, we make the robot briefly pause or fidget its wrist. Such a null event changes nothing the task depends on, yet a released memory VLA counts the interval as work done and stops early. We call this failure phantom progress. It cuts success from 47 to 16 of 50 on one task and from 44 to 10 on the other. When the same frames are withheld from memory, success returns, so the cause lies in memory rather than in the interruption itself. We trace the failure to a temporal shortcut: because demonstrations proceed at a steady pace, elapsed time predicts progress. Indeed, rescaling the time stamps alone makes the policy stop early when the clock runs fast and repeat when it runs slow. Surprisingly, removing the time encoding does not cure the failure, because the frames of a null event still occupy slots of the time-sampled memory. Across RoboMME's released designs, vulnerability follows how memory is indexed. Of the fixes the diagnosis suggests, training with injected pauses does not remove the failure and impairs counting, whereas indexing memory by events recovers half or more of the loss without retraining. A memory meant to remember what happened should count events rather than clock ticks.
authors: Chubin Zhang, Bo An

papers.abstract: Neural networks are increasingly studied not merely as predictive systems, but as complex systems whose internal computations are themselves objects of scientific inquiry. Recent progress in mechanistic interpretability (MI) has made it possible to identify neurons, features, circuits, population structures, and dynamical patterns associated with model behavior. As these tools improve, attention is shifting from what can be observed inside a model to how those observations support mechanistic explanations. We examine the parallel efforts of neuroscience and MI to address this question and identify recurring inferential bottlenecks when inferring mechanisms from complex neural systems. We propose five principles and organize them into a recursive logic for a more rigorous procedure of mechanistic inference. These principles provide a framework that supports scientific discovery in two senses: it helps turn local interpretability findings into cumulative knowledge of mechanisms within models, and it makes those mechanisms sufficiently precise to generate testable hypotheses about domains beyond the models. Evidence beyond MI is ultimately required to establish what model mechanisms reveal about the world.
authors: Zhimin Hu, Chen Jiang, Hanbo Xie, N. Apurva Ratan Murty, Sashank Varma

figures.caption: Figure 1: A recursive logic for mechanistic inference. For a given neural system with behavior of interest, it can be investigated by different candidate objects of study: neurons, features, circuits, population geometry, and dynamics. We propose five principles to organize mechanistic research as a recursive process in which evidence informs further questions and revisions to earlier claims. An individual study may address a subset of these questions and revisit them as needed. Red arrows connect these five inferential questions: which object explains the phenomenon (P1), whether represented information is used in computation (P2), what computational role it plays (P3), how roles are organized (P4), and what remains invariant across conditions or implementations (P5; illustrated here across random seeds). Measurement choices constrain every inference (P0). A, B, and C denote computational roles. This process supports the discovery of candidate model mechanisms (within-model discovery), which can generate domain hypotheses and establish their plausibility beyond the model requires independent evidence (beyond-model discovery).

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a logic of inference for mechanistic interpretability, providing a framework for rigorous scientific discovery within neural network models.
papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs a Logic of Inference

papers.abstract: Visual Question Answering (VQA) imposes substantial computational overhead on vision-language models (VLMs), motivating model-agnostic input reduction methods that can be readily applied across diverse VLMs, including in black-box settings. Simply enforcing a visual-token cap reduces computation, but it can discard information needed to answer the question. A single reduction strategy also struggles to accommodate different scenarios. Our key observation is that cropping and compression are complementary: cropping highlights small targets and local details, whereas whole-image compression better preserves context for large targets or distributed evidence. Based on this observation, we propose C$^2$-Routing, which adaptively selects cropping or compression according to the input image and question. Since both strategies may still discard key information, we further design a safety gate that uses the predicted joint correctness distribution under original and reduced inputs to guide fallback and protect accuracy. To accommodate consumer GPU resource constraints, all training and evaluation experiments run on RTX 3090 GPUs. To measure gains beyond token capping, we use full-image baselines with the same cap of 1,024 visual tokens. We conduct extensive evaluation on three VLMs and 18 datasets spanning local details, global scenes, scene text, and documents. With the visual budget already capped, C$^2$-Routing further reduces end-to-end FLOPs by 36.53% and visual tokens by 42.36% on average, with a mean relative task-score decrease of only 0.77%.
authors: Guorui Lu, Qinyu Chen
bullets: Addresses the information loss and limited flexibility of using a single visual-token reduction strategy for VQA.
Routes each image-question pair to cropping for local details or compression for broader context.
Uses a safety gate based on predicted correctness under original and reduced inputs to trigger fallback when needed.
Evaluated across three VLMs and 18 datasets covering local details, global scenes, scene text, and documents.
With a 1,024-token visual cap, reduces average end-to-end FLOPs by 36.53% and visual tokens by 42.36%, with a 0.77% mean relative task-score decrease.

Fig. 1(a,b). When question-relevant information is concentrated in a small region, whole-image downsampling leaves fewer pixels to represent that region, potentially making answer-relevant details unrecognizable. Cropping removes irrelevant background and increases the key region’s relative prominence, helping the model attend to and recognize the evidence. It can therefore reduce visual tokens and computation while improving accuracy. Conversely, when relevant information spans a large area or is distributed across multiple locations, a crop that retains all relevant content typically removes little background and offers limited computational savings; a tighter crop can discard necessary evidence and context. Moderate whole-image downsampling can instead preserve recognizable evidence and spatial relationships, reducing visual tokens and computation while largely maintaining task performance.

papers.abstract: Policy optimization is central to language model post-training, yet principled guidance remains limited. We revisit its theoretical foundations to identify algorithms that learn near-optimal policies using total samples and gradient steps governed by the base model's response coverage, a measure of how readily it generates optimal responses. We call such algorithms coverage-preserving. This guarantee captures the goal of amplifying capabilities accessible through sampling from the base model. (1) Coverage collapse. REINFORCE, the basis for PPO and GRPO, can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero, even as reward improves. This coverage collapse stalls optimization, and convergence can require exponentially many steps despite good initial coverage. The failure arises even with exact gradients and persists under KL regularization to the base model. (2) Reference resets. We show that repeatedly resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy mitigates coverage collapse. We formalize this intervention in Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), a meta-algorithm that approximately solves a sequence of KL-regularized RL subproblems. APMD enables stronger regularization, making each subproblem easier to solve, while reference resets allow convergence to global optimality. (3) Coverage-preserving algorithms. For softmax linear policies over pretrained features, we use APMD to establish the first global convergence guarantees showing that widely used families of post-training algorithms are coverage-preserving. These include stylized PPO and GRPO variants with explicit KL regularization and reference resets, and squared-loss algorithms that implement them implicitly, including those used to train the Kimi models. These results clarify how regularization, clipping, and objective choice affect the sampling and optimization costs of post-training.
authors: Audrey Huang, Nan Jiang, Sham M. Kakade, Sadhika Malladi, Akshay Krishnamurthy, Dylan J. Foster

(b) Strong regularization controls coverage and keeps the learner close to the reference policy, but far from optimality (marked ✩). (c) APMD resets the reference to the most recent policy, reaching optimality through successive local improvements.

papers.abstract: UTF-8's role as the de facto encoding standard in language models introduces cross-lingual inequities due to its variable-length design. However, the effect that this encoding choice has on model performance remains largely unexamined. In this work, we investigate how text encoding impacts the performance of byte-level language models, comparing UTF-8 with a wide range of other encoding strategies, including other Unicode-based approaches, language-specific encodings, and our own customized encodings. To facilitate our analysis, we propose Aether: a hybrid encoding scheme that uses script-specific encodings for our target setting while maintaining full Unicode coverage through UTF-8 fallbacks, using this framework to model four orthographically diverse languages. Surprisingly, we find that while languages with information-dense characters (Chinese, Korean) significantly benefit from compressive encodings, languages whose characters carry less information individually (Georgian, Tamil) are largely insensitive to encoding choice. In light of these findings, we argue that text encoding should be a language-specific design decision, rather than a universal default.
authors: Eugene Jang, Catherine Arnett, Terra Blevins

papers.abstract: Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG's effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at https://ugg-model.github.io/
authors: Amani Kiruga, Zhiyi Li, Ruojin Cai, Hansen Lillemark, Xiaoshan Wu, Ayush Tewari, Yilun Du

figures.caption: Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of camera-controlled generation. Given the first and last RGB frames and a target camera trajectory, we compare generated intermediate frames against ground truth and baseline video generation methods. UGG better preserves scene identity and dynamic content compared with the generic video completion baselines.

Figure 3: Conditional completion with noise as masking. We specify each task by the clean/noisy pattern over RGB, depth, camera-ray, and text tokens. Clean tokens provide observed context, while noisy tokens are denoised as missing targets, enabling generation and prediction with the same model architecture.

Figure 2: Generative-predictive transformer. We model RGB, depth, and camera pose as spatially aligned tokens, with camera pose represented as dense ray maps. Partial observations are zero-noise context tokens, while missing modalities are noisy tokens to be denoised. A unified transformer processes all tokens with modality-specific projections and feed-forward layers together with shared multimodal self-attention, enabling information exchange across modalities. The decoded RGB, depth, and ray maps form a complete 4D scene representation for cross-modal generation, geometric prediction, and inference-time consistency search.

Figure 1: A unified model for generation and prediction. We formulate visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion in a single joint model over RGB, depth, and camera pose. Given arbitrary partial observations, ranging from a text prompt to RGB sequences with geometric cues, our model jointly uses these modalities to infer a complete 4D scene representation, enabling both generation from sparse inputs and geometric prediction from observations.

Our predictions preserve sharper local structures and object boundaries in the highlighted regions. Evaluation results. Table 2 reports camera pose estimation results. In the dense setting, UGG achieves lower ATE and RPEt than the external baselines across all five datasets. For example, ATE is reduced from 0.190 to 0.087 on ScanNet++ compared with Geo4D. In the sparse setting, UGG obtains the lowest tAE and RPEr across all five datasets. These results suggest that the model can infer reasonable relative camera poses from only the first and last RGB frames, despite the ambiguity of sparse observations.

The dashed line shows the single-sample result, and the solid curve shows the selected result as L increases. Search improves several pose and depth settings, showing that the generative model produces useful candidate diversity.

Ground-truth trajectory is shown in black. The leftmost column shows representative RGB frames from the input video. papers.selection_reason: Introduces UGG, a unified generative model for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations (depth, pose). This fits both World Models (predicting dynamics) and 3D Vision (geometric understanding).
papers.title: UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model

papers.abstract: Deepfake detectors are commonly evaluated on real/fake classification alone, but real-world applications require explanations of the visual evidence behind each prediction. Joint vision-language models struggle with authenticity assessment, producing "real" narratives for manipulated images. To address this, we propose a decoupled predict-then-explain pipeline as our submission to the ACM Multimedia 2026 Explainable Deepfake Detection Challenge, with methods trained and evaluated on the XPlainVerse benchmark. A vision-foundation-model ensemble first classifies the image, then a Qwen3-VL-8B model generates a decision-conditioned explanation of the visual evidence. For fake images, a second Qwen3-VL-8B compresses that text into a short non-expert summary without using the image. We further apply metric-aligned Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to optimize both explainers against the challenge criteria. Under matched conditions, GRPO raises complex BERTScore-F1 from 0.686 to 0.712 and also improves grounding (entity and evidence F1); our submission ranked first on complex BERTScore-F1 and seventh overall.
authors: Luka Dragar, Peter Peer, Vitomir \v{S}truc, Borut Batagelj

figures.caption: Table 4: Post-competition grounding-aware scores on all 200,000 test images.
Table 1: XPlainVerse dataset splits. Test class counts reflect the hidden evaluation reference; labels are not included in the public test release.
Table 2: Selected final CodaBench scores [15]. Complex is Complex BERTScore-F1; Expl. is Explanation Score. Challengewebsite: https://explainable-deepfake-detection.github. io/.
Table 3: Matched SFT vs. GRPO complex-explanation ablation on 10,000 scored test images.

papers.selection_reason: Applies a metric-aligned optimization strategy (GRPO) to explainable deepfake detection using Qwen3-VL. This demonstrates the application of Multimodal Large Language Models to a specific task, relevant to the foundation model taxonomy.
papers.title: Metric-Aligned Group Relative Policy Optimization for Explainable Deepfake Detection

papers.abstract: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $\pi_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.
authors: Ilia Larchenko, Gleb Zarin, Atindra Nair, Keerti Manney, Vitaly Kleban, Mirko Kiefer, Anjana Yodaiken

figures.caption: Figure 1: The 2026 model. The VLM (left) encodes three camera images, register and scratch tokens, the task and stage embeddings and the robot state; the smaller action expert (right) denoises a 30-step action chunk and reads the VLM through a learnable mixture of the keys and values of all VLM layers. The task and stage embeddings also enter the expert directly through two conditioning tokens. Every attention layer of both transformers has a learnable sink. FAST tokens are used only in training.

Each agent-routed episode (right) forks that session. papers.selection_reason: Single VLA policy for 100 long-horizon household tasks in simulation, directly fitting embodied AI.
papers.title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge

papers.abstract: Video world models promise general-purpose interactive simulators, but their training is limited by action supervision: action labels are scarce, fragmented across incompatible specifications, and do not scale with the unlabeled video pretraining corpus. A common workaround jointly trains an action encoder to compress consecutive frames into a latent action and a decoder to reconstruct the next frame from the previous frame and that latent, forcing the latent to capture only new information. This has two limitations: learning the action space from scratch can limit generalization to unseen domains, and the bottleneck trades expressiveness for separation, with tighter settings losing nuance and looser ones risking scene leakage under domain shifts. We argue for a different starting point: rather than learning actions from scratch, we start from a pretrained foundation model (V-JEPA 2), whose embeddings of a frame pair already carry substantial action information after large-scale, diverse video pretraining. The remaining challenge is to extract the action while discarding the scene. We propose a label-free contrastive adaptation framework that pulls together frame pairs sharing the same motion under a different scene and pushes apart pairs from the same scene with different motion, reshaping the geometry of the pretrained space without imposing a reconstruction bottleneck. We introduce a unified evaluation protocol along three axes (action expressiveness, scene invariance, and action-conditioned video generation quality) across robot manipulation, camera navigation, game, and driving benchmarks, most of which are unseen during adaptation. Compared with annotation-free latent-action methods, our representations are substantially more expressive while matching their scene invariance, and they yield world models that transfer demonstrated actions to new scenes more faithfully.
authors: Runjia Li, Minghao Chen, Junyu Xie, Philip Torr, Andrea Vedaldi, Tomas Jakab

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed learning pipeline. Left: Contrastive action adaptation. An anchor frame pair (ot, ot+k) is encoded as a two-frame clip by the OnlyAct encoder ϕθ, a pretrained foundation model with low-rank adapters whose weights are shared across all branches. The positive keeps the action but changes the scene: the moving region of the anchor, found by optical flow, is cut out and pasted at a shifted location onto the background of a different scene (for moving cameras, a different photometric augmentation of the anchor is used instead). The hard negative is drawn from a non-overlapping window (ot′ , ot′+k) of the same video, sharing the scene but corresponding to a different action. In the action space, the anchor is pulled towards its positive and pushed away from its hard negative. Right: Action-conditioned video world model. The frozen OnlyAct encoder ϕθ maps consecutive frame pairs into the learned action space, yielding an action stream α1:t that conditions an autoregressive video world model Gψ. Given past frames o1:t and the action stream, Gψ predicts the next frame ot+1, and is rolled out autoregressively to generate subsequent frames.

Figure 6: Additional action-transfer results. Latent actions extracted from the demonstration frames (top) condition the video world model generations (bottom). OnlyAct reproduces the demonstrated actions across various settings. Best seen as videos in the supplementary material which also includes more examples.

Figure 3: Two control modes. After pretraining the video world model on latent actions from the OnlyAct encoder, the learned action space supports two modes. First, action transfer extracts an action stream from a demonstration video and uses it to condition the world model from a new initial frame, reproducing the demonstrated action with no labels. Second, real-action control learns a lightweight interface from real actions onto the learned latent-action space on a small action-labeled set, so that real actions drive the world model directly.

Figure 5: Action transfer. Latent actions extracted from the demonstration frames (top) condition the video world model generations (bottom). OnlyAct faithfully reproduces the demonstrated action in the new target scene, e.g. in the cross-source example it turns right and then performs the attack action. Best seen as a video in the supplementary material.

Figure 4: Real-action control. Left: OnlyAct learns to generate videos that faithfully respond to different actions, Right: comparison of action representations between OnlyAct and AdaWorld using t-SNE.

(a) Controllability after 800 updates. MetaWorld actions are clipped to [−1, 1]. ◦Videos seen by our encoder during training, without action labels; all other datasets are entirely unseen. †Retrained on the same 168K training pairs as our encoder. V-JEPA 2 (frozen): our backbone, embedded identically but without contrastive adaptation. Avg.: mean R2 over the 12 continuous-action datasets. ∆: ours minus the best other method. Bold: best; underline: second best.

Table 6: The OnlyAct recipe on a multimodal embedding backbone. Left: linear probing of action information (test R2; Procgen: macro-F1; mean over 3 probe seeds) with the protocol, clips, splits and seeds of Table 1. Right: scene leakage (held-out LPIPS↑, higher = less scene information recoverable; mean over 4 decoder seeds) with the decoders and held-out scenes of Table 2. V-JEPA 2: the frozen backbone of OnlyAct; OnlyAct: main-text results; Qwen recipe: the same recipe (168K training pairs, augmentation, loss, optimizer, 10,000 steps) on Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B (Appendix A.3). ∆: Qwen recipe minus OnlyAct; green: better for the Qwen recipe (higher R2, less leakage). Avg.: probe over the 12 continuous-action datasets, leakage over all 13. ◦Videos seen during contrastive training (the same for both backbones).
Table 7: Licenses of existing assets, as stated by each source.

Table 3: Action-conditioned world model. The same world model (AdaWorld backbone, same recipe and data) is trained with each action representation. Self : PSNR↑ (dB) when driven by the clip’s own actions. Transfer: a source clip’s actions drive a different scene; Dir↑ is the cosine between the optical-flow direction of the generated video and of the source (0: unrelated; 1: same). ◦Seen by our encoder without action labels. †Retrained on our data. ∆: ours minus the best baseline. Bold: best; underline: second best (no-action row excluded).

Table 5: Whitening control. DreamDojo† world models trained with their native latent actions (as in Table 3) and with the same whitening rule as OnlyAct (statistics computed on its own embeddings), everything else identical, evaluated on the same clips and source–target pairs as Table 3 (LIBERO and RLBench: 40; SpatialVID: 20). RLBench transfer and nuScenes were not evaluated for the whitened model (–). ∆: ours minus the whitened DreamDojo, tested with a paired t-test over clips (Self PSNR) and a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test over source–target pairs (Transfer Dir); grey: not significant at the 0.05 level. papers.selection_reason: Addresses the action supervision bottleneck in World Models by extracting action representations from a pretrained foundation model (V-JEPA 2) via label-free contrastive adaptation. This is highly relevant to Latent Action Models and Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: OnlyAct: Extracting Action Representations from Foundation Models for World Models

papers.abstract: Formal world models can support planning, verification, and safety reasoning, but constructing them from open-ended natural-language situations is difficult, particularly in multi-agent settings where several formalizations may be plausible. We study whether five LLMs can generate such world models as partially observable stochastic games and whether mechanical validity is sufficient to establish that the resulting model faithfully represents the intended decision problem. We introduce a benchmark of 44 scenarios spanning game, situational, and cultural settings and evaluate generated world models along three dimensions: mechanical validity, reference-relative structural agreement, and semantic criteria. Across three empirical tracks, we analyze 410 first-pass generations. In the reference-backed game track, 134/135 generated world models pass a strict mechanical audit, yet mean permutation-invariant structural F1 is only 0.366, with just 28/134 mechanically valid models exactly matching the authored reference. In the cultural track, explicitly naming the country changes the generated structural representation for most LLMs while producing only small changes in automated semantic scores. These results show that executability is a necessary but insufficient criterion for LLM-generated world models: models that are mechanically valid can still differ substantially in the structure used by downstream neuro-symbolic reasoning and planning.
authors: Souhaila Djaffal, Amna Jamal, Gagana Madhugiri Devaraja, Anidipta Pal, Jobst Heitzig
bullets: Evaluates five LLMs generating partially observable stochastic-game models from natural-language scenarios.
Introduces a 44-scenario benchmark covering game, situational, and cultural settings.
Assesses mechanical validity, reference-relative structural agreement, and semantic criteria across 410 generations.
In the reference-backed game track, 134/135 models were mechanically valid, but mean structural F1 was only 0.366 and 28/134 exactly matched the reference.
Country labels changed structural representations for most models in cultural scenarios, despite only small changes in automated semantic scores.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies generation and evaluation of LLM-based world models for planning and reasoning.
papers.title: Evaluating LLM-Generated World Models for Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning
papers.tldr: LLMs often generate executable world models that nonetheless diverge substantially from the intended structure, limiting their reliability for neuro-symbolic reasoning and planning.

papers.abstract: Local decoding usually fixes one weight precision for the whole generation. We study a different allocation: store 8-bit weights, decode with their top 4 bits, and redo a step at 8 bits only when the low-precision output distribution looks uncertain (entropy above a threshold or a small top-two margin). Quantization is simulated, the model is Qwen3-0.6B, and the benchmark is GSM8K. Cost is counted in weight bytes read per token. On 36724 replayed steps the entropy of the low pass ranks argmax flips with AUC 0.93. At a 15% escalation budget it catches 78% of flips and the margin gate 94%, against the 15% expected for a random gate of equal rate (a computed expectation, not a run). In 150 live problems all-high scores 64.0% and all-low 55.3% (McNemar p=0.053). An entropy gate with a 16% escalation rate scores 62.7% at 0.87 of the all-high weight bytes. Its paired difference is -1.3 (-8.0 to +5.3) points to all-high and +7.3 (+0.0 to +14.7) points to all-low (p=0.080), so the live data do not separate the gate from either end. Verified speculation reaches zero KL at similar bytes in the same cost model. A live random control, a thinking-mode phase rule, a second model and live KL were not run.
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Logesh L, Aliyas Ahmad Misri
bullets: The approach stores 8-bit weights, initially decodes with the top 4 bits, and escalates uncertain steps using entropy or top-two margin thresholds.

papers.abstract: Local language models can save memory by storing weights in fewer bits, and they can reduce sensitivity to the order of answer options by averaging a few reorderings. We ask whether the first makes the second worse, and which is the cheaper way to spend a fixed budget. On Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B with simulated round-to-nearest weight quantization (8, 6, 4 and 3 bits, fp16 reference), read from the logits of the letters A to D on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MMLU and HellaSwag (300 items each), 6 bits lose no accuracy against fp16 (they score +1.8 (+1.0 to +2.5) and +0.9 (+0.3 to +1.5) points higher, which we do not explain), and 8 bits change it by -0.7 (-1.1 to -0.3) and -0.4 (-0.7 to -0.2) points. At 4 bits the answer-slot skew rises from 0.15 to 0.53 (0.6B) and from 0.07 to 0.12 (1.7B); Gaussian noise at the same weight SNR gives 0.15 and 0.37 (two draws) and 0.19 (one draw), so the control is inconclusive on whether rounding adds slot skew beyond equal-power noise. Flip rates rise but stay below an accuracy-matched baseline of independent uniform errors. Averaging four cyclic orders recovers +12.6 points at 4 bits for 0.6B (+5.3 at fp16). We price bits and passes in one machine-independent unit, weight bytes read times passes. In cost-matched pairs, extra orders beat extra bits only when the weights have 6 or more bits, and the decision table reduces to: use 6-bit weights and spend the rest of the budget on up to four orders, one pass each. Everything is simulated on two small models with the simplest quantizer; a title-level search found no earlier study of quantization together with option order.
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Logesh L, Aliyas Ahmad Misri
bullets: The study tests whether lower weight precision increases sensitivity to answer-option ordering under a fixed inference budget.
It evaluates simulated 8-, 6-, 4-, and 3-bit round-to-nearest quantization on two Qwen3 models across four multiple-choice benchmarks.
Six-bit quantization matches or slightly exceeds fp16 accuracy, while 4-bit quantization substantially increases answer-slot skew.
Averaging four cyclic option orders recovers 12.6 points at 4 bits for the 0.6B model, compared with 5.3 points at fp16.
Cost-matched comparisons favor extra orders over extra bits only at 6 bits or higher; findings are limited to two small models and a simple simulated quantizer.

papers.title: Bits or permutations? Spending a fixed inference budget on weight precision or on option-order averaging in small local language models

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by having a draft model propose multiple tokens for the target model to verify in one pass. The speedup is governed by the expected acceptance length (EAL), yet standard training objectives such as cross-entropy, KL divergence, and total variation focus only on distribution matching or single-step overlap. Recent studies instead propose block-level training objectives, aiming to optimize EAL directly. However, these objectives remain surrogates rather than exact formulations of EAL. For example, some average later acceptance over target-distributed continuations rather than the verification branches selected by accepted tokens, introducing a covariance gap that can reverse the gradient direction. We analyze this gap and derive REAL, a real EAL training loss that uses path weights for unbiased estimation and Rao-Blackwellization for variance reduction. In a controlled loss-level comparison with a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B target and a Domino drafter, REAL outperforms WTV, VSD, DBLast, and the static LK baseline on probabilistic serving acceptance length across 9 task subsets and 5 evaluation seeds. These gains require only a change to the training loss, with no modification to the drafter architecture or inference procedure, demonstrating the practicality of real EAL training. A reference implementation of the REAL loss is available at https://github.com/King-ty/speculators/tree/real-loss.
authors: Yu Tian

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the de facto method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks, achieving strong task adaptation with minimal trainable parameters and low optimization cost. Beyond this efficiency, practitioners have observed two striking properties: \textit{robustness to catastrophic forgetting} and the ability to \textit{merge independently trained adapters} into a single model that performs competitively across multiple tasks. These properties are central to continual and multi-task learning, yet remain poorly understood. In this work, we provide a theoretical explanation through a unified \textit{margin-based perspective}. We analyze LoRA in multiclass linear classification under a near-orthogonal task regime with $\ell_2$-regularization, and characterize the optimal LoRA adapter across regularization regimes. Our analysis shows that, in an intermediate regime of regularization parameters, the optimal adapter aligns with the \emph{max-margin solution} on the fine-tuning data. Building on this characterization, we derive two key consequences. First, we obtain closed-form expressions for the margins on pre-training and fine-tuning data, revealing a precise margin trade-off: the regularization parameter controls the balance between retention and adaptation. Second, we analyze adapter merging, proving that merged models achieve positive margin on each task and deriving optimal mixing coefficients that balance margins across tasks and maximize the margin over their union. These results lead to a simple, training-free merging rule, which we term \textit{margin-based LoRA merging} (MaLoRA). Experiments on modern architectures and real datasets validate our theoretical predictions, showing that MaLoRA matches or outperforms several adapter-merging baselines across a range of vision and language classification tasks.
authors: Ziqing Xu, Hancheng Min, Lachlan Ewen MacDonald, Salma Tarmoun, Enrique Mallada, Weijie Su, Rene Vidal
bullets: Analyzes LoRA for multiclass linear classification under near-orthogonal tasks and ℓ2 regularization.
Shows that, in an intermediate regularization regime, the optimal adapter aligns with the fine-tuning max-margin solution.
Derives a margin trade-off between retaining pre-training knowledge and adapting to new tasks.
Proves that merged adapters can maintain positive margins across tasks and derives optimal mixing coefficients.
Experiments on vision and language classification tasks validate the theory, with MaLoRA matching or outperforming several baselines.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have emerged as effective alternatives to autoregressive models for latency-critical tasks, enabling faster token generation. Recent advances employ block diffusion with self-editing capabilities, where each block refines tokens iteratively before advancing to the next one. Yet each block is only as fast as its slowest token, and the next block cannot start before it. We suggest Blurring the Block Boundaries (B3), a novel method with which two blocks are refined in parallel within a shared forward pass. B3 calibrates itself on the fly, opening the next block only once the model is ready to start generating it. It is a training-free and hyperparameter-free acceleration method which seamlessly integrates within any self-editing block diffusion model. Evaluated on state-of-the-art DLMs across 10 diverse datasets spanning varied tasks and difficulty levels, B3 results in on par generation quality and 11.5-14.5% speedup compared to the base model, pushing the Pareto frontier for latency-quality trade-offs in DLM inference.
authors: Amir Mann, Jonathan Fhima, Shaked Brody, Or Avitan, Asif Zamir, Shahar Tsiper, Niv Nayman

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly exhibit capabilities that resemble human Learning by Thinking (LbT), the acquisition of new insight through internal processes such as explanation and reasoning, without new external input. A systematic account of the cognitive mechanisms behind these capabilities, and of their limits, remains underdeveloped. This paper proposes a Cognitive LbT Framework that maps four mechanisms (Reflective Reasoning, Synthetic Memory Formation, Internal Simulation, and Conceptual Self-Organization) onto computational processes in LLMs. Drawing on representative methods, including chain-of-thought prompting, self-consistency, self-reflection, Tree-of-Thoughts search, Self-Instruct, and self-taught reasoning, the analysis argues that selected methods can functionally approximate aspects of these mechanisms and can improve performance on some tasks without additional labeled examples, although this does not always constitute durable learning in model parameters. For example, Self-Instruct generated approximately 52,000 instructions from 175 seed tasks and reported a 33% absolute improvement on Super-NaturalInstructions (Y. Wang et al., 2023). The same mechanisms also produce characteristic failures, including hallucination diffusion, model collapse, concept drift, and high computational cost. These failures are not isolated technical defects but follow from four structural asymmetries between LLMs and human cognition: the identity of generator and monitor, closed learning loops without external grounding, symbolic rather than sensorimotor simulation, and the cost of inference-time computation. The framework yields testable propositions about when LbT in LLMs should succeed or fail and offers a structured basis for designing more reliable autonomous learning systems.
authors: Dong Han, Jin Zhang, Kunyue Yang
bullets: Introduces a Cognitive LbT Framework covering Reflective Reasoning, Synthetic Memory Formation, Internal Simulation, and Conceptual Self-Organization.
Maps methods such as chain-of-thought, self-consistency, self-reflection, Tree-of-Thoughts, Self-Instruct, and self-taught reasoning to these mechanisms.
Argues that these methods can improve some tasks without new labeled examples, but may not change model parameters or produce durable learning.
Identifies failures including hallucination diffusion, model collapse, concept drift, and high inference-time cost.
Attributes these limits to four asymmetries with human cognition: shared generator/monitor, lack of external grounding, symbolic simulation, and costly inference.

papers.abstract: Small, holonomic Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) enable close-range inspection of underwater structures from arbitrary viewpoints, requiring accurate position and attitude tracking under state and input constraints. Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) naturally handles these requirements, but relies on an accurate dynamics model, which is difficult to obtain underwater. In this paper, we present a nonlinear MPCC in all six Degrees of Freedom (DoF) for a holonomic AUV and alleviate the inaccuracies in the dynamics by augmenting the nominal model employed with residual dynamics learned via Gaussian Process (GP) regression. The learned residual is embedded in the optimal control problem through a zero-order robust optimization scheme, which keeps the controller real-time capable at 25 Hz. A simulation ablation shows that residual selection is essential when designing the controller, and simulation and in-water experiments with the Multimodality, Observing, Low-cost, Agile (MOLA) AUV validate the resulting controllers against a nominal MPCC and a field proven Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller.
authors: David D\"orner, Giancarlo Troni, Ignacio Torroba, Ivan Stenius
bullets: Targets accurate position and attitude tracking for close-range underwater inspection under state and input constraints.
Uses a nonlinear six-DoF MPCC with Gaussian Process regression to learn residual dynamics beyond a nominal model.
Embeds the learned residual through zero-order robust optimization, enabling control at 25 Hz.
Ablation results show that selecting appropriate residual dynamics is essential for controller design.
Simulation and in-water MOLA AUV experiments validate the controllers against nominal MPCC and PID baselines.

papers.abstract: Pretrained video diffusion models (VDMs) offer a powerful foundation for World Action Models (WAMs), which jointly predict robot actions and future observations. Building such models requires injecting low-dimensional robot signals (e.g. proprioception, actions, and values) into a latent space shaped by natural videos, and a key design choice is the interface through which these signals enter: existing schemes treat it as a formatting detail, spending a separate latent frame on each signal or bolting on dedicated encoders and decoders. We argue that signal injection is instead a distribution-alignment problem: how well a representation matches the prior of the pretrained VDMs during denoising. Using the relative reconstruction error of a frozen VDM denoiser as a probe, we find that conventional spatial encodings sit far off this prior, whereas frequency-domain packing yields latents that the denoiser corrects far less. Motivated by this diagnostic result, we propose MetaWAM, which folds all robot signals into a single unified meta-frame: each signal is assigned to a disjoint frequency-domain channel band and lifted to the spatial latent by an inverse DCT, yielding a decodable interface aligned with the pretrained VDM prior without any added module or architectural change. A fixed band layout together with slot-aware routing lets the same meta-frame support policy, world-model, and value prediction over a shared set of robot variables. On RoboCasa, MetaWAM reaches 68.9% success while collapsing the per-signal frames into one and cutting inference latency by 39%, and attains 85.0% success on three real-world Franka tasks. Code and models are available at https://github.com/showlab/MetaWAM
authors: Guoqiang Liang, Yiqi Lin, Yanzhe Chen, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Mike Zheng Shou

papers.abstract: Stochastic diffusion samplers often require substantially more neural function evaluations (NFEs) than deterministic samplers to achieve comparable sample quality. Although higher-order discretization accelerates deterministic sampling, its benefits for stochastic sampling remains unclear. We establish matching upper and worst-case lower bounds showing that stochastic samplers with higher-order approximations remain first-order convergent, even with exact score functions. Thus, increasing the approximation order does not generally improve the convergence order. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce forward-value discretization, a training-free framework that evaluates the data/noise prediction model at a lookahead estimate constructed from previous predictions. For deterministic sampling, the resulting Forward DPMSolver (F-DPMSolver), improves sample quality at low NFE budgets through its DDIM-based variant, despite remaining first-order convergent. For stochastic sampling, we develop Forward DDPM (F-DDPM), which evaluates the model at a cleaner lookahead point adjusted for subsequent noise injection. This estimate reuses both the previous model prediction and the previously injected noise. Both variants admit first-order convergence guarantees with one model evaluation per iteration. Across CIFAR-10, ImageNet, FFHQ, and LSUN, F-DDPM consistently achieves lower FID than the evaluated stochastic baselines at matched NFE budgets. With 1.5 times as many NFEs as deterministic baselines, it achieves competitive sample quality, narrowing the practical efficiency gap between stochastic and deterministic sampling. Code is available at https://github.com/Na-Li66/F-DDPM.
authors: Yuchen Jiao, Na Li, Changxiao Cai, Yuting Wei, Gen Li

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon, verifier-rich environments, but current self-improvement mechanisms often write episode-derived lessons directly into memory, making local success an unreliable signal for reusable and safe knowledge. This paper addresses the core question of when an experience-derived behavioral update should be admitted into persistent agent state. We propose Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution (FGSE), a verifier-grounded framework that represents each candidate lesson as a structured hypothesis with an explicit precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier. FGSE applies the hypothesis only in a temporary state, tests it on target-transfer, falsification, and archived-regression probes, and then commits, refines, or rejects it according to measured gain and risk. Across web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory benchmarks, FGSE achieves strong task performance, including 39.8 WebArena success rate, 78.8 AppWorld average completion, and 0.724/0.487 Pass$^1$ on $\tau$-Retail/$\tau$-Airline, while reducing falsification failures to 5.0%, regression damage to 1.3%, and harmful committed updates to 3.6%. These results suggest that testing memory updates as hypotheses supports more reliable long-term adaptation.
authors: Runxuan Tang, Haoyu Gao, Yuyan Ding, Junyi Yao, Zihao Zheng, Zecheng Sheng, Liwei Hou
bullets: Addresses the risk that local episode success leads agents to store unsafe or non-transferable lessons.
Represents each candidate update with a precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier.
Tests updates temporarily using transfer, falsification, and archived-regression probes, then commits, refines, or rejects them based on gain and risk.
Reports strong performance across web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory benchmarks.
Reduces falsification failures to 5.0%, regression damage to 1.3%, and harmful committed updates to 3.6%.

Rows are grouped by the final FGSE decision. Dots denote seed-level outcomes, the shaded halfviolin shows the empirical density, the white box shows the interquartile range, and the diamond marks the mean effect. The right-side annotation reports the sign-consistency score C(h). Committed hypotheses remain consistently positive across seeds, refined hypotheses are still mostly positive but exhibit larger variance, while rejected hypotheses are centered near zero or change sign frequently.

Figure 10: Memory-growth Pareto analysis. We vary the retention budget and evaluate longhorizon self-evolving agents under different memory policies. Left: task success rate versus committed memory size. Right: violation rate versus committed memory size. Each faint point denotes one domain-seed run, while solid lines connect policy means across budgets. Marker area is proportional to retrieval cost Cret. A desirable memory policy should remain close to the upper-left region in the left panel (high success with small memory) and the lower-left region in the right panel (low violation with small memory). FGSE traces the most favorable frontier: it achieves high task success and low violation with substantially smaller committed memory and lower retrieval cost than naive memory growth.

Figure 6: Plasticity–safety Pareto analysis of update-selection strategies. Each point is one configuration obtained by sweeping verifier budgets and acceptance thresholds. The x-axis is update gain ∆upd, and the y-axis is either harmful update rate H (left) or regression damage R (right). Point size indicates verifier cost C (average verifier calls per candidate update), and color denotes the update-selection strategy. The black dashed line shows the empirical Pareto frontier, where larger gain and smaller harm are jointly preferred. FGSE occupies the most favorable lower-right region over a wide range of medium verifier budgets, showing that it improves plasticity without incurring the safety cost typically associated with aggressive update policies.

Figure 7: Falsification discovery curves under different probe-selection policies. The x-axis is the probe budget K. The left panel shows bad-update detection rate D(K), and the right panel shows harmful update avoided A(K). Solid lines denote the mean across repeated trials, and shaded bands denote 95% confidence intervals. The gray vertical band marks the practically relevant low-budget regime (8 ≤ K ≤ 16). Targeted probing consistently dominates random baselines, especially in the low-budget regime, showing that hypothesis-aware falsification is substantially more informationefficient than unguided random testing.

Figure 9: Trajectory-edit Sankey diagram from baseline traces to FGSE traces. The left column shows the dominant behavioral deficiency in the baseline trace, the middle column shows the dominant edit family introduced by FGSE, and the right column shows the resulting FGSE behavior motif. Band width is proportional to the number of corrected trajectories. The diagram shows that most successful transitions are driven by tool-order repair, memory retrieval, and constraint checking, whereas final-answer formatting accounts for only a small minority of improvements.

Figure 2: Exploratory diagnostics for naive episode-derived self-updates. (a) Many updates combine near-transfer gains with boundary harm. (b) Broad and underspecified updates produce substantially higher boundary and archive harm than more specific updates. (c) Sequentially writing free-form lessons into memory can accumulate errors, especially when updates are selected only by source-episode improvement. (d) A post-hoc scope-localization analysis shows that many harmful but useful updates can be repaired by narrowing their applicability, motivating an explicit refinement mechanism.

papers.abstract: Language-model systems use self-judgment to decide which answers to release, review, or recompute. Because intervention is costly, an assurance score must rank errors well at the available budget, not merely over the full ranking. We compare the judge's continuous verdict-token score with a supervised correctness probe trained on attention-head activations from the same prompt. Exact identities link fixed-budget error recall to residual risk and show that AUROC averages recall over all budgets. Across three open 7-12B models on GSM8K and MATH, the probe finds 1.3-22.5 additional percentage points of errors at 5% review in all six model-dataset settings (median 7.4 points). At 10% routing, probe-guided allocation improves accuracy over equal-cost random allocation in both GSM8K experiments, but beats judge-guided routing only for the weaker judge. Cross-dataset transfer lowers probe AUROC for every model in both directions relative to target-domain training. Because dataset, weight precision, and generation budget change together, this measures a joint protocol shift rather than a dataset-only effect. Internal signals can improve supervised, in-domain budget allocation, but are not domain-general confidence estimators.
authors: Mayank Gulati, Gerhard Wunder

papers.abstract: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks, showing that it consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone, while also reducing memory-induced degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace
authors: Yukyeong Lee, Yumin Choi, Jinheon Baek, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: External memory can hurt performance when lessons are incorrect, misapplied, or misread.
WikiTrace stores each insight with a success/failure rationale and its original raw trajectory.
Agents consult linked evidence when an insight is incomplete, conflicting, or derived from failure.
Evaluated on five agentic benchmarks, WikiTrace consistently outperformed existing memory methods and an insights-only baseline.
The system specifically reduces degradation caused by adding memory.

papers.abstract: Adding abstention to a task-adapted multimodal model can discard correct answers, including capabilities acquired during adaptation. We formulate abstention repair as maximizing correct abstention on unanswerable questions under a budget on newly lost correct answers. We propose ReFrain (Regression-Free Abstention), which combines a linear probe on first-token logits, threshold calibration on held-out image clusters, and a deterministic veto that replaces rejected outputs with the displayed "none of the above" option while preserving all other responses. "Regression-free" denotes zero loss on the calibration set at the zero-budget target. All abstention methods in our main comparison start from the same answering-SFT checkpoint; we separately track lost correct answers, repaired errors, and retained SFT gains. On Qwen2.5-VL-3B, ReFrain at zero budget retains all 57 SFT-gained answers with no losses and improves correct abstention by 7.30 percentage points. At a 0.5% calibration budget, it reaches 74.05% correct abstention with 8 losses and retains 55 gains; CLIP-UP EmbLoRA reaches 64.65% with 62 losses, 41 repairs, and 40 retained gains. The same probe at its default threshold loses 298 correct answers. With models and thresholds frozen, confirmation on 228 independent question clusters yields 66.05% correct abstention and no losses at the 0.5% point, exceeding EmbLoRA by 32.72 percentage points. Ordinary refusal SFT achieves higher correct abstention at greater regression cost. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/ModeLiberaL/ReFrain.
authors: Jinyuan Zhang

papers.abstract: System-1 Decision Models directly make structured probabilistic decisions over query-specified options given a state in a single forward pass, without autoregressively generating reasoning trajectories or textual responses. Recent evaluations cover diverse tasks but often rely on existing benchmarks, where prior exposure to test material can obscure generalization. Moreover, real-world decision making often involves long contexts, large option spaces, and complex logical dependencies, challenges that existing benchmarks do not adequately capture together. Thus, we introduce MMDM (Massive Multitask Decision Making), a benchmark of 5,448 high-quality questions across 16 task categories, combining newly constructed tasks with source-grounded recompositions and rewrites for single-select, multi-select, and soft-label decision making in fresh contexts. It covers realistic scenarios such as agent state tracking, tool and skill selection, preference judgments, and rubric scoring, with option spaces ranging from 2 to 1,024 and inputs extending to 64,817 tokens. With MMDM, we conduct a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of 28 decision models, showing that many perform well on common knowledge yet struggle with interdependent options, constrained decisions, and multi-select tasks. For example, Perplexity Decider-V1.2 reaches 78.75% Hard Single-select Accuracy on world knowledge, but only 53.95% on option logic and 47.95% on constraint planning, while the best Hard Multi-select Accuracy across all models is 36.81%. These results highlight joint reasoning, constraint-aware selection, and complete multi-select recovery as key priorities for decision model development, with MMDM providing a testbed for measuring this progress.
authors: Junhao Shen, Qing Zong, Yue Guo, Zhanqiu Zhang, Yiwen Guo, Hong Cheng

papers.abstract: Streaming multi-reference video generation establishes a scene from specified people and objects, then continues it under changing instructions. We introduce TaoMate-R1, a streaming multi-reference generator that organizes adaptation parameters through temporal role specialization. It assigns separate low-rank adapters to scene establishment and continuation on a frozen backbone. Each adapter performs both denoising and context writing for its role; Self Gradient Forcing jointly trains the roles through the history they construct. This allocation contrasts with operation-based specialization, which separates denoising from context writing across all chunks. A fixed-replay gradient analysis characterizes the update directions admitted by the two sharing schemes. On 32 multi-reference cases, we compare the schemes at the same two-adapter budget. Across ten approximately two-minute streams with changing instructions and shared teacher-audio conditioning, TaoMate-R1 reduces the mean boundary luminance jump from 1.96 to 0.613, with higher boundary feature similarity. It also achieves higher mean CLIP and DINO temporal similarity across short interactions, long streams, and public reference compositions. These results support grouping adaptation parameters by scene establishment and continuation for streaming multi-reference generation. Our code and model are released at https://github.com/TaoLiveAIGC/TaoMate-H3.

papers.abstract: Generative driving planners can represent diverse ego futures, but a downstream scorer can choose only among sampled candidates; it cannot recover an absent maneuver. We present ForeseeDrive, which turns future scene evolution into a deployable interface for shaping candidate generation. Rather than reconstructing dense future states or scoring a fixed menu, ForeseeDrive derives query-indexed tokens from logged actor motion, occupancy evolution, route interactions, and TTC margins, and predicts the same token space from present context at deployment. The tokens condition trajectory geometry before candidates materialize. A zero-token-gated residual path and candidate-preservation loss limit unnecessary drift, while a TTC-margin guard targets brittle safe-to-unsafe boundary crossings. Under their respective benchmark protocols, ForeseeDrive reaches 89.2 PDMS on NAVSIM navtest, 0.41\,m average L2 and 0.05\% collision rate on nuScenes validation, and a 76.50 driving score on Bench2Drive. Controlled DiffusionDrive/NAVSIM diagnostics show an exact zero-token no-op, a small aligned-over-shuffled selected-PDM advantage under preservation, mixed oracle-best quality, and localized TTC-boundary failures. Together, the benchmark results and bounded mechanism tests support future-conditioned generation as a practical interface for anticipation. Code is included in the supplementary materials.
authors: Shaokai Wu, Xunchu Zhou, Pinzhi Wang, Bo Dong, Yuting Hu, Yanbiao Ji, Qiuchang Li, Xiao Cui, Qi Kong, Hongtao Lu, Yue Ding

papers.abstract: Remote-sensing foundation models increasingly unify representations across sensing modalities and downstream tasks, yet their prediction mechanisms remain largely task-specific. Separate decoders, prediction heads, and objectives leave prediction fragmented across tasks. This naturally raises a question: can heterogeneous remote-sensing tasks share the prediction process? UniFlow-RS answers this question with a single latent flow-matching predictor shared across tasks. This requires addressing two key challenges: unifying heterogeneous prediction spaces and harmonizing joint optimization across tasks. First, we cast heterogeneous task outputs into structured visual targets in a common latent space, allowing them to be modeled by the same pretrained flow predictor. Task-dependent conditioning further accommodates differences in input configurations. Second, we optimize all tasks with a common Flow Matching objective, eliminating task-specific prediction losses. To mitigate optimization mismatch across tasks and modalities, we introduce Task-Modality Adaptive Timestep Sampling (TMAS), which dynamically allocates training timesteps according to the online learning state of each task-modality group. Using a single shared model, UniFlow-RS handles six tasks and thirteen datasets, surpassing recent task-specific state-of-the-art methods on several benchmarks while remaining competitive on the others. Beyond these benchmarks, the same checkpoint demonstrates strong zero-shot transfer across unseen datasets, task settings, occlusion conditions, and near-infrared false-color imagery, without target-specific adaptation.

papers.abstract: A representation that accurately predicts a deformable object's response is not necessarily the one most useful for choosing manipulation actions. We study this distinction between predictive utility and decision utility in planar single-grasp shape control of Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs). As a common decision backbone, we introduce Geometry-Pointer-Flow (GPF), a geometry-grounded policy that separates grasp-location selection from grasp-conditioned motion generation. Its geometry-only variant reduces one-step executed shape error by 32.8% relative to a DLO-specific diffusion policy, while using 18.7 times fewer parameters and achieving approximately 193 times faster inference. On this backbone, we compare physical context represented by ground-truth parameters, estimated parameters, and learned interaction-history representations, for both forward prediction and executed control. For prediction, ground-truth physical parameters reduce next-shape error by 15.8% over geometry alone, and estimated parameters are slightly more predictive than interaction history. This ordering does not carry over to control: estimated parameters provide no detectable one-step control gain, whereas history-conditioned GPF reduces executed error by 9.9% relative to geometry-only GPF across 470 paired simulation trials. In closed loop, interaction history improves strict-threshold attainment in simulation and yields the strongest zero-shot performance on hardware. All policies are trained exclusively in simulation and transferred to the physical robot without real-world training or fine-tuning. These results show that physical context should be evaluated by the decisions it supports rather than by predictive accuracy alone. Code will be released upon acceptance.

papers.abstract: Biological neural circuits are both modular and recurrent, with dense communities sparsely linked to one another. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) for reinforcement learning are usually feed-forward, and it is unclear how to obtain functional modules in a recurrent SNN or what they buy. In this work, we introduce a class of spiking networks, called Community Recurrent SNNs (CoRe SNNs): recurrent networks partitioned into communities with fixed roles. A controller community receives the stimulus, each action has its own community, and latent communities carry internal state. Spiking activity is then a walk between communities, and the action is the community the walk reaches. All learning is local and three-factor, and the recurrent communities are closer to cortical microcircuits than a feed-forward actor. We compare three regimes for obtaining the communities: dynamic modularity, in which a new learning rule we introduce, Map-STDP, encourages modular structure during learning; partial modularity, in which a stochastic block model (SBM) initialization enforces it partly; and full modularity, in which sealing enforces it fully. On CartPole, across three spiking neuron models, Map-STDP improves learning over the same network without it matches full modularity (sealed communities) on two of the three models, and makes the observed spike walk more compressible. Replacing the feed-forward actor of a TD-STDP actor-critic with recurrent action communities improves on the feed-forward network on CartPole and LunarLander, and matches it on Acrobot. How strongly to enforce modularity depends on the task: full modularity helps most on Acrobot, while on LunarLander the dynamic, partial and full regimes perform alike. Overall, these recurrent modular networks can match or even improve upon feed-forward approaches, with improvements in bio-plausibility and energy efficiency.
authors: Vikram Ramavarapu, Himanshu Udupi, Ashish Gautam
bullets: Addresses how functional modularity can emerge in recurrent spiking networks for reinforcement learning.
Introduces CoRe SNNs with controller, action-specific, and latent-state communities; actions are selected by the community reached by a spike walk.
Proposes Map-STDP, a local three-factor rule that encourages modular structure during learning, alongside partial and full modularity regimes.

On CartPole, Map-STDP improves learning over unstructured networks and can match sealed modularity; recurrent action communities improve or match feed-forward actors across CartPole, LunarLander, and Acrobot.
The best modularity strength is task-dependent: full modularity helps most on Acrobot, while regimes perform similarly on LunarLander.

papers.abstract: World-Action Models improve robot control by predicting future visual dynamics, but iterative video denoising incurs substantial inference overhead. Recent approaches reduce this cost through partial future denoising, yet typically rely on fixed refinement budgets. Our empirical observations reveal that preferred refinement depths vary across tasks and states, while different future regions exhibit varying relevance to action generation. Motivated by these findings, we propose Elastic-WAM, which adaptively allocates world refinement computation across temporal denoising time and spatial future space. A unified spatiotemporal refinement demand field governs when to stop world refinement, how far to advance each denoising step, and which regions to refresh. We parameterize this field with a shared temporal basis and spatial amplitudes, and learn it through a three-stage action-grounded supervised procedure. At inference, the learned field guides recurrent sparse world refinement to improve task success while reducing inference overhead. Evaluations across diverse simulation benchmarks and real-world long-horizon manipulation demonstrate state-of-the-art control performance with reduced inference latency.
authors: Haitian Li, Tianfu Li, Xuxi Zhao, Zizheng Liu, Yangcheng Yu, Yiwen Hou, Zeyu Xiao, Mutian Xu, Ziqian Yang, Haonan Chen, Lin Shao

papers.abstract: Recent work shows that multimodal agents increasingly self-improve without recurring human annotation. However, each self-improvement mechanism is designed and evaluated within a single scenario, leaving its preconditions unverified under cross-scenario transfer. This survey investigates the structural source of asymmetric mechanism transfer across four scenarios: multimodal reasoning, multimodal generation, GUI and Web navigation, and embodied manipulation. We first formalize the self-evolving multimodal agent by four criteria and a differentia of self-reference, and adopt the three-stage self-evolving loop of experience generation, feedback acquisition, and update consolidation as our analytical framework to position the scenarios along ceilings on rollout count and feedback fidelity. Comparing self-evolving with fixed loops within each scenario separates the limitations that the scenario imposes from those inherent in the self-evolving design. We then recast each mechanism as a trade-off that raises a scarce factor by presupposing a task-structural resource, such as output equivalence or checkable outcomes, and judge it portable, conditional, blocked, or redundant across scenarios. We attribute the asymmetry to divergent combinations of scarce factors and resources across opposite transfer directions, and identify the matched-budget measurements that could overturn these still untested verdicts.
