(2) On-Policy Rollout & Distillation: The student generates continuations from prefix prompts and receives dense teacher guidance through a student-weighted Top-16 log-ratio reward at each rollout step. (c) Performance Dynamics: OPMD completely eliminates NTP policy collapse and achieves substantial, stable reasoning gains across benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models are pretrained on satellite and aerial imagery, but whether such an encoder beats a strong generic one for few-label land-use/land-cover mapping remains unclear, as prior comparisons rarely isolate the pretraining data. We study five matched pairs of Earth-observation (EO) and generic encoders sharing objective and architecture (DINO/SatDINO, DINOv3/DINOv3-SAT, MAE/SatMAE, MAE/Scale-MAE, CLIP/RemoteCLIP) within a benchmark of 14 frozen encoders on five RGB scene-classification datasets (0.06-30 m GSD). With native preprocessing, we evaluate k-NN, linear and attentive probes and image retrieval over six low-label splits, using paired per-image significance tests. EO pretraining is not uniformly helpful: on most datasets and metrics, it significantly improves three pairs (SatDINO, Scale-MAE, RemoteCLIP, the latter evaluated only on unseen datasets) and significantly hurts two (linear probe: DINOv3-SAT by up to 22.5 points, SatMAE by up to 8.8), with opposite outcomes even for two MAEs pretrained on the same fMoW-RGB imagery. These effects are robust to patch-token pooling and attentive probing, concentrate on small man-made objects, and are largest with 1-5% labels. Across encoders, the silhouette score of frozen embeddings predicts k-NN accuracy and retrieval mAP almost perfectly (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.96$ on four of five datasets). Pretraining on satellite imagery is thus not a reliable selection criterion; candidate checkpoints must be validated on target data.
authors: Sandarbh Agrawal, Rakshith Sathish, Ashwathi Nambiar

papers.abstract: Typed-decision encoders answer a question about a text in one forward pass, but their behaviour outside English is rarely measured on a fixed yardstick. We release PolyRoute: 322 native-language support messages in 12 languages and 9 writing systems, 156 code-mixed or romanised messages (Hinglish, Spanglish, Arabizi), 967 optional native training rows, and a protocol for a three-way department-routing decision. Labels come from Qwen3.8-27B with a blind second pass (91% of candidates kept); an independent model, gemma4-31b, agrees on 97.2% of test items, and the largest character 5-gram similarity between any test text and any training text is 0.33. A leaderboard of 13 systems gives 61.2% for the English-root checkpoint, 77.3% for the shipped multilingual one and 96.6% for the best fine-tune; TF-IDF with logistic regression reaches 91.9%. On four withheld languages the three multilingual systems score 77%, 90% and 93%. On code-mixed text the English root (85%) is nominally ahead of the shipped multilingual checkpoint (79%; p=0.134). The split resolves differences only above about 4 points. All texts and labels are LLM-generated.

papers.abstract: Music editing transforms existing recordings while preserving their original attributes. Recent approaches adapt pretrained text-to-music models for tasks like inpainting, event insertion, or restoration by conditioning them with context audio. It was recently proposed for image editing to unify generation and editing by treating the source image as in-context information. However, applying this directly to music is computationally expensive due to long audio sequences. In this work, we develop MusicFlux, a text-guided music editor built on an efficient pretrained flow-matching text-to-audio model. We introduce two conditioning approaches that trade off editing performance and computational efficiency. Experiments show that both are competitive with strong baselines, with one achieving better editing quality and the other preserving the original sequence length and substantially improving computational efficiency.
authors: Teysir Baoueb (IP Paris, LTCI, IDS, S2A), Leonardo Boulitreau de Menezes Martins Marques (IP Paris, LTCI, IDS, S2A), Paraskevas Stamatiadis (S2A, LTCI, IDS), Ga{\"e}l Richard (S2A, IDS, IP Paris, LTCI)

(Right) MusicFlux-CAR: Condition-Aware Reparameterization uses lightweight auxiliary networks (µsrc, µtgt) to shift the noise start-point z0 and target endpoint z1. Diffusion operates directly in the shifted space over L frames, reducing complexity.

Fig. 1. MusicFlux formulates text-to-music generation, music inpainting, and SFX restoration under a shared latent conditioning paradigm (the source latent s represents the input audio to be transformed). The source-target latent fusion module combines (s,m, xt) to construct the latent trajectory zt used as an input to the DiT.

papers.title: MusicFlux: Flexible Conditioning for Text-Guided Music Generation and Editing

papers.abstract: Human gameplay supplies paired observations, actions, and visual consequences that can supplement robot-policy training. We study event-and-foresight pretraining for InternVLA-A1.5, combining recorded keyboard/mouse event prediction with history-conditioned visual supervision through a frozen video model. Coverage-preserving anchor selection constructs one-second targets, and an attention mask prevents teacher-forced future actions from entering foresight queries. The selected corpus contains 394 recordings across 20 games, with 223.36 hours of recorded timestamp span and 2,072,084 training anchors. After 12,400 game-pretraining updates, we compare the resulting initialization with the public base under the same suite-specific robot fine-tuning protocol. Across four LIBERO suites, aggregate success increases from 1,718/2,000 (85.90%) to 1,811/2,000 (90.55%), a gain of 4.65 percentage points. Suite gains are 9.2, 6.8, 0.2, and 2.4 points on Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long. The 40-task breakdown shows 24 improvements, 10 declines, and six ties. These results support the practical value of the complete game-pretraining stage in this evaluated setting, while revealing heterogeneous task outcomes. The comparison includes additional optimization and does not isolate the effects of game data, the two objectives, or training variability.
authors: Lianlei Shan, Han Jin, Yaunchao Ma, Xinpeng Chen, Linhao Zhou, Xin Bin

papers.abstract: This work presents the 2nd-place solution (Team IF1001) to the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge, which evaluates mobile manipulation across 100 household tasks. Our method is built on a powerful world action model (WAM), Cosmos 3. We improve Cosmos 3 by using richer visual history, task-progress conditioning, and task-group and skill-specific LoRA adapters. During inference, we apply a separate progress estimator to supply task-progress context, and use task- and progress-conditioned routing to select a task-group or skill-specific policy, complemented by action-candidate aggregation, rolling inpainting, and task-specific temporal and gripper control. To meet the minimum inference requirement of 1 FPS, we use neither recursive self-improvement (RSI) nor agentic harness methods and rely on no closed-source models; during official private-test evaluation, our system handled concurrent requests across 100 evaluation ports with limited hardware resources, sustaining an average end-to-end inference rate above 2 FPS per port. Our method achieves a mean Q-score of 0.613 and a full-task success rate of 40.9%, averaged over 3 self-evaluation rounds across all 100 tasks. On the official private test set, with 20 instances per task, our system achieves a mean Q-score of 0.615 and a full-task success rate of 41.2%.
authors: Yelin He, Jiaquan Ye, Xinming Wei, Wenjie Xiao, Gengming Zhang, Guoting Wei, Xianbiao Qi, Rong Xiao

papers.abstract: Real-robot benchmarks of learned visuomotor policies often record room illuminance as the lighting condition. We show that, on a typical low-cost rig, room light and image light can be almost unrelated. Four imitation-learning policies (ACT, SmolVLA, Diffusion Policy and pi0.5) were trained on the same 50 demonstrations of a pick-and-place task on an SO-101 arm. Each was run for ten rollouts at about 520 lux and again at about 45 lux, an 11.5x reduction. Success was 20/40 in normal light and 19/40 in low light: a change of -2.5 percentage points (95% CI -23 to +19), with no evidence that the policies differed in sensitivity (interaction p = 0.86). The recorded video shows why: mean image brightness was only 3% lower in low light on the front camera and 19% lower on the wrist camera. Both cameras were set to automatic exposure and white balance, which most likely absorbed the difference; exposure was not locked in this experiment. An accidental repeat of one 10-rollout block reproduced its success count (7/10) but matched the first block at only 6 of 10 placements, consistent with chance. We conclude that lux alone does not describe what a policy sees. Camera settings, and image statistics compared with the training recordings, are the quantities to report and control. Data and code are public.
authors: Simon Cowling

papers.abstract: Internet photos of a scene differ in exposure, illumination and transient objects such as passers-by, so one set of Gaussian colours cannot explain all photos (the in-the-wild setting). Recent in-the-wild Gaussian Splatting methods mostly report hours of per-scene optimization. We present FastWild-GS, which describes each photo by a 128-dimensional Photo Appearance Token and a per-channel transform, a scale and an offset applied to the rendered image (six parameters); a small MLP predicts the colour of each Gaussian from this token and a per-Gaussian feature, replacing the spherical-harmonics colour. The same transform is applied to the renders that score Gaussians for densification and pruning, so appearance differences between photos are not counted as reconstruction error. On PhotoTourism, FastWild-GS trains in 8.8 minutes per scene with the lowest LPIPS among the compared methods, 23x faster than AsymGS, the next best in LPIPS. On NeRF-OSR, it has the best average PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS among the compared methods in 9.7 minutes per scene.
authors: Donghun Ryu, Seokhyun Kim, Minhyeok Lee

(2) Colour-matched densification: Gaussians are grown and pruned from the error of renders of 10 training views that use the stored SfM colour and the same per-image transform (sj , bj); the PAT is not used there. papers.abstract: Multimodal remote sensing pretraining commonly relies on exact instance-level correspondence across modalities, implicitly treating strictly paired observations as a prerequisite for learning transferable representations. In this work, we revisit this assumption by relaxing cross-modal correspondence from the instance level to the semantic level. We introduce Semantic Pairing (SemPair), a pairing-relaxed pretraining strategy that replaces exact instance pairs with class-consistent cross-instance pairs. To characterize the effect of correspondence relaxation, we formulate a latent-factor model that separates cross-modal dependence into shared semantic structure and instance-specific correlation, showing that SemPair preserves the former while marginalizing instance-specific cross-modal correlations in expectation. We further introduce Mixed Pairing (MixPair) as a controlled interpolation between semantic and exact pairing to study correspondence granularity along a continuous spectrum. Extensive experiments consistently show that SemPair achieves transfer performance comparable to exact pairing (ExaPair), while MixPair reveals a non-monotonic relationship between downstream transfer and the instance-pairing ratio. These results demonstrate that exact instance correspondence is not a prerequisite for effective multimodal remote sensing pretraining and establish cross-modal correspondence granularity as an important design dimension for transferable multimodal representation learning. More broadly, this finding suggests a practical route toward scaling multimodal pretraining with reduced dependence on costly instance-aligned data.
authors: Xianping Ma, Yu Zhang, Mingzhe Jiang, Wanxin Xie, Qing Zhu, Nan Xu, Xiaokang Zhang, Yuanxin Ye
bullets: Reframes cross-modal pairing from exact instance alignment to class-consistent semantic alignment.
Uses a latent-factor analysis to show semantic structure is preserved while instance-specific correlations are averaged out.
Introduces MixPair to continuously control the degree of exact versus semantic pairing.
Experiments find SemPair performs comparably to exact pairing, while transfer varies non-monotonically with the exact-pair ratio.
Suggests reducing reliance on costly instance-aligned multimodal data for scalable pretraining.

Different instances from the same semantic class can still share common semantic structure despite variations in appearance and geometry. This motivates SemPair, which preserves semantic consistency while relaxing exact instance identity.

papers.title: Relaxing Cross-Modal Correspondence for Multimodal Remote Sensing Pretraining
papers.tldr: SemPair shows that multimodal remote sensing pretraining can learn transferable representations from semantically matched, non-identical cross-modal pairs rather than requiring exact instance correspondence.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems increasingly rely on generating multiple trajectory candidates and selecting one for execution. In this setting, a central challenge is no longer only candidate generation, but how to evaluate candidates according to their long-horizon consequences under uncertainty. Existing methods still mainly use deterministic point scores, heuristic subscores, or single-outcome evaluations, which makes it difficult to capture delayed failures, tail risk, and ranking instability under plausible future perturbations. We present RiSE-Drive, a framework for risk-sensitive long-horizon candidate evaluation in end-to-end autonomous driving. RiSE-Drive first performs candidate-conditioned latent future rollout, then estimates long-horizon outcome distributions instead of single scalar scores, and finally ranks candidates using a tail-risk-aware and perturbation-robust decision criterion. This reformulates candidate scoring from deterministic oracle-style evaluation into distributional outcome assessment with explicit risk control. As a result, the evaluator is encouraged to prefer candidates that are not only strong under nominal conditions, but also reliable under long-horizon rollout and safety-critical deviations. Experiments on the NAVSIM-v1 and NAVSIM-v2 benchmarks, as well as the closed-loop HUGSIM benchmark, show that RiSE-Drive achieves state-of-the-art performance and significantly improves the robustness of candidate selection.
authors: Yu Zhao, Hongyi Duan, Ming Yin, Hongyuan Zhang, Fan Yang, Hongzhi Wang, Xiubo Liang

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the RiSE-Drive pipeline. Multi-view observations are encoded, and the proposal generator produces 𝐾 ego-trajectory candidates. A future-condition generator predicts 𝐿 branch-specific condition codes that parameterize plausible downstream evolutions. For each candidate–condition pair, RiSE-Drive initializes a latent consequence state, propagates it along the trajectory, and decodes one branch-level long-horizon outcome sample. The resulting branchwise consequence traces are pooled over time and across branches and mapped to ordered outcome quantiles by a distribution head. The final ranking score combines the mean estimate, lower-tail CVaR, and cross-condition instability, thereby favoring candidates that remain reliable under plausible future deviations rather than merely optimal under a single nominal forecast.

Figure 3: Qualitative results of RiSE-Drive on representative NavSafe safety-critical scenarios. From left to right, columns (a)–(d) correspond to UNPL (unprotected left turn), EXR (exit ramp), YLD (yielding), and RDBT (roundabout). Each column shows two temporal snapshots of one representative case. Magenta denotes the RiSE-Drive plan, green the human future trajectory, orange dashed the ego history, and blue the future trajectories of surrounding vehicles. Across all four cases, RiSE-Drive produces smooth, route-consistent, and interaction-aware behaviors while remaining close to safe human driving in conflict-prone regions.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce Predicate-State Video Reasoning Segmentation (PS-VRS), where a query defines a dynamic predicate $P(o,t)$ over objects and time rather than a fixed object identity. Existing methods typically treat the target as permanently active once identified, leading to over-emission of masks during vacant intervals and failure to handle target switching. To address this, we construct PS-Bench, a large-scale benchmark with 2,077 videos and 16,250 queries annotated with explicit active/vacant predicate states, temporal intervals, and pixel masks. We further propose Predicate-State Grounding (PSG), a State-Bind-Emit pipeline that: (1) predicts [ACTIVE]/[VACANT] state tokens; (2) aligns them to video frames via dense cross-modal similarity; and (3) emits masks via SAM2 only for active states. Experiments show that PSG outperforms existing baselines by +9.32 J&F on PS-Bench and significantly reduces false-positive mask emissions. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of explicit predicate-state modeling for video reasoning segmentation with dynamic visual witnesses.
authors: Yuhuan Hong, Yiming Ren, Zhiqiang Lin, Feize Wu, Xingyun Liu, Yitong Xie, Lei Zhou, Lisheng Wu, Junjie Wang, Yujiu Yang

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the Predicate-State Grounding (PSG) Segmentation architecture. PSG decouples semantic validity from mask generation via a strict State-Bind-Emit pipeline. (1) State: A Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) infers the dynamic predicate states by generating discrete structural reasoning tokens ([ACTIVE], [VACANT], and [SEG]). (2) Bind: The Span-Frame Projecting module performs dense cross-modal alignment, binding these abstract state tokens to continuous video frames to establish frame-level temporal boundaries. (3) Emit: The [SEG] token acts as a semantic prompt for SAM to decode masks exclusively during active spans. Mask decoding is bypassed during predicted vacant intervals, substantially reducing invalid mask emission.

Figure 4: Explicit baseline prompt. System prompt used to adapt generalist MLLMs to predicate-state temporal segmentation with explicit active/vacant states, target-set transitions, and bounding-box localization.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on dynamic predicate-state transitions. For the query about the cleaning implement currently being used, the valid visual witness changes over time and is absent in the initial frames. PSG suppresses mask emission during the vacant state and rebinds the active state to the query-valid witness when the used implement changes. In contrast, existing baselines often segment visually plausible but query-invalid objects, or continue emitting masks across invalid states.

Figure 1: Task formulation comparison. Referring Video Object Segmentation segments explicitly referred targets, while Video Reasoning Segmentation introduces implicit reasoning queries but typically lacks explicit target switching and temporal predicate-state boundaries. PS-VRS treats the query as a predicate over objects and time, requiring reasoning, target switching, active/vacant temporal grounding, and pixel-level masks for active segments.

Figure 6: Qualitative cross-platform comparison of bounding-box annotations generated by Qwen3-VL8B-Instruct. Each row corresponds to the same query and candidate key frame, with the NVIDIA prediction shown on the left in red and the Ascend prediction shown on the right in cyan. Pairwise IoU is reported in the upper-left corner. The examples include both consistent and inconsistent predictions across the two deployment stacks.

papers.abstract: Learning representations from multimodal observations is difficult in reinforcement learning with limited interaction data. Multimodal Joint Predictive Representation combines multimodal latent prediction with contrastive learning across modalities, but its recursive rollout depends on earlier predictions and its pairwise alignment focuses on correspondence between modalities. We propose Improved Predictive Representation, which combines prediction from action prefixes with alignment at the observed anchor based on Contrastive Multimodal learning. At each horizon, it predicts future representations directly from the observed anchor and the corresponding sequence of actions. We evaluate two crop configurations: IPR-S with a minimum retained crop area of 10%, and IPR-H with 50%. Across five DeepMind Control Suite tasks, IPR-H achieves an average return across tasks that is 10.0% higher than the baseline with visual and depth images and 3.4% higher with visual images and position vectors. The relative performance of the two configurations varies across tasks. In Webots, both IPR configurations achieve higher mean final returns than the baseline without LiDAR, but not when LiDAR is available.
authors: Sijie Xu, Francisco Cruz
bullets: Addresses recursive prediction errors and limited pairwise modality alignment in multimodal representation learning.
Predicts future representations directly from the observed anchor using action sequences, while aligning modalities at that anchor.
Evaluates two crop configurations: IPR-S (10% minimum retained area) and IPR-H (50%).
Across five DeepMind Control Suite tasks, IPR-H improves average return by 10.0% with visual/depth inputs and 3.4% with visual/position inputs.
In Webots, both variants outperform the baseline without LiDAR, but not when LiDAR is available; performance varies by task and crop configuration.

papers.abstract: Remote sensing disaster assessment is moving from simple damage classification toward comprehensive report-level analysis. In this setting, responders need not only damage descriptions but also verifiable evidence to guide response and recovery. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) and tool-augmented agents offer strong multimodal reasoning and perception, but they struggle to provide the evidence required for high-stakes verification. To address these limitations, we propose DisasterAgent, an evidence-driven agent that uses a Perception-Augmentation-Generation workflow to generate verifiable disaster reports from bitemporal optical imagery. DisasterAgent first invokes a specialized vision expert toolkit in the perception phase to build a Spatiotemporal Perception Graph (STPG), serving as a structured memory to store and organize disaster-induced changes across space and time. Evidence-based Augmentation (EA) then extracts evidence from the STPG, attaching inline citations that form a closed evidence loop from each statement to the supporting visual evidence. Extensive experiments on the DisasterM3 and RSCC benchmarks demonstrate that DisasterAgent consistently outperforms general-domain VLMs, remote sensing-specialized models, and existing remote sensing agents. Notably, compared with the original model, it improves the average score for disaster report generation on DisasterM3 by 13.5\% and ST5-SCS on RSCC by 15.34\%, providing a more accurate and verifiable solution for disaster emergency response. The code will be available at https://github.com/ZhijianLi2003/DisasterAgent.
authors: Zhijian Li, Jiawei Song, Chao Ren, Yidan Zhang, Peijin Wang, Xian Sun, Kun Fu
bullets: Addresses the lack of verifiable evidence in report-level disaster assessment using vision-language models and agents.
Uses a Perception-Augmentation-Generation workflow over bitemporal optical imagery.
Builds a Spatiotemporal Perception Graph to organize disaster-related changes across space and time.
Extracts graph evidence and attaches inline citations, creating a link from each report statement to supporting imagery.
Outperforms compared baselines on DisasterM3 and RSCC, with reported gains of 13.5% and 15.34% on the respective metrics.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. The overall architecture of DisasterAgent. The framework processes multimodal inputs through two primary stages. (1) Skill Routing: Driven by the VLM’s interpretation of the query, the system dynamically routes to appropriate skills within a pre-defined repository and seamlessly registers the required functional tools. (2) Skill-Guided Workflow: Guided by the registered skills, the framework sequentially executes a three-step pipeline comprising Perception, Evidence-based Augmentation, and Generation.

Fig. 4. Illustration of the SCE extraction pipeline. The VLM first reasons over the STPG to generate atomic factual claims. Each claim is then independently verified against the raw bitemporal images to obtain a confidence score. Finally, claims with scores above the threshold are filtered to form the robust SCE set.

papers.abstract: 3D reflection removal is crucial in applications demanding high-fidelity visualization, such as museum exhibitions. In this work, we propose Reflection-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting (RF3DGS), a novel method for superior reflection removal. RF3DGS exclusively leverages a widely-adopted photometric prior for reflection removal: that the minimum pixel intensity across multi-view images corresponding to the same 3D point strongly correlates with reflection-free information. However, generalizing this principle to a 3D Gaussian Splatting within a multi-view context is non-trivial. To address this, RF3DGS first optimizes a vanilla 3DGS model using a geometric prior to estimate a coarse, reflection-free depth map for each view. Leveraging these depth maps and photometric prior, a 3D warping process aggregates reflection-free information from auxiliary views to construct a clean transmission pseudo-label for a given reference view. This pseudo-label provides a robust self-supervised signal for optimization. We further introduce an Adaptive Twin Rendering (ATR) loss to synergistically utilize this pseudo-label while preserving high-frequency details from the original, reflection-degraded images. By adeptly fusing these internal 3D self-priors with the ATR loss, RF3DGS demonstrates state-of-the-art reflection removal performance across both synthetic and real-world scenarios. Furthermore, we establish the first 3D reflection removal benchmark, based on the Unity rendering engine, for rigorous quantitative evaluation.
authors: Qiang Wen (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology), Guotao Meng (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology), Junhong Ruan (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology), Hongyu Liu (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology), Chenyang Lei (Huawei Research), Qifeng Chen (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology)

Subsequently, for re-rendering each specific view, a minimum value-based photometric prior is applied to extract preliminary clean transmission information; 4) During Comprehensive Optimization, three 3DGS models are jointly optimized for producing transmission image T̂n, reflection image R̂n and reflectance factor β̂n, respectively.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth foundation models make it tempting to replace depth sensors on mobile robots with a single RGB camera. We show that, used off the shelf, this is unsafe: in a simulated indoor navigation benchmark, a standard Nav2 stack driven by Depth Anything V2 (metric) collides in 63\% of 120 episodes, because the model systematically over-estimates the distance to nearby obstacles. We propose a lightweight plug-in module that turns predicted depth into \emph{safe depth}. A 0.58\,M-parameter head on top of the \emph{frozen} depth model predicts, per pixel, a log-depth correction $\mu$ and an uncertainty $\sigma$, trained with a $\beta$-weighted Gaussian negative log-likelihood. The navigation stack consumes the one-sided bound $\hat d_{\text{safe}}=d\,e^{\mu-k\sigma}$, where $k$ is set by conformal calibration on a held-out world, and uncertainty also decides which pixels may be treated as floor. The correction halves the depth error (AbsRel $0.262\rightarrow0.134$) and reduces near-range over-estimation from 59.8\% to 12.0\%. In navigation, safe depth raises the success rate from 37\% to 70\% and lowers collisions from 63\% to 3\%, close to the 2\% of ground-truth depth. A constant safety margin calibrated to the same pixel coverage reaches only 30\% success because it freezes the robot; uncertainty-aware safety wins 52 of 56 discordant paired episodes against it. Gains hold on glass, texture-less walls and dark regions.
authors: Saeid Firouzi Daghigh, Saeed Ayat

papers.abstract: Weight-space programming allows language models to read a trained neural network's weights and edit them. This opens the door to ``training'' by reasoning rather than through gradient descent. Prior work has demonstrated its functionality and promise for game-playing networks and fixing specific failures in language models, even extending to diffusion models. In this work, we present its applicability to models trained on biosignal data, specifically EEG and ECG data. We show that frontier models are not only able to debug specific faults planted in biosignal-based models without being told what these faults are, but are even capable of writing all the weights of a network from scratch, given only the architecture, the task, and a minimal set of training subjects. In particular, in one set of experiments, a language model was able to match standard gradient-descent training using $6\times$ fewer training subjects, through reasoning alone and without any gradient descent step. Networks written by Claude Opus 5.5 also scored higher than classic hand-crafted EEG pipelines (alpha band power, and common spatial patterns with linear discriminant analysis) when built from the same 5 subjects. We also highlight some of the limitations, which include the inability of language models to improve already well-trained classification models, and their incapacity to reliably recognize, from the weights alone, the task a network was trained on. Overall, our results indicate that weight-space programming can be useful for small networks, such as those deployed on edge devices and wearables, but the concept still requires further investigation before it can be used in practice.
authors: Dara Varam, Taraneh Aminosharieh Najafi, David Atienza

papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations contain reusable manipulation knowledge, but transferring this knowledge across embodiments requires representations that bridge differences in control interfaces. Action reconstruction alone does not ensure that similar behaviors across robots share a representation. To address this gap, we introduce CIALLO, an action codec that aligns actions, visual changes, and observation-grounded language in a shared space of short-horizon behavioral intent. An embodiment-conditioned decoder maps this intent back to robot-specific actions, allowing a shared representation to support different control interfaces. After pretraining on eight embodiments, CIALLO adapts to a new robot from one recording of at most 10 seconds by updating only its embodiment embeddings. The calibrated codec then remains frozen while a policy learns to predict intent from observations and instructions. We instantiate this policy with Qwen3.5-4B to form Qwen-CIALLO, whose backbone requires no large-scale robot-action pretraining before policy finetuning. With 20 demonstrations per task, Qwen-CIALLO achieves 76.7\% average success across real SO-101 and single-arm Piper robots, compared with 70.0\% for fully finetuned $\pi_0$. In simulation, we additionally finetune the action decoder, achieving 97.3\% success on LIBERO and 52.7\% on RoboTwin 2.0. The LIBERO policy also achieves 80.8\% on LIBERO-Plus without further finetuning. Together, these results support a shared action codec as a transferable control interface that separates embodiment calibration from task learning.
authors: Choo Sin Wai, Dake Zhong, Jingye Zhang, Zhifang Liu, Siyao Xiao, Zirong Ding, Yuhong Zhang, Kangjie Chen, Dongbin Zhang, Guorui Song, Guocun Wang, Peng Jiao, Haoqian Wang

We align their outputs with contrastive losses and train a shared decoder to reconstruct the demonstrated actions from each intent, conditioned on the robot’s embodiment parameters. (B) To learn a policy, Qwen-CIALLO predicts intent from observations and instructions, using the frozen action encoder as a teacher and the demonstrated actions to supervise the decoder output. CS denotes cosine similarity loss. (C) To transfer the codec to a new robot, we first calibrate its essential vector and arm and axis embeddings while keeping the shared weights fixed, then train the policy with the calibrated codec frozen.

The decoded action is the softmax expectation over the bin centers.

papers.abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning enables language models to adapt using rewards derived from their own answers. However, majority voting can reinforce incorrect solutions even when correct alternatives are available. Our training audit shows that false positives (incorrect responses receiving positive rewards) dominate reward errors. We focus on a practical regime where ground-truth rewards are difficult to obtain at scale, while a limited labeled source set is available. We introduce TRUER, a framework that uses limited supervision to train a reward rectifier that distinguishes correctness from consensus. To achieve this goal, we train the rectifier with an emphasis on incorrect majorities and correct minorities, targeting cases where consensus and correctness disagree. After that, we freeze the rectifier and use it to correct rewards during subsequent test-time adaptation. By improving reward accuracy and thereby model performance, TRUER consistently outperforms naive TTRL in both metrics across all evaluated configurations.

papers.abstract: Video overlay removal recovers the scene beneath burned-in subtitles, karaoke lyrics, titles, credits, logos and watermarks. Generative video models now fill a known region convincingly, but in practice the region comes from a detector or a segmenter, and it is wrong in both directions: it misses strokes, halos, whole frames and whole objects, and it covers background between characters, around boxes and on genuine scene text. Erasers that treat the mask as a hole, regenerating inside and copying outside, inherit every one of these errors. We present HintErase, which treats localization as a hint, not a hole. The model sees the full, unmasked video together with a hint channel; during training the hint is corrupted the way real localizers fail, while supervision follows the true overlay. The result is a single model that removes overlay the hint missed, keeps background the hint wrongly covered, and is trained to keep genuine scene text even when the hint lands on it. For full-length releases, a streaming pipeline handles interlaced sources, shot cuts, missed and jittering hints, paste-back and audio, with memory independent of the length of the video. This report describes the approach, the pipeline that turns it into full-length deliveries, and qualitative results; video results, with input, hint and output side by side, are on the project page.
authors: Dongyang Zhang, Wei Zhang, Renjie Zou, Zhiwei Huang

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of HINTERASE. The unmasked video and a separate hint channel condition a video diffusion transformer. In training, the hint is a corrupted copy of the true overlay region G, while the loss is defined by G itself and by background the hint wrongly covers, so supervision never trusts the hint.

Figure 5: Ultra-HD delivery of old footage. Crops from three low-resolution karaoke videos, each shown as a pair: the input, enlarged to the same size, and the delivered video: lyrics and the channel logo are erased by HINTERASE at the source resolution, and the result is upscaled 4× by our in-house super-resolution model, designed to preserve the original colors and faces (#uhd).

Figure 6: Time slice through the lyrics band. Each image is one pixel column through the lyrics of the karaoke clip that opens the project page, with 18 seconds of frames running left to right. In the input, lyric lines appear as striped blocks that change color as the wipe passes; in the output, the streaks of the background run through them without vertical steps.

Figure 4: The same weights under five hints. Top: the hint (orange) on the input. Bottom: the output of HINTERASE, which reads the hint as evidence. A mask-as-hole eraser cannot change pixels outside the hint (Proposition 1), so it would leave the outlines just outside the character mask (a), the halo outside the eroded mask (b), the lower strokes of the last two characters (c), and all of the lyrics inside a detection box drawn as its outline (e); with a filled box (d) it would have to regenerate all the clean background inside the box. HINTERASE removes the lyrics under every hint.
Figure 2: Three ways to localize the same title card. (a) and (b) are too large and too small when read as a hole; (c) is coarser than both, yet sufficient when read as a hint. Red: text; blue: logo.

Table 1: From model to delivery. Each stage of the long-video pipeline, the problem it addresses on full-length releases, and how it is solved in general. Cost scales with the duration of the overlays, not with the length of the video.

papers.abstract: Existing sequential user modeling methods mainly focus on improving the backbone encoder or learning task-specific user representations for a single prediction objective. We instead study how to export the multi-layer user states of a frozen long-history backbone as compact, timestamp-addressable representations for downstream training backfill and serving. In this setting, the user state at a given timestamp summarizes the user's actions before that time, so downstream systems need only the state aligned to each target timestamp rather than the full hidden-state timeline. To this end, we present \texttt{SeqFold}, a compressed-state interface that combines learned multi-channel fusion, channel-specific temporal decay, and Lookup-Free Quantization (LFQ) to produce compact discrete codes from frozen backbone states. Task-specific decoders then map these shared codes into flexible embedding spaces for downstream models. To make timestamp-addressable export practical at scale, we further develop a fused streaming implementation that updates the fusion recurrence after every action while materializing states only at target timestamps. On large-scale proprietary datasets, SeqFold reduces per-state representation storage by $3{,}400\times$ while preserving most of the downstream ranking performance of the uncompressed model, showing that SeqFold is an effective interface for reusing long-history sequence backbones in downstream models.
authors: Mianwei Zhou, Duo Zhang, Henry Tsai, Yuqi Zheng, Jian Li, Juexin Lin, Sujay Khandagale, Vijay Rajaram, Dong Jiao, Tao Cheng
bullets: Targets efficient export and reuse of multi-layer backbone states for downstream training backfill and serving.
Combines learned multi-channel fusion, channel-specific temporal decay, and Lookup-Free Quantization (LFQ).
Uses task-specific decoders to map shared compressed codes into downstream embedding spaces.
A fused streaming implementation updates states per action but materializes them only at target timestamps.
On large-scale proprietary datasets, reduces per-state storage by 3,400× while preserving most ranking performance.

figures.caption: Figure 3: SeqFold compression training and downstream serving. A frozen multi-layer action sequence backbone first produces layer-wise history states, which SeqFold compresses into shared LFQ bit codes. During compression training, a training-only layer-wise learning path (bottom zoom-in; one representative layer shown) decodes the compressed states and applies crossattention to the current action states to supervise the compressor with the upstream prediction loss. During serving, each downstream application reuses the shared codes and learns its own task-specific LFQ decoder with a configurable output dimension for layer-wise cross-attention.

Figure 4: Fused streaming compression with sparse timestamp export. SeqFold updates the fusion recurrence after every action, but materializes compressed states only at requested timestamps. The right panel illustrates the grouped training special case, where evenly spaced checkpoints 𝜏1, 𝜏2, . . . are exported and queries between two consecutive checkpoints reuse the most recent exported state. More generally, the requested export set can be arbitrary, including backfill timestamps or the latest online serving timestamp.

Figure 1: SeqFold as a timestamp-addressable interface between a frozen action sequence backbone and downstream applications. Given a target timestamp, SeqFold returns timestamp-aligned compact codes that downstream tasks decode with task-specific decoders for downstream training backfill and serving.

papers.tldr: SeqFold compresses frozen long-history user-sequence states into timestamp-addressable discrete codes, greatly reducing storage while retaining most downstream ranking performance.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems provide a convenient framework for the massive deployment of agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs). It provides a sound framework where agents can interact with existing software to perform actions in an autonomous way. Agentic AI is the new term to denote these AI-based autonomous systems. In real multi-agent systems, agents need to deal with malicious agents some of which can exploit security vulnerabilities to do harm. A memory poisoning attack is an example of exploiting a vulnerability to modify agents knowledge and, thus, affect its behavior. In an agent, there are different types of memory systems (semantic, episodic, and short-term) which have their own characteristics and for which different memory poisoning attacks may be developed. In this paper we focus on semantic memory, we discuss its attack, and mitigation strategies. We introduce private knowledge retrieval and private inference. We propose a signature system in the knowledge base to prevent from undesired manipulation. This should avoid memory poisoning attacks by introducing security by design in the construction of the semantic memory. In our architecture, an agent contains a local Prolog-like inference system (i.e., using Horn clauses to represent knowledge) which accesses an external knowledge base to get the required knowledge. This externally signed knowledge base is accessed privately. We provide different implementations in Python using different privacy levels including k-anonymity and information-theoretical privacy (IT-PIR).
authors: Vicen\c{c} Torra, Maria Bras-Amor\'os

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Key-value pairs for the knowledge-base considering only Prolog-like inference systems and queries. Key values correspond to predicate names and arity.
Table 2. Execution time statistics for different knowledge base access mechanisms, five runs, each accessing the knowledge bases as first time (i.e., case Non-cached).

Table 3. Execution time statistics for different knowledge base access mechanisms corresponding to two runs with cache. That is, first execution of the queries uses external access, and the second never does (case Standard caching).
Table 4. Execution time statistics for different KB access mechanisms corresponding to five runs with no external access (i.e., baseline, case All cached).

Table 1. Costs on bits for private knowledge retrieval implemented using k-anonymity, b-buckets, two non-colluding databases (2-PIR), and 2d knowledge databases. 64 above represents the length in bits of integers (assuming long long int). Here, r is the number of bits associated to each index in the knowledge base, k the parameter associated to k-anonymity, b is the number of buckets and m = npa/b is the number of rows retrieved by b-buckets.

papers.selection_reason: Discusses memory poisoning attacks and mitigation strategies for multi-agent systems, focusing on semantic memory and secure knowledge retrieval for agents.
papers.title: On Private Knowledge Retrieval and Private Inference for secure multi-agent systems

papers.abstract: Reliable state feedback of excavator front-end mechanisms is essential for autonomous excavation, yet retrofitting existing machines with dedicated joint sensors, external cameras, or visual markers can increase deployment and maintenance burdens. This paper proposes a closed-loop autonomous excavation framework for continuous inference of excavator joint states using onboard visual observations and control-related temporal information. The framework encodes structural cues from the current cab-view image, models short-term motion trends from historical joystick commands, and introduces a rolling state buffer for the bucket joint to preserve temporal continuity under severe occlusion. Mechanical joint-range constraints are incorporated into the learning objective to suppress infeasible estimates. The current cab-view image and inferred states are supplied to an Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT)-based control policy for online action generation. Experiments in an AGX Dynamics for Unity simulation environment under diverse operating conditions evaluate joint-state inference and end-to-end task execution. Across 20 autonomous excavation trials, the framework achieved a 95% task-completion rate, with an average joint-state-inference-and-control latency of 10.11 ms per step. The bucket-joint inference achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.965 degrees. These results demonstrate a sensor-light and computationally efficient joint-state-inference approach that can support closed-loop autonomous excavation with reduced dependence on additional sensing infrastructure.
authors: Junwei Li, Jian Pan, Mengchi Cai, Shuai Zhao, Xizhuo Jiang, Zheng Wang, Qing Xu, Keqiang Li, Jianqiang Wang

The upper panel shows swing and bucket, whereas the lower panel shows boom and stick. Colored curves denote predictions; dark-gray curves with open-circle markers denote target angles.

The bucket and distal working-mechanism structures can be partially or fully obscured during digging and loading, reducing the reliability of singleframe joint-state inference.

papers.abstract: We present Walrus, a unified 8B speech-and-audio foundation model handling speech recognition (including code-switching and multi-talker speech), speech-to-text and speech-to-speech translation, text-to-speech, emotion recognition, audio captioning, and general audio understanding. Our main contribution is not a new architecture but a data-centric training recipe; we use a standard decoder-only backbone initialized from Gemma 4, so that gains can be traced to the data. For speech generation, Walrus predicts low-bitrate discrete speech tokens, and a lightweight token-to-waveform decoder converts them into high-fidelity audio. The recipe is a three-stage data curriculum that moves from broad multilingual data to multi-talker, code-switching, and domain-specific data. At each stage, task-aware and dataset-aware weighting balances tasks with very different token budgets and protects core skills from forgetting. Trained on over 600M samples covering more than 20 tasks and 100 languages, Walrus leads on most multilingual, multi-talker, and code-switching ASR, speech translation, and audio understanding benchmarks, outperforming both open speech language models of comparable size and dedicated task-specific models. On most benchmarks, it even matches or surpasses the $4\times$ larger Qwen3-Omni's performance. Results suggest that data engineering is a primary driver of quality in multi-task speech and audio modeling.
authors: Alkis Koudounas, Osamu Take, Hayato Futami, Quentin Jodelet, Emiru Tsunoo

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Walrus, our most capable SpeechLLM yet. Input speech is encoded by the USM encoder into continuous representations, which are passed to the decoder-only Gemma 4 backbone together with a natural-language task prompt. For recognition, translation, and understanding tasks, the backbone generates text. For TTS and S2ST, it generates discrete speech tokens at 25 Hz (325 bits per second), which a VQ decoder and a Vocos-based vocoder convert into a waveform. The vocoder is also conditioned on the source speech to transfer speaker identity and prosody.

Figure 3: Training data composition of Walrus. Recognition dominates the mix (45%), followed by translation (27%) and understanding (21%), while generation is deliberately kept small (7%). The detailed breakdown shows that standard ASR and instruction-following data anchor the recognition and understanding families. This distribution reflects our data-centric design: core recognition is heavily represented to protect it from forgetting, while token-heavy generative tasks are downweighted.

Figure 2: Walrus against the best previous system (among AF3, Gemma4, Qwen2.5-Omni7B, Phi4-MM) across recognition, translation, and understanding benchmarks. Scores are normalized so that higher is better (ASR and CS-ASR shown as word/character accuracy, translation as BLEU or ASR-BLEU, understanding as accuracy, captioning as CLAP-Sim×100). Both Walrus variants advance the frontier on most axes, and the Research variant extends it further, most notably on code-switching, internal entertainment ASR, and audio understanding.

papers.abstract: Answering spatial questions about multi-source scenes requires a model both to identify each sound and to locate it. Existing spatial audio-language models obtain spatial information from a dedicated encoder, which separates spatial and semantic processing into distinct feature spaces. We study whether a general-audio codec trained without spatial supervision can serve both purposes. A controlled layer-wise analysis shows that the frozen codec retains spatial information, with lateral cues carried by the difference between the two ear channels. This information, however, is not readily accessible: in dual-source scenes, a model trained on these features predicts left/right at chance and, on the remaining axes, assigns the detected direction to the queried and the non-queried source equally often. We attribute this failure to an audio--text information asymmetry, in which the audio contains both sources while the answer describes only the queried one. A controlled $2\times2$ experiment shows that either completing the scene description or exposing the inter-channel difference lifts left/right accuracy above chance, whereas binding directions to the queried source requires both. Building on these findings, AURA keeps the codec and the language model frozen and exceeds the strongest dedicated system on SpatialSoundQA by 10.31 points in dual-source direction accuracy, with about 40\% of its trainable parameters.
authors: Boyan Han, Xiaoyan Wang, Zhe Sun, Ziqi Wang, Yujun Cai, Hongli Cao, Yiwei Wang, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Liang An
bullets: A general-audio codec retains spatial information despite being trained without spatial supervision, with lateral cues encoded in the left–right channel difference.
Naively using these features fails in dual-source scenes because audio describes both sources while the answer refers to only the queried one.
A controlled 2×2 study finds that complete scene descriptions or exposing inter-channel differences improves left/right accuracy; both are needed for source-direction binding.

AURA freezes both the codec and language model, yet surpasses the strongest dedicated system on SpatialSoundQA by 10.31 points in dual-source direction accuracy with about 40% of its trainable parameters.

figures.caption: Figure 5: AURA architecture. (a) Existing dedicated spatial pathways and general-audio pathways are separate and rely on different feature spaces, so features cannot be shared for unified perception. (b) AURA provides a shared, frozen general-audio codec representation that unifies perception in a single audio feature space. (c) Details of the AURA pipeline: for each ear, RVQ layers L0–L2 and L3–L7 are summed into content-oriented (S) and acoustic-oriented (A) bands, and adding the band-wise interaural difference yields six slots. A shared projector maps these slots to audio tokens for the language model, which generates a scene description and, for relation questions, a geometric analysis before the final answer.

Figure 1: Spatial and general-audio understanding with AURA. Left: illustrative questions and responses covering general-audio understanding, source descriptions, and geometric relations. Source coordinates in responses are model outputs. Right: performance overview for AURA and the evaluated spatial baselines; AURA attains results comparable to dedicated state-of-the-art systems on spatial audio understanding and generalizes well to general-audio understanding. Matterport3D imagery is subject to the Matterport3D Terms of Use.
Figure 6: AURA training-target examples for scene supervision (top) and geometric supervision (bottom). The question is shown in gray; the remaining text is the model’s target.

Figure 3: Overall results of the 2 × 2 controlled experiment on the dual-source direction questions. The four-slot answer-only baseline (red) fails to exceed the majority baseline on left/right discrimination, whereas every other intervention clearly surpasses the baseline level. The best value for each metric is in bold and the second best is underlined; the majority baseline is not ranked. H1: scene supervision; H2: six-slot representation with interaural difference slots; AO: answer-only supervision. Each pie spans 100 points: the grey sector is the majority-baseline level, the blue sector the gain over it, and the number below the pie the metric value (%); for DER (∗) lower is better, so the pie shows 100 − DER.

Figure 4: Dual-source direction accuracy stratified by whether the non-queried source lies on the same side as the queried source along each axis. Except for the full intervention, the direction gains of every intervention are confined to the same-side stratum (open markers); only the full intervention effectively improves the opposite-side questions (filled markers), which require binding the semantic and acoustic attributes to the queried source, lifting them above the majority-baseline level. n is the number of questions per stratum. H1: scene supervision; H2: six-slot representation; AO: answer-only supervision.

Figure 2: Layer-wise similarity analysis of RVQ representations. Top: schematic illustration of acoustic variables on Matterport3D scene wc2JMjhGNzB. (a,d) Interaural similarity for simulated (fixed source and BRIR) and real (MRSSpeech) binaural audio; the RVQ vectors diverge markedly as the layer index increases. (b,c) Room variation: right-ear similarity when the same audio is rendered at another placement in the same building or with an impulse response from a different building; the similarity of the RVQ vectors still decreases clearly with depth. (e,f) Full versus early-reflection-only and direct-path-only impulse responses for the same placement, and the additional reduction from removing early reflections. These comparisons reveal increasing sensitivity to spatially relevant acoustic changes in deeper RVQ layers. Scene data under the Matterport3D Terms of Use.

Figure 7: Text-to-audio attention across layers. Attention concentrates on more specific frames with depth and, depending on the question, is finally directed to different slots. Columns show the first (layer 0), an intermediate (layer 15), and the final (layer 35) transformer layer after prefill. Attention is averaged over heads. In each panel, the wide map sums attention over the six slots at each audio frame and the narrow map sums it over frames for each slot; rows are text tokens. Each map is normalized to its own maximum.

Figure 8: Layer-wise similarity on reconstruction-only codecs. Left: DAC; right: EnCodec. Top: interaural similarity for simulated (fixed source and BRIR) and real (MRSSpeech) binaural audio; the RVQ vectors diverge markedly as the layer index increases. Bottom: room variation: right-ear similarity when the same audio is rendered at another placement in the same building or with an impulse response from a different building; the similarity of the RVQ vectors still decreases clearly with depth. These comparisons reveal that the increasing sensitivity to interaural and room changes in deeper RVQ layers is not specific to X-Codec.

Table 2: Main results: system-level comparison on SpatialSoundQA. AURA performs comparably to current dedicated spatial audio understanding systems on SpatialSoundQA and achieves the best results on single-source DER, dual-source DoA and DER, and the relative-direction relation questions. All spatial metrics are reported in percentage points. The first group lists references: the random predictor, the majority-class baseline, and the zero-shot general-purpose models. The best result in each column is in bold and the second best is underlined; reference rows are not ranked.

Table 3: General-audio accuracy (%). AURA generalizes well to general-audio understanding and outperforms the current spatial understanding systems. The two general-purpose models are zero-shot references trained with large-scale audio instruction data and are not ranked; among the spatial systems, the best result is in bold and the second best underlined.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language models by distilling teacher predictions on student-generated trajectories, while on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) removes the need for an external teacher by using a reference-conditioned copy of the model as the teacher. Despite its great early improvements, we find that OPSD does not remain consistently effective under continued training and can eventually suffer substantial performance degradation. We study this training behavior and link the degradation to a growing mismatch between the evolving reference-free student and the frozen privileged teacher. In the early stage of OPSD, the privileged teacher remains closely aligned with the student and provides useful guidance for improving the student's generation trajectories. However, as training progresses, the growing distributional mismatch between the privileged teacher and reference-free student can cause the teacher to provide misleading supervision, ultimately degrading student performance. This phenomenon motivates us to first leverage privileged reference supervision to acquire useful knowledge and then transfer it to a fresh student. We introduce Bootstrapped On-Policy Distillation (BOPD), a two-stage framework that first uses OPSD to internalize task-relevant information from reference-conditioned supervision into an intermediate model, and then distills this reference-free intermediate model into a fresh copy of the initial model. Experiments across models show that BOPD improves mathematical reasoning and code generation beyond both the initial models and the constructed OPSD teachers. These results suggest that privileged reference supervision can be more effectively exploited by first transferring its task-relevant signal into a task-adapted model and then distilling from that model without reference conditioning.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is bottlenecked by the token budget of large language models: feeding long documents into the context window is expensive, while aggressive textual compression discards fine-grained information that is irreversibly lost in a one-dimensional token sequence. We argue that this bottleneck is not fundamental to information density but to the choice of compression \emph{modality}. Modern visual encoders can pack the contents of a rendered text page into roughly a hundred visual tokens with little semantic loss, opening a new compression-fidelity tradeoff that purely textual methods cannot reach. We present \textbf{OpticalRAG}, a framework that renders documents as page images, encodes them with a frozen vision encoder, and distills the retrieved visual tokens into as few as $16$ injected tokens before passing them to the LLM. Two ingredients make this work without expensive cross-modal training: (i) \emph{Encoder-Bridged Retrieval}, which projects text-query states into the visual feature space of the frozen encoder, through a projection shared with the compressor, to retrieve visual tokens from a text query, with no contrastive training; and (ii) \emph{Query-Driven Distillation}, a lightweight cross-attention compressor that condenses the retrieved visual tokens into a small set of query-conditioned prefix tokens. On LongBench-v2, BAMBOO, and LooGLE-v2, OpticalRAG achieves the best compression-aware accuracy (CAP) on all three benchmarks while injecting only $16$ tokens, and improves the closed-book Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone by $5.17$ points on LongBench-v2.Code is available at https://github.com/brighterr/OpticalRAG.
authors: Senhao Liu, Yuheng Zhang, Chunyu Wei, Yueguo Chen, Xinran Zhang

papers.abstract: Reasoning about people's plans and goals based on their actions is fundamental to human social interaction and essential for cooperative, embodied artificial intelligence. Formalizing this capacity in naturalistic, embodied settings has been a longstanding challenge. Here, we present GenEA, a novel agent representation capable of reasoning over multi-step, long-horizon embodied plans. At the heart of GenEA lies a multilevel state-space that couples the coarse biomechanics of an articulated body and its interactions with nearby objects by extending the task-and-motion planning framework from robotics with simulation-based intuitive physics. By embedding this state-space in a generative model, GenEA yields a joint probability distribution over goals and embodied plans. Across several experiments spanning the qualitatively distinct domains of object manipulation and navigation, featuring diverse tasks and multiple behavioral measures, we show that GenEA, through simple transformations of this joint distribution, recapitulates how humans reason about embodied plans. Crucially, GenEA consistently outperforms strong alternative models, including plausible heuristics, standard task-and-motion planning, and a state-of-the-art vision-language model. GenEA thereby offers a new perspective on the architecture of human reasoning and social cognition, suggesting that embodied artificial intelligence systems seeking to seamlessly interact with humans should adopt GenEA-like generative models of action planning.
authors: Aalap D. Shah, Basil Saeed, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Tobias Gerstenberg, Hyowon Gweon, Ilker Yildirim

papers.abstract: The complex interactive dependencies between human behavior and 3D scenes make accurately predicting human intent a major challenge for human motion prediction (HMP). While recent studies use human gaze to infer intent, gaze signals suffer from ambiguity, drift, and a reliance on eye-tracking hardware. Research in cognitive science indicates that egocentric views inherently encode potential interactions, while head motion serves as a crucial precursor in motion planning. Motivated by this, we propose EgoHMP, a novel framework that uses egocentric views and head motions as robust carriers of interaction intent. By translating this intent into an envisioning of future interactions, EgoHMP achieves precise HMP in 3D scenes. EgoHMP first employs a vision-motion alignment encoder to align the visual and motion feature spaces. Based on these aligned features, an egocentric intent predictor with a modality-aware modulation mechanism adaptively suppresses invalid interaction cues to predict an accurate interaction probability map. Furthermore, to enhance the stability and realism of the generated motions, we propose a contact-aware motion decoder. Specifically, inspired by the human cognitive process of planning trajectories prior to action execution, we first predict a global trajectory to serve as a self-prompt, effectively mitigating the optimization conflict in diffusion models. Subsequently, we introduce a multi-stage denoiser, which relieves motion artifacts by incorporating human contact modeling through a multi-stage optimization strategy. Finally, a GCN-based motion decoder is employed to synthesize physically plausible and semantically consistent motions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EgoHMP achieves state-of-the-art performance.

Finally, guided by this probability map, a contact-aware motion decoder synthesizes the final human motion sequence (Sec. 3.4).

papers.abstract: Transformer feed-forward blocks combine several design choices: squared activations, gating, and tied versus untied parameter sharing, whose separate contributions to expressivity remain poorly understood. We introduce CP-MLPs, a tensor framework in which each multiplicative unit contributes a rank-1 interaction with three roles: detecting an input feature, reading a value, and writing to the output. Tied gated blocks such as ReLU$^2$ force the detector and value roles to share the same direction; untied gated blocks such as ReGLU and SwiGLU let them differ. We show that this distinction yields exact, degree-wise tensor-rank separations: untied detector-value units are strictly more width-efficient for indefinite quadratic interactions and role-asymmetric monomials, while tied units are structurally matched to symmetric pure-power targets. The width advantage of untying therefore depends on the target structure. Experiments show loss plateaus below the exact-representation width, but these plateaus alone do not establish a positive approximation gap: arbitrarily accurate approximation is governed by border rank. In trained gated MLPs, untied blocks retain an advantage in selected comparisons at matched input-projection budget. Code is available at https://github.com/rarefin/CP-MLPs.
authors: Md Rifat Arefin, Farzaneh Heidari, Irina Rish, Guillaume Rabusseau

papers.abstract: Privacy concerns have been raised in Large Language Models (LLM) inference when models are deployed in Cloud Service Providers (CSP). Homomorphic encryption (HE) offers a promising solution by enabling secure inference directly over encrypted inputs. However, the high computational overhead of HE remains a major bottleneck. To address this challenge, we propose MOAI, an efficient HE-based, non-interactive framework for secure transformer inference. MOAI gains significant efficiency improvement from: (1) a novel evaluation flow that combines column and diagonal packing with consistent strategies across all layers, eliminating expensive format conversions. (2) rotation-free algorithms for Softmax and LayerNorm that significantly reduce the number of costly HE rotations, removing 2,448 HE rotations in BERT-base inference. (3) Column packing removes rotations in plaintext-ciphertext matrix multiplications and interleaved batching further reduces the rotations in ciphertext-ciphertext matrix multiplications. MOAI uses at least 1.7x fewer HE rotations compared to the state-of-the-art works across all matrix multiplications of BERT-base. As a result, we achieve a $52.8 \%$ reduction in evaluation time compared to the state-of-the-art HE-based non-interactive secure transformer inference, THOR (Moon et al., CCS 25). We then apply MOAI on the Powerformer's framework and achieve a $55.7 \%$ reduction in evaluation time compared to Powerformer (Park et al., ACL 25), which approximates Softmax and LayerNorm with simpler functions in transformer and proposes HE-based non-interactive transformer inference. We report an amortized time of 2.36 minutes per input on a single GPU environment. We show the extendibility by applying MOAI in LLaMA-3-8B. Our implementation is publicly available as open source.

papers.abstract: Real-time disaster recognition from aerial imagery requires deep learning models that operate under strict memory, compute, and latency constraints. While recent approaches achieve high accuracy, their computational cost limits deployment on resource-constrained UAV platforms. This work introduces picoEmergencyNet, an ultra-lightweight convolutional neural network designed for aerial image disaster classification. The proposed architecture combines depthwise dilated convolutions with efficient channel attention and channel shuffling to enable multi-scale feature extraction at minimal computational cost. picoEmergencyNet has 23k parameters and 7M FLOPs, requiring only 0.1 MB of model storage. Evaluated on the AIDER and AIDERv2 disaster datasets, it achieves up to 96.1% accuracy, matching or exceeding state-of-the-art lightweight models that are orders of magnitude larger. Deployment experiments on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin show that, without hardware-specific optimizations, picoEmergencyNet achieves 258 FPS on GPU and 46 FPS on CPU with a 7x lower activation memory footprint compared to competing models. These results demonstrate that careful architectural specialization, rather than model scaling, enables highly efficient and accurate TinyML-ready disaster recognition for real-time UAV-based emergency monitoring.

papers.abstract: Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as an efficient representation for novel view synthesis, offering fast differentiable rendering and high visual fidelity, and has increasingly been extended to surface reconstruction. However, the relationship between depth information and reconstruction error remains insufficiently explored, limiting the principled design of geometric optimization strategies. To fill the above gap, we propose DepthGS, a depth-guided Gaussian splatting framework. We derive theoretical relations between depth discrepancies and reconstruction error under single-view and multi-view settings, and rigorously establish corresponding upper bounds on reconstruction error. The above analysis informs the design of adaptive regularization strategies in both single-view and multi-view optimization. More specifically, for single-view optimization, we propose a depth-difference-guided adaptive normal regularization strategy that modulates the normal constraint strength using a geometric reliability weight computed from local depth differences. For multi-view optimization, we introduce a cross-view depth consistency regularization strategy that promotes consistency between neighboring-view depth maps and the corresponding depth predictions obtained by transforming the current view's depth predictions into those neighboring views. Extensive experiments on DTU, Mip-NeRF360, and Tanks and Temples demonstrate that DepthGS achieves competitive performance in both surface reconstruction and novel view synthesis.
authors: Xiao Ren, Yu Liu, Ning An, Jian Cheng, Xin Qiao, You-Fu Li, He Kong

In the multi-view branch, coordinate transformations establish depth correspondences between neighboring views to construct the cross-view depth consistency constraint Lmv D . The proposed constraints are jointly optimized with the baseline objectives to improve surface reconstruction and multi-view geometric consistency.

papers.abstract: Generative video compression offers a promising solution for compressing and reconstructing videos under extremely low bitrate constraints, among which the diffusion-based solutions still achieve the best performance by providing the powerful generative latent prior. However, their effectiveness critically depends on when the compressed latent is introduced into the diffusion process, which directly governs the trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and perceptual realism. To address this limitation, we identify denoising start-timestep selection as a key factor governing this trade-off and formulate it as a geometric optimization problem. Based on this formulation, we propose a novel adaptive diffusion entry method for generative video compression (ADE-GVC), the first timestep-aware generative video compression framework, featuring a lightweight predictor that estimates an adaptive denoising start point from the compressed latent. A temporal adapter further extracts compression-aware conditions and injects them into a pretrained video diffusion model, enabling the reconstruction of videos with both high fidelity and realism. More importantly, we observe a strong quantitative relationship between the predicted timesteps and the distortion between the original and compressed latents, providing empirical support for our optimization formulation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ADE-GVC achieves the state-of-the-art performance on perceptual metrics and substantially improves reconstruction realism over existing generative video compression methods. Notably, our ADE-GVC achieves an average bitrate savings of 40.99\% (on DISTS) and 95.24\% (on PSNR) compared to the latest open-source baseline GLC-Video.
authors: Zifu Zhang, Yuqiao Li, Ding Ding, Shengxi Li, Mai Xu, Daowen Li, Kai Li, Ying Chen

figures.caption: Figure 3. The overall architecture of ADE-GVC consists of a latent compression network (LCN), temporal adaptor (TA), timestep predictor (TP), and video diffusion model. The input video Vg is encoded into the clean latent x1, which is compressed by the LCN into xc and a compression-aware feature ft. The TP predicts the denoising entry τ from xc, while the TA converts ft into the visual context cv . Conditioned on cv , the VideoDiT denoises xc τ , into x̂1, which is decoded to reconstruct V̂1.

The strong negative correlation indicates that τ varies inversely with ρe, indicating that more severely distorted videos require an earlier denoising start timestep.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents reuse execution experience to improve reliability on complex tool-based tasks. Systems such as Sentry call large models to generate failure diagnoses before retrieving advice, adding inference cost to experience reuse. We present Synapse-Control, an agent runtime whose lightweight control plane selects advice and determines when to send it to the task-executing model. Rules shortlist relevant advice, and a lightweight 1.7B classifier fine-tuned on teacher-labeled state-suggestion pairs scores those candidates instead of generating a diagnosis. Micro-contracts encode reusable interface checks, such as required arguments or valid options, without prescribing complete task programs. A Prompt Value Table records earlier guidance and feedback to limit repeated suggestions through cooldown and token-budget checks. Across 1,308 attempts per method in AppWorld and WebShop, Synapse-Control achieves 270 successes (29.8% more than Base), replaces 4,987 generative diagnosis calls, and reduces auxiliary control time relative to Sentry by 50.2% and 51.0%, respectively.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human video (EHV) records close-range hand-object interaction (HOI) and the temporal structure of everyday activities, offering a potentially scalable source of experience for robot manipulation. Using this experience for robot control requires recovering useful supervision without recorded robot actions and accounting for differences in morphology, viewpoint, and action space. We define Ego2Robot learning as the process of learning or adapting robot manipulation policies from EHV, organized into four learning paradigms: explicit embodiment transfer, explicit action and task supervision, egocentric video representation pretraining, and latent action and dynamics modeling. The four paradigms differ in what they derive from human video: robot-format demonstrations, interpretable supervision, visual representations, or predictive models of actions and dynamics. For each paradigm, we trace what EHV information is extracted, how robot policies use it, and when the additional data is required. Besides, we review the benchmark datasets that cover EHV, robot demonstrations, and synthetic and simulated resources. This paper links EHV data's contribution to the task information preserved and the robot-specific grounding used during training or deployment. Finally, we identify challenges in physical feasibility, agent coordination, in-context adaptation, controlled evaluation, and predictive control.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for multimodal and embodied tasks, yet aggregate accuracy or consistency alone does not reveal whether a judge changes its verdict for the right reason. We propose State-Conditional Invariance (SCI), a reliability principle requiring a judge to remain stable under semantics-preserving changes in presentation while responding to causal interventions that change the task outcome. We instantiate SCI in GridWM-Judge, a simulator-grounded diagnostic benchmark built from deterministic MiniGrid trajectories with aligned Full, evidence-removal, and counterfactual variants, plus presentation and representation probes. Across five diagnostic tasks, GridWM-Judge tests local perception, action-conditioned transitions, presentation stability, representation exchangeability, and Full-CF causal discrimination. Our diagnostic evaluations reveal heterogeneous failure modes, including sensitivity to evidence presentation and encoding, low activation on successful trajectories, and weak paired counterfactual discrimination. Perception-controlled analyses further indicate that visual grounding and objective recovery are substantial, model-dependent bottlenecks. These results motivate jointly reporting correctness, presentation stability, and causal sensitivity instead of relying on a single score.
authors: Qinan Zhang, Xinyu Wang, Qihang Jin, Tianyuan Wang, Hongbing Luo, Pengfei Li, Wenjun Lv, Yu Kang, Jian Di

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress on complex reasoning tasks, yet the mechanisms by which they acquire reasoning capabilities and the efficiency of their reasoning remain poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the path-finding problem over directed graphs, a symbolic abstraction of multi-step reasoning. We first characterize the architectural requirements for this task, proving that one-layer transformers require $\Omega(N^2)$ size on dense graphs to implement the key DFS child-selection primitive. While a two-layer transformer implements full DFS with $O(N\log(N))$ size. Thus, a second layer is necessary and sufficient for near-linear DFS reasoning. We then extend this expressivity analysis to deeper models: for every $k\geq3$, a $k$-layer transformer implements a bounded-reachability DFS policy with look-ahead horizon $1+2^{k-3}$, establishing an exponential increase in reachability horizon with depth. Finally, going beyond expressivity, given appropriately curated training data, we show that two-layer transformers can provably learn to execute DFS via gradient flow and generalize to unseen graphs. Together, our results provide a mechanistic account of how transformers implement graph search, how depth expands bounded look-ahead, and how such reasoning algorithms can emerge through training.
authors: Xutao Ma, Somayeh Sojoudi
