A k-layer transformer achieves a bounded-reachability DFS policy with look-ahead horizon 1 + 2^(k−3) for k ≥ 3.
Under appropriately curated training data, two-layer transformers can learn DFS through gradient flow and generalize to unseen graphs.
The analysis is theoretical and focuses on directed-graph path finding as a symbolic model of multi-step reasoning.

papers.abstract: Pretrained latent world models can support visual planning and control, but their predictions may fail when physical dynamics change at deployment. We study whether such models can adapt from only a few interactions without modifying their pretrained weights or identifying the changed physical parameters. We introduce a few-shot residual adaptation approach that learns self-supervised corrections from latent prediction errors. The corrections are applied both inside the latent predictor and directly to its predicted latent state, while the pretrained world model remains frozen. We evaluate the approach in simulation and on a real robot under center-of-mass and friction shifts. These changes reduce the success of the frozen model to near zero. Using three interaction episodes for adaptation, our dual-site approach recovers 90\% success under the center-of-mass shift and 100\% under the modified friction on the real robot. Ablations show that correcting both locations outperforms single-site adaptation. Our diagnostics further suggest that much of the learned correction reduces a general prediction mismatch, while successful control also depends on shift-specific information captured during adaptation.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across diverse applications, making both safety and utility essential for reliable deployment. Jailbreak attacks use diverse forms of adversarial prompting to bypass alignment safeguards and induce LLMs to generate harmful responses. Some representation-based defenses regulate internal activations using predefined steering directions or learned safety regions. However, adapting intervention to each input without a predefined representational target while limiting over-refusal remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose Target-free Entropy-guided Residual Modulation (TERM), an inference-time defense that uses prompt-calibrated attention entropy deviations to guide adaptive modulation of the model's own residual updates. Attention patterns vary across prompts and decoding steps, making raw entropy values difficult to interpret as a consistent signal for intervention. We therefore calibrate attention entropy against each prompt's own prefill baseline to establish an input-specific reference for reducing unnecessary intervention on benign requests. Adaptive scale normalization and temporal accumulation then account for differences in deviation scale and persistence to determine intervention strength. The resulting signal controls bounded scaling of the model's own residual updates, without relying on a predefined safety direction. We compare our method with seven defenses on seven jailbreak attacks and two over-refusal benchmarks across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models, including Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B. Results show our method improves jailbreak robustness while maintaining low over-refusal on benign safety-sensitive requests with modest inference overhead.
authors: Haoyi Wu, Yunkai Dang, Wanyu Zhang, Lei Wang, Wenbin Li

papers.abstract: As text-to-video (T2V) models are increasingly positioned as world simulators, it is essential to evaluate whether their videos conform to physical commonsense. However, existing benchmarks rely on annotators who rate each video with a single score based on intuition, yielding ratings that are subjective and do not tell which physical principle is violated. We introduce PhyRubric, a rubric-grounded diagnostic framework for evaluating physical commonsense in T2V generation. For each caption, PhyRubric constructs a caption-specific rubric before any video is seen, decomposing the caption into semantic and physical items, and derives scores from item-level verdicts grounded in timestamped evidence. We instantiate this framework as PhyRubric-Bench, which spans 34 categories across five physical domains, and scale it up to PhyRubric-Train with 3,788 videos, on which we fine-tune the open-source PhyRubric-Judge. Empirical results across ten T2V models show that physical commonsense remains far from solved, and that PhyRubric-Judge correlates more closely with human judgments than existing open-source judges while matching the frontier proprietary Gemini 4 Argon. Further analysis provides actionable insights for T2V models.
authors: Huiyi Chen, Weitai Kang, Shicheng Fan, Xinshuo Wang, Zhixiang Shen, Yan Yan, Philip S. Yu, Baoxin Li

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PhyRubric. Videos from 10 T2V models are pre-annotated by an agent and verified by humans. (3) Train & Judge: an agentic annotator labels training videos to build PhyRubricTrain, on which we train PhyRubric-Judge. Given a video and its caption, the judge outputs an SA score, whether PC is assessable, a PC score, and a diagnosis of the violated expectation with timestamped evidence.

papers.abstract: Edge NPU performance depends not only on hardware capabilities, but also on model transformation and the overall deployment pipeline. We propose a benchmarking methodology that separates these effects by comparing three configurations: Baseline, Vendor Guided NPU Only (VG-NPU), and Vendor Guided End-to-End (VG-E2E), where VG-NPU preserves common model I/O and host-side processing while VG-E2E follows the vendor-native deployment pipeline. We apply this methodology to four edge NPUs and three vision workloads. VG-NPU improves both accuracy and Runtime-call latency in 10 of 12 NPU--workload combinations, whereas VG-E2E reduces System-level latency in all combinations but improves accuracy in only four. Moreover, NPU-level performance rankings do not always match End-to-End rankings, and VG-E2E provides an additional 10.4--70.7\% reduction in System-level latency over VG-NPU. These results demonstrate the importance of evaluating vendor-guided optimization separately at the controlled model-transformation and full deployment levels when comparing heterogeneous commercial Edge NPU platforms in practice.
authors: Youngjin Jo, Jihwan Kim, Minseok Choi, Kwanghoon Choi, Jusung Kang, Jaein Kim
bullets: Evaluates Baseline, Vendor Guided NPU Only (VG-NPU), and Vendor Guided End-to-End (VG-E2E) configurations.
Tests four edge NPUs across three vision workloads while separating model-transformation effects from deployment-pipeline effects.
VG-NPU improves accuracy and Runtime-call latency in 10 of 12 NPU–workload combinations.
VG-E2E reduces System-level latency in every combination, with an additional 10.4–70.7% reduction over VG-NPU, but improves accuracy in only four.
NPU-level rankings do not always match end-to-end rankings, highlighting the need for deployment-level evaluation.

papers.abstract: Traffic cameras continuously record urban road-user behavior, providing proactive safety evidence beyond crash reports. Yet safety-critical events - conflicts, near misses, unsafe turns, sudden braking, and crosswalk interactions - are rare and brief, buried in hours of routine footage. Existing traffic-video pipelines extract detections, trajectories, and risk scores but process footage uniformly, without adapting to an analyst's query. Vision-language methods improve scene understanding but often lack traffic-specific verification of participant-level conflicts. We introduce AgenticConflictLens, an agentic, query-conditioned framework for efficient, auditable conflict extraction from long fixed-camera traffic videos. Given a natural-language safety query, a Traffic-Aware Controller combines structured traffic memory with specialized conflict-analysis tools to choose where to search, which road users to examine, and which evidence to verify or reject. A coarse-to-fine search retrieves candidate intervals and applies detailed verification selectively. The framework produces conflict records with refined time intervals, participant pairs, semantic regions, trajectories, motion evidence, uncertainty, rejection reasons, and supporting clips. On 96 annotated hours from Bellevue and NYC DOT, AgenticConflictLens achieves the highest conflict-existence F1 and temporal IoU on both datasets: 0.84 F1/0.77 tIoU on Bellevue and 0.80 F1/0.73 tIoU on NYC DOT, while inspecting only 8.7% and 11.9% of video, respectively. These results support scalable, evidence-grounded urban traffic-safety analysis.
authors: Boshra Khalili, Sonia Moshfeghi, Jinwoo Jang, Andrew W Smyth

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) have opened up new possibilities for generating rich interleaved text-image content. However, they generally lack native support for coordinating the two modalities, and translating coarse user requests into coherent multimodal compositions also requires explicit planning. We propose UniWeaver, a structured, model-agnostic harness framework that integrates multimodal planning, generation, and visual feedback to produce coherent interleaved outputs. To train UMMs for this task, we construct UniWeaver-10K, a dataset of 10,000 tasks across 20 task families, paired with execution trajectories guided by UniWeaver. We also introduce UniWeaver-Bench, a task-oriented benchmark systematically assessing text coverage, writing quality, visual coverage, and image-text alignment. Experiments show that UniWeaver achieves state-of-the-art performance and improves interleaved text-image generation across multiple UMM backbones.

papers.abstract: Photorealistic and metrically consistent world representations are a primary requirement for LiDAR--inertial--visual SLAM systems that serve robots over continuous operation. 3D Gaussian splatting makes such representations attainable by supplying an explicit, renderable, and queryable scene model. We present GEMOR-GS (Global Extrinsic-calibration-refined Mapping and Online Relocalization for 3D Gaussian-Splatting SLAM) to make the Gaussian map geometrically accurate, globally refined, and re-enterable, providing a better appearance for robot perception and decision-making. To improve the 3DGS map, the LiDAR--camera extrinsic is first estimated offline by direct-method alignment over dedicated calibration segments and reused by all following online and offline processes. Under the calibrated geometry, keyframe poses and Gaussian parameters are refined alternately under a gated differentiable-rendering and LiDAR--projection objective. The final global reconstruction is then rebuilt from the refined keyframe schema with all online constraints lifted. For the robot SLAM lifecycle, the method recovers the pose from the 3DGS map after tracking loss through an XFeat bypass map, RANSAC-PnP coarse localization, and Gaussian RGB-D warp refinement. Experiments on one self-collected and five public sequences quantify each element: the offline reconstruction wins all paired keyframes against the online map by 14.3--19.9 dB, improves PSNR by approximately 9 dB over Gaussian-LIC2, and achieves 86--100% held-out relocalization success tied to extrinsic quality. The results show that GEMOR-GS improves the geometric accuracy, appearance fidelity, and re-enterability of the 3DGS map, serving as a dependable robot world model for SLAM and downstream tasks.
authors: Yuchen Yang, Ming Ding, Xinyu Wu, Hesheng Wang

figures.caption: Figure 1: System overview. The calibration refinement 3O is an independent process: the extrinsic is estimated once per sensor rig by direct-method calibration and reused by both tracks. The bypass relocalization path 4O matches descriptors against the relocalization database upon tracking loss and hands the refined pose back to the front end.

papers.abstract: Remote sensing imagery acquired by Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) supports wide range of applications; however, deploying machine learning (ML) models on resource-constrained aerial platforms introduces challenges beyond predictive accuracy, particularly when deployment data differ from the distributions observed during training. Such shifts are common in remote sensing due to geographic, sensor, seasonal, and other visual variations. A practical solution is to equip deployed models with mechanisms that detect emerging distribution shifts and support subsequent responsive actions. This paper presents an empirical case study of three open-source detection tools: (i) Alibi-Detect; (ii) NannyML; and (iii) PyTorch-OOD. Using cross-dataset remote-sensing shifts, we evaluate both detection effectiveness and computational latency of these tools. Our results reveal differences in detection behavior and processing cost across methods and implementations, highlighting trade-offs between detection capability and response-time. These findings motivate further work toward lightweight, and latency-aware monitoring mechanisms for resource-constrained systems.
authors: Abdullah Almansour, Ozan K. Tonguz
bullets: Distribution shifts arise from geographic, sensor, seasonal, and other visual changes between training and deployment data.
The study evaluates Alibi-Detect, NannyML, and PyTorch-OOD using cross-dataset remote-sensing shifts.
It examines both shift-detection behavior and processing latency.
Results show differences among tools and implementations, motivating lightweight, latency-aware monitoring for resource-constrained aerial platforms.

papers.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) running on mobile devices can keep user data private and work without connectivity. But they perform well only when fine-tuned for the target task and sized for the target device, a process that today requires repeated expert tuning. We present {\it Mobile AI Factory}, an agentic system that builds a fine-tuned, quantized SLM for a given task and phone. Given a task specification and a target phone, an orchestrator LLM chooses whether to tune hyperparameters, mine real data, or generate synthetic examples, while fixed rules roll back changes that hurt accuracy. The factory searches from small to large models across base models and quantizations, adapts its accuracy goal as it searches, and uses real measurements of the target phone across inference engines and backends. We evaluate Mobile AI Factory on ten tasks and four Android phones. On an unseen testset, its on-device models outperform two five-shot frontier models on five tasks, by up to 0.34, and match them on three more. Its search comes within 0.03 of exhaustively training all 27 model variants on an entity extraction task, while using 19$\times$ less GPU time. Phone measurements also matter: the best configuration changes across phones. Without phone measurements, Claude Opus 5.5, given the full hardware and model specifications, misses the app's requirements in 25\% of easy and moderate cases and in 60\% of hard ones. Code is available at: https://github.com/evanly-gh/SLM_Factory.
authors: Evan Li, Krishna Deshpande, Wen Cheng, Shyamnath Gollakota

papers.abstract: SDR-to-HDR reconstruction is an ill-posed problem in which clipped highlights, crushed shadows, and quantization artifacts must be recovered while preserving the original content. Latent diffusion models provide powerful generative priors for restoring missing detail, but their effectiveness is constrained by how HDR signals pass through the pretrained VAE. We find that common log-like encodings suppress low-luminance chromatic differences before generation, producing a dark-side collapse in the frozen-VAE latent. We introduce EquivFlow, a compact, invertible exposure-equivariant encoding that maps exposure changes to additive shifts while retaining a scale-independent chromatic component, without modifying the VAE. Encoding-level tests across pretrained image and video VAEs show that its exposure structure and deep-dark chroma transport persist across the tested hosts. Integrated into SDR-to-HDR video diffusion, EquivFlow delivers consistent chromatic-fidelity gains across the tested settings while retaining competitive reconstruction fidelity.
authors: Donghoon Cha, Bomseok Park, Hansl von Kwon, Ku DoHyung, Hanwool Sul
bullets: Addresses highlight clipping, shadow crushing, and quantization artifacts in the ill-posed SDR-to-HDR problem.
Identifies dark-side chroma collapse caused by common log-like encodings in frozen VAE latents.
Introduces a compact, invertible, exposure-equivariant encoding with additive exposure shifts and scale-independent chroma.
Tests across pretrained image and video VAEs show persistent exposure structure and deep-dark chroma transport.
Integrated diffusion experiments achieve consistent chromatic-fidelity gains while maintaining competitive reconstruction fidelity.

papers.abstract: End-to-end navigation in cluttered environments relies on compact visual representations to support collision avoidance and goal-directed motion. Existing methods typically learn these representations jointly with the policy or through observation reconstruction, which does not explicitly specify what information the representation should preserve. Moreover, they are usually evaluated with a single downstream policy learner, although the benefit of a representation may depend on how the policy is learned. It therefore remains unclear how different representation-learning objectives affect downstream navigation performance and robustness. This work proposes DeRep, a navigation-oriented representation-learning method that combines local bird's-eye-view reachability supervision with depth reconstruction. To compare representation objectives under controlled conditions, we pretrain encoders with a common architecture and freeze them during downstream learning. We evaluate the representations using a linear policy probe, flow-matching imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with PPO. DeRep achieves the lowest linear policy probe prediction error and outperforms reconstruction alone across all six tested PPO conditions. In imitation learning, both reachability-based objectives achieve higher mean success rates than reconstruction alone, with similar mean success rates between the reachability-only and joint objectives. These results demonstrate consistent benefits of incorporating reachability supervision into depth representation pretraining across different downstream learning methods and evaluation conditions. We further deploy the PPO policy with the frozen DeRep encoder in Gazebo and on a physical quadrotor without fine-tuning, demonstrating its capability for zero-shot sim-to-sim and sim-to-real transfer.
authors: Hanyu Jin, Kenji Shimada

papers.abstract: Compositional generalization is an important form of out-of-distribution generalization, defined as the ability to train on some combinations of modules (e.g., functions such as sort, filter) and then generalize to unseen combinations. Despite substantial empirical work evaluating compositional generalization in transformers, findings have been inconsistent because evaluations were often conducted on a limited set of train-test splits, defined in an ad hoc manner. Through a systematic evaluation, we identify two key aspects of the train-test distribution that strongly affect performance: composition equivalence and module coverage. We show that the apparent performance of direct models (trained only on final outputs) results primarily from exploiting composition equivalences, meaning different sequences of modules that reduce to identical end-to-end functions. When benchmarks eliminate these equivalences, performance drops significantly, showing their inability to generalize to compositions of known modules that produce novel end-to-end functions. We further demonstrate that performance degrades monotonically as module coverage shifts increase (when modules appear in different contexts between train and test), affecting both direct and step-by-step models (trained on intermediate and final outputs). These findings have concrete implications for benchmark design: benchmarks that include compositional equivalences can lead to significant overestimation of the generalization abilities of direct models, and benchmarks that include both module coverage violations and compositional equivalences can exacerbate shortcut learning. As a case study, we demonstrate the role of compositional equivalence on the generalization performance of the pre-trained model Llama3-8B on the code-output prediction task in the coding benchmark LiveCodeBench.
authors: Purva Pruthi, Andrew Yuan, Alexander D'Amour, David Jensen
bullets: Systematically evaluates how train–test distribution design affects compositional generalization.
Finds direct models often appear strong by exploiting different module sequences with identical end-to-end functions.
Removing composition equivalences causes substantial performance drops on novel functions built from known modules.
Performance declines monotonically as module contexts shift between training and testing, for both direct and step-by-step models.
Shows benchmark design can overestimate generalization and encourage shortcut learning, including in a Llama3-8B LiveCodeBench case study.

figures.caption: Figure 9: Generalization performance of bigger transformer architecture: We observe that the performance of the bigger architecture shows similar performance trends as seen for the smaller architecture (N_heads = 6, N_layers = 3) in Figures 2(b) and (d).

Figure 4: Isolating the effect of composition equivalence in the diverse benchmark (k = 6): (a) Generalization performance increases with the degree of shared composition equivalence classes between train and test. (b) The direct model generalizes primarily to test sequences that share equivalence classes and fails on classes exhibiting novel end-to-end behavior.

Figure 6: (a) Code output prediction performance of Llama3-8b on LiveCodeBench benchmark: We show the accuracy of the base model (No LoRA) and three LoRA fine-tuned models on splits with varying ratios of shared equivalence classes (defined by the same function names) (held out h=0, 0.5, 1.0). As splits share composition equivalences, accuracy improves substantially. (b) Performance grouped by equivalence classes: We observe that performance on most functions only improves when equivalences are leaked into the fine-tuning set.

Figure 1: (a) A sequential composition task combines “atomic” functions (e.g., sort, mode, filter). Task-based compositional generalization is the ability to generalize to unseen sequences after training on a subset. (b) Composition equivalence: Different sequences are composition equivalent if they reduce to the same end-to-end function. For example, one equivalence class consisting of the first four sequences reduces to returning the most frequently occurring vowel in a set of strings; direct models succeed on the test sequence (mode ◦ filter ◦ sort) from this class but fail on the remaining two test sequences from a different composition equivalence class. (c) Module coverage: Examples of coverage failures include position-wise (e.g., function 2 never appearing in the first position, shown with dashed lines) and pair-wise (e.g., missing pair (2,1) in the training set, shown with solid lines).

Figure 3: Cross-k evaluation: For the diverse benchmark (a–b), direct models perform well near training k as equivalences persist across nearby k values. Direct models fail on the uniform benchmark (c–d) regardless of identity tokens, since identity-based equivalences in the uniform benchmark are k-specific. Step-by-step models are more robust but still exhibit significant variability.

Figure 2: Within-k evaluation: Direct models fail completely (0% accuracy) on uniform bijections without identity tokens (Figure (d)), while step-by-step models maintain near-perfect performance across all conditions. We observe that including identity tokens or diverse function types seems crucial for the generalization performance of direct models.

Figure 7: Uniform benchmark (without identity), N_heads = 6, N_layers = 3, Direct (Relative): We observe that the models learn to predict the outputs of training compositions for both K=2 and for K=6, while the test accuracy on unseen compositions remains 0% throughout. We report two metrics: (1) sharp accuracy, where a prediction scores 1.0 only if the entire output sequence is correct and 0.0 otherwise; and (2) mean token accuracy, average accuracy of predictions in the output sequence, with both metrics averaged across compositions from each split. For reference, 100 epochs correspond to roughly 20k iterations (batch size 512, 100k training samples, 195 iterations per epoch).

Figure 8: Diverse benchmark, N_heads = 6, N_layers = 3, Direct (Relative): We observe non-trivial compositional generalization, as the models perform well on training and validation compositions, the test performance also increases. We observe better generalization for K = 6 than for K = 2 due to more training diversity and shared equivalences.
Figure 5: Effect of position-wise distribution shift: As the position-wise KL divergence increases, the compositional generalization performance of both direct and step-by-step models decreases.

Figure 10: Equivalence class necessity and training requirements: (a) Generalization performance to unseen sequences is strongly correlated with the degree of shared composition equivalence classes between train and test. (b) Models need to see at least 4–5 composition equivalences (per class) in training to generalize to the corresponding test equivalences.

Figure 14: Composition equivalence encourages shortcuts in step-by-step models: We observe that composition equivalences in the diverse benchmark cause discrepancies between final output accuracy and full output (intermediate and final output) accuracy for both within-k evaluation and cross-k evaluation. Final accuracy > full accuracy implies the model is learning shortcuts to reach the final answer. If we eliminate composition equivalences, the performance difference is zero between full and final outputs (see Figures 15(a), 15(b))

Figure 15: Eliminating composition equivalences removes shortcut learning in step-by-step models : We observe that the lack of compositional equivalence in the uniform benchmark removes shortcut-learning behavior in step-by-step models. This is shown by the exact same step-by-step accuracy, and the final accuracy is the same for both within-k evaluation (k = 6) and cross-k evaluation (train-k = 6).

Figure 19: Effect of pairwise-wise distribution shift: (a) As the pairwise-wise KL divergence increases, the compositional generalization performance of both direct and step-by-step models decreases in the diverse benchmark. (b) For the uniform benchmark, the effect of divergence is primarily observed at the extreme right end for support violations.

Figure 25: Effect of number of samples per composition (diverse benchmark, direct model): For the diverse benchmark, direct models are less sample efficient than the uniform benchmark to generalize on the validation set, especially for K= 2. We observe significant compositional generalization behavior, as seen in Figure 2(b) for large samples, especially for K=6.

Figure 24: Effect of number of samples per composition (uniform benchmark, step-by-step model): We observe that step-by-step models are more sample efficient than direct models due to access to intermediate outputs providing extra information.

Figure 23: Effect of number of samples per composition (uniform benchmark, direct model):. Number of training compositions N = 24 for K = 2, and N = 576 for K = 6. We vary the number of input-output samples per training composition in this experiment. We observe that with a small number of training samples, the train/val gap is large, and the model struggles to generalize to training compositions with novel inputs. The train-val gap reduces as the number of samples increases. Test accuracies remain 0%, as expected.

Figure 26: Effect of number of samples per composition (diverse benchmark, step-by-step model): Step-by-step models are more sample efficient than direct models, and a similar difference between uniform and diverse benchmarks for K=2 is observed as for direct models.

Figure 22: Effect of number of unique training sequential compositions (randomly sampled, K=6):: We observe that (a) step-by-step models with relative global embedding need fewer training compositions to generalize faster than absolute embedding models, and (b) For the diverse benchmark, as compared to direct models, step-by-step models need fewer unique training compositions due to extra information available using intermediate outputs.

Figure 16: Gemma-1B visualization of per-class distribution for 100% sharing: We observe that most of the equivalence classes are shared and the model has overall high accuracy over test sequences in the shared equivalence classes.

Figure 17: Gemma-1B visualization of test accuracy for the split with no shared equivalences: We observe that none of the equivalence classes are shared, and the model has poor accuracy over test sequences in those classes.

Figure 13: Leaking test equivalence classes without swapping (K = 6): (a) Generalization performance to unseen sequences is strongly correlated with the number of shared composition equivalence classes between train and test. (b) The mean accuracy of shared equivalence classes is significantly higher than that of non-shared equivalence classes.

Figure 20: Combined effect of position-wise shift and reduced diversity: Shows (1-accuracyKL) to demonstrate accuracy degradation as in Figure 5, revealing combined effects of coverage shift and reduced compositional diversity due to biased sampling. Here, accuracyKL is the performance with biased sampling.

Figure 21: Isolating position-wise shift by controlling diversity: Shows accuracyzero_shift − accuracyKL, where accuracyzero_shift and accuracyKL are accuracies under random and biased sampling with n unique compositions at each Dpos, respectively. For the diverse benchmark, positionwise shift alone has a reduced but still significant effect compared to Figure 20, indicating that both coverage shift and reduced diversity contribute to degradation. For the uniform benchmark, the negligible difference confirms that degradation is driven primarily by coverage shift alone.

Figure 11: Visualization of learned equivalence classes for the diverse benchmark (K=6): We show two equivalence classes (out of a total of 14 classes). First, we can note that the degree of equivalence varies significantly within an equivalence class. The test sequences are marked in red, and the training sequences are marked in green, indicating whether an equivalence class is shared. We observe that accuracy is significantly higher for compositions in the shared equivalence class and near zero for those in the non-shared equivalence class.

papers.abstract: Open-Vocabulary Scene Graph Generation (OV-SGG) requires models to recognize visual relationships beyond the training vocabulary, yet existing methods often rely on dataset-specific object--predicate co-occurrence patterns. Under long-tailed distributions and noisy object localization, such reliance leads to biased, entangled relation representations, limiting both rare-relation recognition and generalization to unseen predicates. To address these challenges, we propose RaRe, a reasoning-aware relational representation learning framework that transforms MLLM-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) rationales into structured relation embeddings. Rather than using CoT only as an intermediate reasoning trace for final prediction, RaRe directly optimizes the rationale-derived representation space to improve inter-relation discriminability. Specifically, RaRe first aligns rationale embeddings with textualized relation descriptions through self-supervised contrastive learning, and then refines rationale generation with a specificity-oriented reinforcement learning objective that encourages semantically object-pair-specific relational evidence. Experiments on VG150 and PSG demonstrate improved category-balanced recognition over existing baselines, while the additional gains from learning vary across datasets and proposal settings. Code available at: https://artanic30.github.io/project_pages/RaRe.
authors: Jiawei Xiao, Boya Wang, Longtian Qiu, Shan Ning, Xuming He

papers.abstract: Existing cooperative end-to-end driving works at Class A (status-sharing) of the SAE J3216 classes of cooperative driving automation (CDA): vehicles exchange what they perceive, not what they intend, so each plans alone when to go, which limits cooperation and leads to deadlock when both vehicles yield or to collisions when both go. We present When2Go, a cooperative end-to-end driving system that learns when to go by sharing intent under CDA Class B or higher. Each vehicle broadcasts its LiDAR detections with forecast motion as instance tokens, together with its plan and intended trajectory. The receiver draws the fused detections, forecasts and partner plans into a route-time conflict map, the occupancy along its route over the planning horizon, on which a planner scores candidate speed profiles. Where two intended trajectories conflict, an order gate, a precedence network distilled from a right-of-way rule, decides who goes first; both vehicles evaluate it on the same messages and so reach the same order. When2Go imitates the rule-based expert of V2Xverse, which sees the simulator's ground truth; stops that When2Go cannot observe within its 2 s planning horizon are relabelled, so that it does not learn to wait without an observable cause. For our runs only, the benchmarks' PID controller steers by When2Go's waypoints instead of the route, and its forced push of long-waiting vehicles is off. With one model, When2Go sets the state of the art on three closed-loop CARLA benchmarks: 97.8 and 90.7 driving score on InterDrive without and with traffic (best published 90.1 and 78.9), 70.0 on the public V2Xverse protocol (best of sixteen rerun methods 59.1) and 88.2 on MDrive (best rerun 85.1), with 95.0% of its vehicles collision-free (87.7%).
authors: Haohua Que, Mingkai Liu, Tianle Zhu, Zhipeng Bao, Yiping Li, Handong Yao
bullets: Addresses the limits of perception-only cooperation, which can cause mutual yielding deadlocks or collisions when vehicles proceed simultaneously.
Vehicles share LiDAR detections, predicted motion, plans, and intended trajectories as instance tokens.
A route-time conflict map represents predicted occupancy along the ego route; a planner evaluates candidate speed profiles.
An order gate based on a distilled right-of-way precedence rule gives vehicles a consistent crossing order.
Achieves reported state-of-the-art driving scores across three closed-loop CARLA benchmarks, with 95.0% of vehicles collision-free.

papers.abstract: Event cameras record asynchronous changes in brightness. To use a general visual model as a recording trigger, a system must represent these measurements in a form the model can interpret. We compare direct grayscale accumulation, two temporal encodings, and two intensity reconstructors on paired real event data. On 192 windows from four held-out DSEC recordings, thresholds calibrated only on development data yielded 40 of 52 person detections and 12 of 140 background positives with E2VID. The strongest direct temporal encoding at an admissible fixed cutoff yielded 14 detections and seven background positives. A retrospective comparison at a common 10% background-positive cap yielded 40 detections for E2VID and at most 19 for any direct encoding. FireNet+ had lower preparation cost and produced 21 detections with zero observed background positives at its frozen cutoff. On the same 192 windows, Qwen3-VL-4B yielded 33/52, 2/140 with E2VID and 9/52, 9/140 with the highest-recall direct rendering, the three-bin image (person detections, background positives). A 96-second exploratory replay illustrates the sensitivity of episode capture and recording starts to cutoff selection. The experiments identify a detection benefit from reconstruction under controlled input history and distinguish it from the cost and false starts of continuous triggering.
authors: Yifan Shuai

With Qwen3-VL-4B, E2VID achieved 33/52 person detections and 2/140 background positives; the best direct rendering achieved 9/52 and 9/140.

A replay study shows that cutoff selection strongly influences episode capture and recording starts.

papers.abstract: This paper tackles the task of hand-object contact transition detection in egocentric video, which aims to localize the two temporal boundaries of a contact episode: the moment a hand first establishes contact with an object (touch) and the moment contact is released (release). We propose a unified framework that jointly models the interacting hand and object to accurately localize both transition types. The proposed framework augments hand-centric spatiotemporal representations with object-aware features learned directly from the video and introduces a transition-aware event spotting formulation tailored to contact transitions, without relying on external object or hand-object interaction detectors during inference. To support this task, we present ContactTransition, a dataset comprising 4,021 egocentric videos with 8,498 touch and 8,077 release annotations, together with object-of-interest supervision. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms strong two-stage and end-to-end event-spotting baselines on both transition types. Finally, we show that detected contact transitions provide effective temporal anchors for downstream egocentric hand-object reasoning.
authors: Huy Anh Nguyen, Chang Dong, Feras Dayoub, Minh Hoai

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of OASIS. Starting from the hand-enhanced feature map produced by HiCE [37], OASIS predicts an object-of-interest heatmap and pools object-aware features from the predicted regions. A presence gate controls when object evidence should be used, and the resulting object-aware representation is fused into the temporal spotting stream. The final head predicts touch and release transitions with event scores and class-specific displacement refinement.

Fig. 2: Predicted object-of-interest heatmaps. Top: input frames around a contact transition, with the predicted transition frame highlighted in red. Bottom: heatmaps predicted by the object-of-interest branch of OASIS. Although object annotations are used only during training, the model learns to highlight the object involved in the hand interaction at inference time, providing object-aware evidence for precise touch–release localization.

We report overall mAP, together with AP at frame tolerances δ ∈ {0, 1, 2} for touch and release detection. Bold and underline denote the best and second-best results.

papers.abstract: Predicting long action chunks, often spanning dozens of timesteps, has become a key ingredient in increasingly capable robot policies. In this paper, we find that adapting these long-chunk policies with existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods can require many online samples due to the high dimensionality of the action chunks being optimized, making such adaptation impractical in real-world scenarios where interaction data are costly to collect. Our key insight is to shift adaptation from optimizing actions to optimizing how long to execute each predicted action chunk. This keeps the adaptation space low-dimensional while its expressivity grows with the chunk size. We thus introduce Execution at the Right Length (ExRL), a simple approach which augments the base policy with a lightweight adapter that predicts the execution length of each chunk and is trained using off-policy RL algorithms. Across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks, ExRL enables sample-efficient adaptation of a diverse range of long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific hyperparameter tuning.
authors: Xu Luo, Jiaying Yang, Hao Wu, Junlin Xie, Zijin Hong, Ji Zhang, Lianli Gao, Jingkuan Song

papers.abstract: As AI agents become increasingly capable, users must still recognize when and how to ask for help, leaving many opportunities for useful support unrealized. Proactive agents hold the promise to close this gap, but effective proactivity requires understanding users' real-time activities and personalizing intervention timing so that assistance is offered when it is likely to be helpful rather than disruptive. We introduce deep personalization, a closed-loop process that connects continuous context observation with continual agent adaptation: an agent observes user activity, selectively retains long-term context, and adapts intervention decisions from implicit feedback. We initiate deep personalization in Coco, a proactive desktop agent, by having a separate Observer Agent that monitors desktop activity, maintains compact long-term user modeling context, and learns when assistance is desirable from implicit signals such as engagement, dismissal, explicit requests, and repeated work patterns. We further develop efficient on-device strategies to enable the Observer Agent to run on local AI compute platforms without streaming raw activity data off-device. For evaluation at scale without collecting sensitive real-user activity, we introduce a data-synthesis pipeline that transforms existing computer-use trajectories into OSWorld-Persona, a benchmark with persona-conditioned intervention labels. On OSWorld-Persona, deep personalization improves macro F1 across three model backbones from 0.12-0.19 under direct prompting to 0.35-0.48 after adaptation, a 2.4-3.0x relative gain. In a week-long user study, we observe that Coco improves its macro-averaged F1 score from 0.199 to 0.515. These results suggest that on-device deep personalization can make proactive agents more timely and increasingly aligned with each user's everyday work.
authors: Yijia Shao, Song Bian, Junxian Guo, Jindong Jiang, Zhen Dong, Huizi Mao, Diyi Yang, Song Han

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction (3R) from unconstrained multi-view images has recently emerged as a prominent research direction in 3D computer vision. Various foundational reconstruction models have been proposed with different architectures and reconstruction paradigms. Despite being trained on large-scale perspective datasets with substantial computational resources, these models generally struggle to generalize to non-perspective images. This limitation hinders their deployment in applications involving arbitrary, unknown, and potentially heterogeneous camera models. To build on the capabilities of existing reconstruction models with minimal retraining, we propose Camera3R, a low-rank adaptation framework that efficiently extends perspective-pretrained 3R networks to any other camera models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, with only 0.5% additional parameters and less than a day of training, Camera3R adapts a foundational 3D reconstruction model to non-perspective cameras while fully preserving its original performance on perspective inputs. Code is available at https://github.com/android-xr/camera3r.
authors: Ruxiao Duan, Yunwen Zhou, Erin Hong, Dongxu Zhao, Eric Turner, Federico Tombari, Alex Wong

figures.caption: Figure 1: 3D reconstruction from heterogeneous cameras. Given an image sequence of arbitrary, unknown, and mixed camera models, our method reconstructs the scene in a single forward pass.

Figure 2: Camera-agnostic feed-forward reconstruction. Given an input sequence from arbitrary, unknown, and mixed camera models, we adapt a perspective-pretrained reconstruction network by camera-specific LoRA experts. Each frame is passed to a camera router, which selects the corresponding LoRA expert to adapt the model to the frame’s camera geometry, enabling pose and dense geometry (depth, ray directions, etc.) prediction from non-perspective cameras. Perspective frames bypass the adaptation, preserving the original behavior of the pretrained backbone.

Figure 3: Cross-camera data augmentation for model adaptation. Multi-view 3D reconstruction data from fisheye and panoramic sequences are augmented by synthesizing diverse camera projections. For fisheye sequences, we randomly preserve the original views, create additional fisheye distortions, and undistort the image to obtain perspective views. For panoramic sequences, we randomly preserve the original views, apply rotations, and render fisheye or perspective images by sampling from the panoramic sphere. Dense ground truth quantities such as depth and ray maps are transformed together with the image, providing geometrically aligned supervision across various camera models.

papers.abstract: Most language models deployed outside the United States and China are fine-tuned descendants of a small number of pretrained families. We argue that fine-tuning leaves the decisive properties of a model inherited from its base: vocabulary, knowledge, cultural alignment, memorized data and license. We contribute (i) an updated, reproducible measurement of the tokenization premium across 31 languages and 7 tokenizers released in 2023-2024, on 27 articles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, with explicit correction for unknown-token collapse. Premiums reach 10x for Amharic in older tokenizers and remain at 6.8x in the newest commercial one; Indigenous South American languages pay between 1.6x and 2.7x under global tokenizers. A vocabulary built from Portuguese lowers the premium for 11 of 13 Latin-script Global South languages relative to every global tokenizer tested, by about 24% for Guarani and Quechua. (ii) An eight-test black-box sovereignty audit that a buyer can run without access to weights. (iii) A regime argument: under energy and liability constraints, accuracy per joule, calibration and selective risk should replace raw accuracy as design objectives, with metrics that abstention cannot inflate. We close with preliminary internal measurements from a proprietary architecture built around these objectives, reported with their limitations. Data and measurement code are included.
authors: Paulo Camara (LUA Vision)
papers.selection_reason: Measures tokenization and inherited properties of language models, relevant to LLM design and deployment.
papers.title: Inherited Weights: Measuring the Tokenization Premium and the Sovereignty Cost of Language Models for the Global South

papers.abstract: How should we understand memorization vs. generalization in in-context learning (ICL) tasks, and when does one happen vs. the other? To investigate, we study how rotation-invariant kernel machines learn the ICL linear regression task proposed by Raventos et al. (2023). By decomposing the task in the kernel eigenbasis, we obtain a spectral picture of learning in this ICL setting. This picture reveals that as sample size grows, kernel machines learn successively-higher-degree components of the memorizing solution, which depend upon successively-higher-degree statistics of the training task set. The generalizing solution is approximately a low-degree truncation of the memorizing solution, and so the model first generalizes, then degrades into memorization as training proceeds. The takeaways are threefold. First, if this case is indicative, learning a "generalizing" solution on an ICL task is really just underfitting the memorizing solution! Second, the fact that kernel machines can generalize on this task means that feature learning is inessential to ICL. Third, transformers empirically trained to do ICL are shown to memorize tasks through the higher-order statistics of the training tasks that the kernel-based theory predicts, suggesting it applies even to models capable of feature learning.
authors: Joseph Turnbull, Jamie Simon
bullets: Studies rotation-invariant kernel machines on an ICL linear-regression task using a kernel-eigenbasis decomposition.
As sample size grows, models learn increasingly higher-degree components tied to higher-order statistics of the training tasks.
Generalization appears first, then degrades into memorization as training proceeds.
The results suggest feature learning is not essential for ICL in this setting.
Empirically trained transformers show the predicted memorization through higher-order task statistics.

Figure 4: Task diversity trades pretraining-task accuracy for novel-task accuracy. Following Raventós et al. (2023), we sweep the number of training tasks T and report test MSE on the pretraining tasks Dtr (left) and on novel tasks Dnovel (right). Our data is drawn with d = 8, L = 15, ϵ2 = 0.25. In blue, we show a fit random features network trained with SGD (see Section B for random feature network details), with the memorizing (dMMSE) and generalizing (ridge) oracles shown. As T grows, the training task distribution’s cumulants approach that of the prior’s (Gaussian) and all three curves converge. Evaluated on novel tasks, the random features model initially tracks the memorizing solution up to a task diversity T of 4, continuing to approach the generalizing solution until T ≈ 26 = 64 tasks. All models are trained with enough samples such that they can fully realize the optimal degree-3 term, indicated by the green background. We note two exceptions: a blue background for one training task is used to signify that the model uses the mean task alone, and the seafoam background for two tasks signifies the mean task still being heavily utilized. The trained models do not exactly reach the generalizing solution, in part due to the finite context length L we use for training (see Section 7). Further experimental details are in Section B.

Figure 7: One-dimensional ICL data breaks Gaussian universality. We compare the eigenframework’s predicted test MSE (line) against kernel regression trained on true ICL contexts (circles) and on a Gaussian surrogate with matched moments (diamonds), for T = 4, d = 1, L = 8. We use a Gaussian kernel with kernel width σker = √ 3 and in-context data with covariance Σx ∼ Id/(dL). The left panel is ridgeless (δ = 0) and the right uses a small ridge (δ = 5× 10−3). The Gaussian surrogate tracks the theory at every n. The true contexts agree away from the interpolation peak but exceed the prediction near it, most visibly at small ridge. Both datasets share the same theoretical curve, so the mismatch comes from the non-Gaussianity of one-dimensional ICL data rather than from the predicted eigenstructure. We observe no such failure for d > 1.

Figure 3: Random feature models can perform ICL even with only T = d+ 1 tasks. We train a random feature network using SGD with exactly T = 4 = d+ 1 tasks (d = 3), with context length L = 96. We manually construct a training task pool such that Σ̂ = Id and µ̂ = 0. As is predicted in Section 7, this training task distribution allows the model to near-perfectly generalize once the optimal degree-3 term ∑ i yix ⊤ i xL+1 is learned. We evaluate the random features model’s test error on novel tasks β⋆ ∼ Dnovel, normalized by E[y2]. When the model has not seen many samples in phase one, the model uses the average training task, which we manually set to 0. At approximately 106 samples, the model enters phase two and begins fitting the generalizing degree-3 term. Even though there are only 4 training tasks, the model does not memorize the tasks with up to 109 samples! Given infinite training samples, the model will eventually memorize. Further details in Section B.

Figure 5: Transformers memorize through non-Gaussian statistics of their training tasks. We train 12-layer GPT-2-style transformers with Adam on T = 256 training tasks (d = 8, L = 16, ϵ2 = 0.25) and evaluate the test MSE on (a) fresh tasks and (b) the training tasks. All pools are centered and whitened (see Section 7.2 for a discussion of the implications) and differ principally in their fourth cumulant. Whiten consists of i.i.d. Gaussian draws, partial kurtosis is made of a symmetric pool whose κ̂4 is rescaled to 0.3× that of its initial Gaussian pool, no kurtosis uses a symmetric pool with κ̂4 = 0. Dashed and dotted lines mark the generalizing (ridge) and memorizing (dMMSE). In (a), each pool’s dMMSE is shown to highlight that the slight difference in oracle does not explain the onset of task memorization. All models first approach the generalizing solution, with the scale of the kurtosis setting when memorization begins. Further experimental details are in Section B.

Figure 1: As sample size grows, kernels learn successively higher-degree target function components in in-context linear regression. They first learn the mean training task (phase 1), then approximate the degree-three generalizing solution (phase 2), and finally memorize the training tasks (phase 3). (Left) A visualization of a kernel machine’s inferred task in task space B = Rd decomposed into vector components learned in each phase (arrows). Grey dots indicate training tasks Btr = {β(t)} and a grey star indicates an unseen task β∗ /∈ Btr. In phase 1, the kernel learns the mean training task µ̂β := Eβ∼Btr [β]. In phase 2, the kernel learns approximately β∗− µ̂β , nearly recovering the true task β∗. In phase 3, learned higher-degree terms pull the prediction towards the nearest task in Btr. (Right) We plot learning curves for KR on the in-context linear regression problem with d = 5, L = 7, T = 16. (Top) Evaluated on the training tasks, the error falls monotonically, eventually reaching that of the memorizing solution (Equation (3)). We show both theoretical predictions (lines) and experimental values (dots) in the experimentally-accessible region n ∈ [1, 5 × 104]. (Middle) Evaluated on novel tasks (β ∼ N (0, Id)), error is minimized at the end of phase 2, approaching that of the generalizing solution (Equation (4)), before rising to that of the memorizing solution in phase 3. Background shading indicates the three phases of learning. (Bottom) We also plot the predicted overlap between the function f̂ker learned by KR and various polynomial functions gi. The functions gi correspond to the vector components in the cartoon on the left, and are given explicitly in Section B. The function gi is determined by the i-th order statistics of Btr. The component g1 is responsible for generalization and is learned in phase 2. We show theoretical predictions (lines) for the kernel’s error out to 1012 samples, finding excellent agreement between theory and experiment in the experimentally accessible region.

Figure 2: Transience is explained by learning higher order task statistics. We train lazy random features networks (RFNs) (see Section B.2 for a description of RFNs) with online SGD on ICL linear regression data. Using RFNs, we empirically find that the error on novel tasks rises when the higher degree terms are learned, as was theoretically predicted in Figure 1. We observe the same three phases of predicting from the mean task alone, then generalizing to any task, followed by memorizing using higher-degree terms. (Top) Test MSE on novel tasks β ∼ Dnovel, with the memorizing (dMMSE) and generalizing (ridge) oracles for reference. Unlike the kernels trained in Figure 1, the random feature networks train with enough samples to empirically probe phase 3. (Bottom) Overlap of the learned predictor with the leading terms of the memorizing solution, E[f̂gi]/E[g2i ]. Similar to Figure 1, the functions gi are determined by the i-th order statistics of Btr, and are explicitly given in Section B. Novel-task error drops below the memorizing oracle as ϕ3 is learned (n ≈ 105–106) and is lowest once ϕ3 (g1) saturates. The error then rises back toward the memorizing oracle as the network learns higher order statistics through g2 (n ≳ 107). Further experimental details are in Section B.

Figure 6: Analytically solved random feature models outperform the memorizing oracle on novel tasks. We show test MSE on novel tasks (Dnovel) and on the training tasks β ∈ Dtr of a random feature model whose readout layer weight has been analytically solved, as a function of the number of training samples n. The limiting kernel function is the ICL kernel of Equation (11), set with kernel width σ = 3. We use T = 8, L = 4, d = 4, ϵ2 = 0.05, and tasks drawn from an isotropic prior. Shading shows the standard deviation over 5 trials. Past n ≈ 4× 103, the model’s error drops below that of the memorizing oracle (dMMSE). It remains well above the generalizing oracle (ridge) throughout.

Figure 9: Gaussian kernel learning curves on ICL Regression data. For four different settings (colors) of the task diversity T , we compute the expected test MSE as a function of the number of training samples n, and compare it to empirical errors obtained across 20 trials. Theoretical learning curve equations are provided in Section D, with validation of the eigensystem the equations are built off of provided in Sections E and F. Our data uses a Gaussian kernel with kernel width σker = √ 3, d = 5, L = 7, ϵ2 = 0.1 where our data is drawn x ∼ N (0, Id/(dL)). Additionally, as T → ∞, we find that the errors on the pretraining distribution match those of the true distribution, as expected. Further experimental details are in Section B.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential in biomedical applications, while agentic memory systems have emerged as a promising approach to preserving and utilizing information across tasks and interactions. However, a fundamental question remains: how effectively and reliably do these systems retain, retrieve, update, and utilize biomedical information? In this study, we systematically investigate agentic memory in the biomedical domain, focusing on task effectiveness, retrieval quality, information fidelity, and long-term robustness. We evaluate five memory approaches across four LLMs in three representative settings: biomedical knowledge reasoning, clinical prediction, and long-term conversational memory. Our analyses reveal how memory construction, evidence relevance, and conversational history shape downstream biomedical performance, highlighting the distinct challenges of retrieving relevant information, preserving its fidelity, and effectively utilizing it for reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce Hybrid Memory Retrieval and Utilization (HMRU), a training-free framework that jointly enhances evidence accessibility and task-aware utilization to improve biomedical reasoning and long-term conversational memory. HMRU achieves an average relative improvement of 8.6% across biomedical question-answering and conversational memory benchmarks, with additional gains in selected clinical prediction tasks. It further reduces conversational answer errors by 24.9% and closes 48.0% of the performance gap to full-context inference. Our findings provide a systematic characterization of biomedical agentic memory and practical insights into developing more effective and reliable memory-augmented LLM systems.
authors: Mingchen Li, Yongkang Xiao, Rumeng Li, Rui Zhang, Hong Yu

papers.abstract: Automated segmentation in multi-view echocardiography is essential for comprehensive cardiac assessment, yet remains challenging due to substantial anatomical and appearance variability across standard acoustic windows. In this paper, we present P2Echo, a unified framework capable of segmenting diverse cardiac structures across multiple standard echocardiographic views using a single model controlled by structured view-aware text prompts. Unlike recent foundation model adaptations that rely on implicit latent priors, P2Echo explicitly conditions the segmentation process via a novel Dynamic Image-Text Alignment (DyITA) module. DyITA integrates a differentiable routing mechanism and token differential operators to dynamically modulate decoder features according to the requested view and target structure. This allows the network to adaptively switch its processing pathways for different views without architectural changes. Extensive experiments on a large-scale internal dataset (seen during training) and held-out evaluation on three external datasets demonstrate that P2Echo matches or exceeds both view-specific specialists and state-of-the-art universal models at a fraction of their computational cost, offering an efficient, controllable solution for multi-plane cardiac analysis. Code is available at: https://github.com/moeinheidari7829/P2Echo.
authors: Moein Heidari, Alvin Kimbowa, Mahdi Tabatabaei, Afshin Bozorgpour, Sina Ghorbani Kolahi, River Jiang, Wenjin Chen, David J. Foran, Jasmine Grewal, Dorit Merhof, Ilker Hacihaliloglu

papers.abstract: Quantifying uncertainty over an entire LLM completion is critical for selective prediction and adaptive compute. Zero-cost signals such as mean token entropy and log-probability are local to tokens or to one completion, and self-consistency needs many extra completions. We show that Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding for power sampling already estimates the normalizing constant of the power distribution, which gives the sequence-level R'enyi entropy (SRE) of the model's completion distribution at zero marginal cost, with a guarantee at every particle budget. A R'enyi chain rule extends this readout to a family of stepwise entropies of any order. We prove that orders above one are tied to the most likely token of each step, which explains why they track log-probability, while the order-1/2 member accumulates the log of per-step search effort. This member is the best zero-cost selective-prediction signal in 10 of 13 settings. On MATH500 its AUROC is 0.022 to 0.044 above log-probability with all four models and within length quartiles, and the same order is selected when each setting is held out. An 8-particle probe identifies the problems that benefit from more particles, and a two-pass policy matches 64-particle accuracy on MATH500 with 34.2% fewer particles over three seeds.
authors: Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo, Milad Heidari Sorkhehdizaj, Shahab Rahimirad, Aliasghar Pourghani, Seyedarmin Azizi, Souvik Kundu, Abolfazl Hashemi, Joseph Campbell, Vijay Gupta
bullets: Sequence-level uncertainty is needed for selective prediction, but token-level scores and self-consistency have limitations.
Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) power sampling estimates the completion distribution’s normalizing constant, yielding sequence-level Rényi entropy at every particle budget.
A Rényi chain rule provides stepwise entropy signals; order 1/2 captures cumulative per-step search effort and outperforms log-probability in 10 of 13 settings.
On MATH500, order 1/2 improves AUROC over log-probability by 0.022–0.044 across four models and length quartiles.
An 8-particle probe enables adaptive compute: a two-pass policy matches 64-particle accuracy while using 34.2% fewer particles over three seeds.

papers.abstract: DeepSeek-V4.1's 203 GB of Engram n-gram tables sit in host DRAM today, taking 190 of the 223 GiB a 4-GPU serving process uses. Row indices depend only on input tokens, so reads can start with each step and overlap earlier layers. V4.1's two Engram layers have windows that differ by 30x (0.3 vs. 9.3 ms). We show that this deadline, together with session reuse and contention on a shared device, decides which tier each table can use and which layers need cache, and we give a model that predicts the resulting slowdown from measured read times. Agent and chat traffic reuse rows within sessions, and static hot sets transfer poorly. We build SlackTier, a table tier for SGLang that issues all lookups at step start. It reads the short-window layer first and splits a small GPU row cache across layers. The path runs inside the decode CUDA graph and is bit-exact with the original gather. Layer 14's table can go to NVMe uncached with no measurable decode cost. With both tables on four NVMe disks, mean time per output token on agent and chat replays rises at most 1.4% over unmodified SGLang, and host memory falls from 212 to 34 GiB. Both tables need no cache when read over RDMA (remote direct memory access) from another node's memory; one copy serves two instances. On a KV-constrained agent workload, using the freed memory as host KV cache at the same memory budget raises median throughput by 36% and cuts median p90 time to first token from 38 to 24 s.
authors: Wen Huang, Jack Liu
bullets: Engram table reads can begin at each decoding step and overlap earlier-layer computation, but layers have very different deadlines (0.3 ms versus 9.3 ms).
The proposed model accounts for deadlines, session reuse, and shared-device contention to select storage tiers and cache requirements.
SlackTier prefetches all lookups at step start, prioritizes the short-window layer, and partitions a small GPU row cache across layers within SGLang’s CUDA graph.
With both tables on four NVMe disks, agent and chat replays slow by at most 1.4% while host memory drops from 212 to 34 GiB.
Freed memory used for host KV cache improves median throughput by 36% and reduces median p90 time to first token from 38 to 24 seconds on a KV-constrained agent workload.

papers.title: Placing LLM Lookup Tables by Per-Layer Prefetch Deadlines
papers.tldr: SlackTier places LLM lookup tables according to per-layer prefetch deadlines, preserving near-baseline decoding while greatly reducing host-memory use.

papers.abstract: LLM agents drive inference engines with closed-loop sessions whose context grows every turn, and serving them economically depends on prefix caching: a hit costs an incremental prefill of about a thousand tokens, a miss recomputes a 10--40K-token context. We show that this makes prefix-cached agent serving metastable. With an identical base workload, a few minutes of extra arrivals leaves a vLLM server in a degraded regime--a ~10% hit ratio, about half the throughput, and a backlog that grows for the remaining 70 minutes--while its no-burst twin stays healthy (9 of 12 pairs; none in the reverse direction). The regime appears at loads the cache-warm server sustains, is absent without prefix caching, and also appears with Qwen3-32B on SWE-bench agent trace shapes and on SGLang, which tolerates larger triggers. Slower service keeps more sessions in the system, their working set outgrows the KV pool, and every turn becomes a recomputation; a first-order workload-balance condition, calibrated independently, brackets when the regime can drain. Getting out is the harder problem: throttling new admissions recovered 1 of 7 matched collapsed runs, while suspending admitted sessions against a capacity-based limit recovered all of them within minutes. A CPU offload tier delays the collapse but does not prevent it. A budgeter that bounds the resident KV demand of active sessions to the pool, with thresholds that need no per-workload tuning, prevented the failure in every run we tested.
authors: Wen Huang, Jack Liu

papers.abstract: Hyperbolic vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as a rapidly growing area of research, reporting strong zero-shot performance alongside an interpretable embedding space in which radius orders representations by generality. But how hyperbolic are hyperbolic VLMs in practice? We investigate this at the exponential map, the single operation through which curvature enters an otherwise Euclidean network. We show that across MERU, HyCoCLIP, ARGENT, and PHyCLIP, the exponential map is well approximated by the identity function, i.e., pairwise distances and angles in the pre-map Euclidean space barely change under projection, and removing the map at inference leaves evaluation scores unchanged. Motivated by this observation, we train Euclidean VLMs on CC3M from scratch under the same hierarchy losses. Over roughly the final 90% of the training steps, the training statistics are nearly indistinguishable from those of their hyperbolic counterparts, and the resulting models match the evaluation scores and recover the same radial distributions. Our findings establish Euclidean space as a sufficient substrate for hierarchical vision-language learning as it is currently practiced, and motivate new paradigms in which hyperbolic geometry can deliver on its theoretical promise. Code is available at https://github.com/fbyrman/hyperbolic-vlms.
authors: Freek Byrman, Partha Das, Stijn Verdenius, Pascal Mettes
bullets: Analyzes the exponential map, the main point where curvature enters hyperbolic VLMs.
Across MERU, HyCoCLIP, ARGENT, and PHyCLIP, projection barely changes pairwise distances or angles.
Removing the exponential map at inference leaves evaluation scores unchanged.
Euclidean VLMs trained with the same hierarchy losses match hyperbolic models’ training behavior, scores, and radial distributions.
The results suggest current hierarchical VLMs do not yet exploit hyperbolic geometry’s theoretical advantages.

papers.abstract: Looped language models deepen computation without adding parameters, yet caching full-context key-value (KV) states across layers and rounds severely bounds serving batch size. We design a looped causal encoder-decoder (CED) that achieves recurrent depth with zero round-wise KV growth, addressing where and how to loop an asymmetric stack in which only sparse encoder layers generate global KV. We find that recurrence must be placed in the encoder to iteratively refine global KV representations rather than re-reading static decoder projections, which both drives language-modeling gains and preserves long-context scaling. Furthermore, training the encoder loop under stochastic recurrence depth induces a fixed-point equilibrium where every round losslessly shares the last round's KV cache. Compounding cross-layer and cross-round KV sharing, the resulting Looped CED matches an unlooped CED's minimal memory footprint and recovers 86-93% of a looped Transformer's gain with 1/6 of its global KV. To test serving at production scale, we loop the 552B-parameter DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash for 8 rounds on one 4xGB200 node: with per-layer and per-round KV the loop cannot fit a single 128K-token request, whereas Looped CED holds 36.8x less KV per token, fits 38 such requests (as many as the unlooped model), and serves 3.6x higher throughput on 8K-token prompts.

papers.abstract: Protein engineering requires navigating rugged fitness landscapes, where small sequence changes can produce large functional differences, but experimental screening can only sample a small fraction of sequence space. Thus, a central challenge is to efficiently traverse the large combinatorial space of mutations in silico. We introduce ProTEUS, a mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution. Pretrained on deep mutational scanning assays, ProTEUS learns a joint representation of sequence, evolutionary, and structural information using MutationFormer, a mutation-biased attention architecture. Variants are represented as states in this joint latent space, and mutations define actions whose functional consequences are predicted. To support exploration of many mutants, we developed a fast, physics-constrained all-atom predictor that utilizes explicit geometric constraint enforcement to achieve >10 fold increase in speed than AlphaFold3 with guaranteed physical validity. Lastly, ProTEUS refines its prediction and understanding of protein activity through closed loop experimental feedback to guide evolution toward a desired phenotype. ProTEUS surpasses established models in both zero-shot and supervised fine-tuning mutation prediction tasks. We experimentally demonstrate its utility in two closed-loop multi-objective engineering campaigns on aldehyde dehydrogenase and levansucrase, yielding variants with >10 fold higher activity than wild type. ProTEUS provides a world-model framework that connects virtual evaluation of mutational outcomes with experimental learning for efficient protein evolution.
authors: Yikun Zhang, Minghao Guo, Guangxue Xu, Peter Yichen Chen, Wojciech Matusik, Wengong Jin, Jingjing Chai, Kaiyi Jiang
papers.selection_reason: ProTEUS is a mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution, using a physics-constrained predictor and feedback loops. This fits World Models (Latent Action Models, Interactive World Models).
papers.title: ProTEUS: A mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution

papers.abstract: Vision-language models widely adopt Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding (MRoPE), an extension of Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) that incorporates temporal, height, and width axes to encode the spatial structure of visual tokens. However, MRoPE also assigns height and width coordinates to text tokens that lack inherent spatial structure, introducing spatial positional effects into text-vision attention. Existing MRoPE variants explore different frequency allocations and coordinate layouts, with their designs suggesting different intuitions about these cross-modal effects: they may provide useful spatial references for associating language with visual regions, or introduce unnecessary positional preferences that hinder text-vision interactions. In this work, we disentangle intra-visual spatial structure from cross-modal spatial effects to investigate this question. We identify a constraint of shared coordinate layouts that prevents eliminating cross-modal spatial effects while preserving intra-visual spatial encoding, and develop controlled experiments to isolate their respective contributions. Our results across multiple model scales, MRoPE variants, and benchmarks show that cross-modal spatial effects provide little additional benefit as spatial references and can even impair model performance, while intra-visual spatial encoding remains useful for fine-grained grounding.
authors: Zhaoyi Liu, Haichuan Zhang, Xiaochuan Gong, Yancheng Zhu, Bowei Tian, Wanghao Ye, Yufan Zhang, Ang Li
bullets: MRoPE assigns spatial coordinates to both visual and text tokens, potentially affecting text–vision attention.
The work separates intra-visual spatial structure from cross-modal spatial effects to study their distinct roles.
It identifies a limitation of shared coordinate layouts that prevents removing cross-modal effects without also losing visual spatial encoding.
Controlled experiments across model scales, MRoPE variants, and benchmarks find that spatial references for text tokens provide little benefit and can impair performance.
Intra-visual spatial encoding remains useful for fine-grained visual grounding.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large-scale foundation models across resource-constrained, distributed clients presents significant computational and communication challenges. While merging Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with Federated Learning (FL) enables rank-based flexibility, the interdependence of the adaptation matrices ($\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$) often complicates optimization. In this work, we theoretically demonstrate that LoRA fine-tuning with Gaussian initialization and a frozen $\mathbf{A}$ matrix acts as a stochastic approximation of full fine-tuning, where batch gradients are subject to a random, rank-dependent perturbation. Motivated by this insight, we propose freezing and periodically resampling $\mathbf{A}$ matrices at the client level. This strategy decouples the $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ gradients, diminishes LoRA low-rank constraints and reduces both computational and uplink communication overheads by 50\%, allowing for the reallocation of resources toward higher adaptation ranks. Furthermore, we show that in this frozen-$\mathbf{A}$ regime, the adaptation rank $r$ directly governs the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the perturbed gradients. Specifically, we find that the SNR increases linearly with $r$, implying that clients' learning rates must be dynamically scaled with their adaptation ranks for higher utility. Building on these foundations, we introduce SPRA-LoRA (Stochastic Projection Rank-Aware LoRA), a federated rank-aware fine-tuning strategy that utilizes frozen, resampled $\mathbf{A}$ matrices and rank-dependent learning rates for clients. We also prove its convergence with heterogeneous client resources. Our experiments across benchmark datasets demonstrate that SPRA-LoRA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with half the overhead on clients.
authors: Saber Malekmohammadi, Kevin Kuo, Virginia Smith, Golnoosh Farnadi
bullets: Shows that frozen-$\mathbf{A}$ LoRA with Gaussian initialization approximates full fine-tuning through rank-dependent stochastic gradient perturbations.

Finds that gradient signal-to-noise ratio increases linearly with adaptation rank, motivating rank-aware client learning rates.
Proves convergence under heterogeneous client resources.
Experiments on benchmark datasets report consistent outperformance over state-of-the-art baselines with half the client overhead.

papers.abstract: Accurate localization of abnormalities in three-dimensional (3D) CT scans is essential for linking automated predictions with clinically relevant pathological findings. We propose Uni-Loc, a vision-language framework that unifies pathology classification and 3D localization using scan-level supervision. Uni-Loc derives both predictions and localization maps from spatial similarities between pathology-conditioned queries and image features. A token-to-voxel upsampling module enables high-resolution localization, while gradient-guided thresholding identifies pathology regions without additional learned parameters. Evaluated on five localization tasks comprising 355 annotated CT scans, Uni-Loc achieves macro-averaged voxel-level AUROC/AUPR of 96.1\%/34.5\%, outperforming relevance propagation (80.7%/13.9%) and gradient saliency (88.7%/8.1%). Uni-Loc also achieves classification AUROC of 88.39% on CT-RATE and 78.03% on RAD-ChestCT, improving over a matched baseline. These results demonstrate effective 3D pathology localization without requiring pathology-specific voxel-level supervision.
authors: Hao-Chih Lee, Zahi A. Fayad, Xueyan Mei
bullets: Addresses the challenge of clinically meaningful 3D pathology localization from weak, scan-level supervision.

Across five tasks and 355 annotated CT scans, achieves 96.1% voxel-level AUROC and 34.5% AUPR, outperforming the compared saliency methods.
