papers.abstract: Few-shot abstract reasoning on ARC-AGI requires inducing algorithmic transformations from 2 to 5 demonstration pairs without task-specific pretraining. Because few-shot demonstrations under-constrain the hypothesis space, program synthesis suffers from the Rashomon effect (predictive multiplicity): heuristic search finds spurious programs with low training error that fail on test inputs, while unconstrained library growth degrades latency. We introduce F3-AGI v4.0, a CPU-native neuro-symbolic and active inference architecture comprising three mechanisms: (1) F3-Metabolic-Optim, combining mistake-gated plasticity, Fisher-EMA preconditioning, and virtual ATP gating; (2) Adaptive Complexity-Guided Program Synthesis (AACR) with a Cycle-3 ResidualPatchSynthesizer and smallest-pair early rejection; and (3) a 512D L2-normalized random projection driving Expected Free Energy (EFE) exploration with dead-signature pruning. Across three empirical studies: (i) on a synthetic 5-task class-incremental stream without replay, F3-Metabolic-Optim achieves 91.67% final accuracy with 9.17% forgetting, skipping 93.47% of updates, cutting L1 plasticity cost by 65.7%, and running 2.19x faster than EWC; (ii) on the 400-task ARC-AGI-1 public evaluation set (offline CPU, zero LLM calls), F3-AGI v4.0 solves 57/400 tasks (14.25% pass@2; 56/400 pass@1) with a mean latency of 1.62 s/task, decomposed into 19/50 (38.00%, 1.19 s/task, a 42.5x paired speedup over Horizon 2) on the 50-task calibration slice and 38/350 (10.86%) on the 350 strictly uninspected hold-out tasks (with 7 autonomous Cycle-3 patch solutions); and (iii) in a local 5-game (15-level) ARC-AGI-3-inspired interactive suite, our agent completes 15/15 levels with 89.44% level-weighted RHAE (90.72% unweighted).
authors: Henrique Oliveira
bullets: Targets spurious program selection and search-cost growth when reasoning from only 2–5 demonstrations.
Uses mistake-gated plasticity, Fisher-EMA preconditioning, virtual ATP gating, residual patch synthesis, and early rejection.
Adds 512D random-projection EFE exploration with dead-signature pruning for CPU-native search.
Achieved 57/400 ARC-AGI-1 tasks at pass@2 with 1.62 s/task, including 38/350 strictly uninspected hold-out tasks.
Also reported 91.67% final accuracy with 9.17% forgetting in a synthetic continual-learning stream and 15/15 levels in a 5-game interactive suite.

papers.abstract: Lenses that decode hidden states into words are a popular way to look inside language models, but a heatmap of decoded words only shows what a vector reads as and cannot distinguish whether, or how much, the model uses the information. We present an interactive viewer that puts reading, tracing and editing on the same layers-by-tokens grid of the residual stream. In the viewer, every cell can be decoded with two lenses, the logit lens and the Jacobian lens (J-lens), traced back to the tokens it drew from, and edited, with the rest of the model rerun on the spot. We demonstrate three usage scenarios on Gemma-3-4B-it, backed by sweeps over a few hundred prompts, to show what this tool can discover. First, the two lenses give different directions to write with, each suiting a different edit: the logit lens's word direction sets what a token outputs, while the J-lens's direction changes what later tokens read. Second, in two-hop trivia questions (the capital of the state or country containing a given city), the state or country is readable at the city token from as early as layer 7, and swapping it there can redirect the answer 92-98% of the time; however, at the answer position, the state or country information is not used. Third, when a chat model answers questions with a step-by-step reasoning prompt, the correct answer is often already the top word in the residual stream before any reasoning is written: for 89-92% of retrieval questions and 39-63% of multi-hop and serial ones, far above their respective distractors (at most 5%). However, ordering puzzles are an exception, as the model works them out only once it writes its final reasoning steps. Furthermore, for answers that are visible in the residual stream, the J-lens reads them a layer or two earlier than the logit lens across the different types of question.
authors: Nika Zahedi, Fangyi Zhu, Anna Wu

figures.caption: Figure 8: Two-hop recall in Gemma-3-4B-it (“Fact: the capital of the state containing Dallas is”, 25 U.S. items the model answers correctly). (a) At the city token, the J-lens reads the state among its top five words from about layer 7, the logit lens from layer 22. As a control, a wrong state (one belonging to another item, such as California for Dallas) never enters either lens’s top five. (b) At the last token, both lenses read the state before the capital; the J-lens begins to read it a few layers before the logit lens does. (c) Swapping the state for another item’s at the city token (s = 4, 40 pairs) gives the new state’s capital, nearly as often as the copy cell edit (black line), until the handoff. (d) The same swap at the last token fails, although the state is readable there and copying the cell works after the handoff. Bands are bootstrap 95% CIs.

Figure 6: The Dallas question in the viewer (Gemma-3-4B-it). (a) At Dallas, layer 21, the J-lens reads Texas second. (b) Swapping Texas for California there (J-lens directions, s = 4) changes the answer from Austin to Sacramento. (c) At the last token, layer 25, the J-lens reads Texas first. (d) The same swap there makes the model name a state instead of reasoning on to its capital.

Figure 9: Scenario B in one picture (Gemma-3-4B-it, 34 layers; “Fact: the capital of the state containing Dallas is”, 25 U.S. items). Each token has one lane per lens, shaded from the median layer at which the state (Texas, light) and then the capital (Austin, dark) enter the lens’s top five. (a) At the city token "Dallas", the J-lens reads the first hop from layer 7, well before the logit lens (layer 22), and swapping Texas for California there makes the model answer Sacramento. (b) By the handoff (layer 25), the last token "is" has copied the state from the city token, and both lenses read the state before the capital. Swapping the state here leaves the answer Austin: the state is readable at this token but not used. World items (not shown) read the capital as early as the country, as a memorized shortcut would.

Figure 10: The two patterns we look for (a schematic, not data), for the prompt “The Sydney Opera House is in a country. What is the capital of that country? Think step by step.” Each cell can only use the tokens to its left. (a) If the model resolves both hops in its layers while reading the question, a lens reads Australia and then Canberra in the question’s cells, before any reasoning is written. (b) If the model needs its written steps, Canberra becomes readable only after it has written Australia. Figure 11 counts how often each case occurs.

Figure 3: Each direction suits one edit (country–capital, Gemma-3-4B-it). (a) Pushing the answer token toward another country’s capital: the logit lens direction succeeds for 90% of items from layer 7, the J-lens direction only from layer 28 (n = 79). (b) Swapping the country for another at its own token: the J-lens direction succeeds in the middle layers (n = 100 pairs), up to the handoff, where copying the cells after the country starts to beat copying the country’s own cell (black lines, 20 pairs). Bands are bootstrap 95% CIs. (c) Cosine between the two directions for the same word, over the 203 words pushed toward (band: interquartile range): nearly perpendicular through layer 12, converging near the top.

Figure 4: A J-lens swap in the viewer (Gemma-3-4B-it, antonym prompts with five examples). (a) At layer 18 the J-lens reads the undue cell as undue and related words, and (c) swapping undue for rural there (strength 4) changes the answer to urban. (b) The J-lens reads the comfortable cell as formatting tokens (layer 12 shown), and (d) the same swap toward unfold leaves the answer uncomfortable. A J-lens swap points the right way only when the J-lens shows the word in its own cell; undue→rural is the only antonym pair of 100 for which it succeeds.

Figure 5: Finding the handoff in the viewer (Gemma-3-4B-it, “. . . Q: Russia\nA:”). Left: the last four tokens, each cell labeled with the J-lens’s top word and shaded by how much it feeds the output (Trace back from the outlined cell). Right: the answer after copying the Russia cell, at that layer, from the same prompt ending in Japan. The copy changes the answer up to layer 21 and not after. Teal outlines: cells with trace-back weight of > 0.04 to the output cell (red outline).

Figure 7: Reading the Dallas question in the viewer (Gemma-3-4Bit): the last four tokens at every layer, each cell labeled with the J-lens’s top word. Shaded: Texas is among the top five; outlined: Austin is. Texas is readable at Dallas from layer 6, long before the cell’s top word changes, and reaches the last token at layer 23, three layers before Austin.

Figure 11: Is the final answer readable before the reasoning? Gemma-3-4B-it, correctly answered questions out of 100 per task type. (a) Share of answers that a lens ranks first at some cell before the first reasoning token; the black ticks are a plausible wrong answer (control). (b) For those answers, the median first layer at which the lens reads it, with the number of answers beside each point.

Figure 2: Schematic of the four edits to a cell h. (a) Push adds a word’s direction d̂w, scaled by the cell’s own length. (b) Swap removes the cell’s component along the old word and adds s times its size along the new word, leaving the rest of the cell unchanged. (c) Copy replaces the whole cell with the same cell from another prompt. (d) Add a difference adds the difference between two prompts’ cells.
Table 2: The four task types of the chain-of-thought study, 100 questions each, and how many Gemma-3-4B-it answers correctly.

Table 1: Edits on Gemma-3-4B-it (34 layers), n = 25–100 items per task. Push: the first layer from which the pushed word is the top prediction for at least 90% of items. Swap: success at each direction’s best layer, with that layer in parentheses. Random: a control edit that changes the cell by the same amount as the J-lens swap, but along a random direction. Copy cell: success when the whole entity cell is copied from a prompt naming the new entity, our empirical ceiling for a single-cell edit. Random pushes succeed on at most 4% of items at any layer. The rates are not sensitive to choosing the best layer on the same pairs it is scored on: choosing it on a random half and scoring the other half (20 split trials) changed them by at most 5 percentage points.

papers.abstract: Temporal Sentence Grounding (TSG) aims to localize temporal segments in untrimmed videos that correspond to natural language queries, a critical task for video understanding with applications in video retrieval, summarization, and human-computer interaction. Despite significant progress driven by transformer-based models, existing TSG methods suffer from two key limitations: quantization errors due to temporal downsampling, which misalign segment boundaries, and suboptimal ranking of predictions based on semantic matching rather than localization precision. To address these challenges, we propose the Adaptive Boundary Refinement and Ranking (ABRR) framework, a novel, model-agnostic post-processing approach that enhances the performance of any TSG model without retraining. ABRR integrates three innovative components: (1) Temporal Distribution Smoothing, which mitigates noise in predicted score distributions using Gaussian kernel convolution; (2) Boundary Refinement via Optimal Transport, which leverages the 2-Wasserstein distance and Sinkhorn iterations to align coarse segment boundaries with true temporal moments, grounded in Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport theory; and (3) Quality-Driven Re-Ranking, which reorders predictions using a composite score balancing localization precision and semantic relevance. By correcting quantization errors and prioritizing accurately localized segments, ABRR achieves substantial improvements over state-of-the-art TSG models. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, including Charades-STA, ActivityNet Captions, and QVHighlights, demonstrate consistent gains at stringent IoU thresholds (e.g., IoU=0.7), alongside enhanced ranking performance. The framework's computational efficiency and compatibility with existing models make it a versatile and impactful solution for real-world TSG applications.
authors: Xiang Fang, Wanlong Fang, Junhao Dong, Daizong Liu

papers.abstract: AI coding agents can now construct scientific workflows, but operating them on shared cyberinfrastructure (CI) raises problems that code generation does not solve. Agents need current knowledge of the workflow system and its execution sites and access to the runtime state of distributed executions, while facilities need to attribute every agent action to a user and bound it by that user's privileges. We present PegasusAI Studio, an AI-assisted science gateway built on the Pegasus and HTCondor stack. Studio makes CI legible to agents by projecting one facility-curated knowledge base into the native configuration of several coding agents, by introspecting workflow interfaces and execution sites, and by grounding diagnosis in workflow and scheduler telemetry. Agent actions operate within a trust envelope that combines federated authentication, per-user execution environments and scheduler credentials, provider-neutral model access, observability, and approval controls for state-changing actions. The same application runs as a JupyterHub-based gateway on a research cloud and as an Open OnDemand application on HPC systems. We evaluate Studio through case studies of legacy CASA weather workflow modernization, a gravitational-wave reanalysis, an EEG analysis built with an open-weight model, and an Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) M87 image reconstruction that recovered from two failed runs to a zero-failure execution. The evaluation establishes that these mechanisms operate as designed.
authors: Komal Thareja, Mats Rynge, Berent Aldikacti, Angelina Ju, Ian Lumsden, Anirban Mandal, Rajiv Mayani, Kin Wai Ng, Hamza Safri, Michael Stealey, Sai Swaminathan, Michela Taufer, Karan Vahi, Michael Zink, Ewa Deelman
bullets: Addresses the gap between AI-generated workflow code and safe, observable execution on shared scientific infrastructure.
Projects a curated knowledge base into multiple coding agents and introspects workflow interfaces and execution sites.
Grounds agent diagnosis in workflow and scheduler telemetry for distributed-run awareness.
Constrains actions through federated identity, per-user environments and credentials, observability, and approval controls.
Case studies across scientific workflows, including EHT M87 reconstruction, show the mechanisms operating as designed, including recovery from two failed runs to a zero-failure execution.

Model access goes through a provider-neutral gateway with a prompt guard, and usage telemetry flows to a collector inside the platform.

The home page offers four starting actions and four example requests that each hand a prompt to the assistant, and a link that starts the guided tour.

Figure 4: The run panel of a workflow project in Studio, here for a streamflow workflow the assistant built from one chat prompt. The settings (gauge list, lookback window, retry policy, minimum number of gauges, and an optional site catalog) are derived from the generator’s argparse interface by abstract-syntax-tree introspection, without executing user code. Every field, default, and help string comes from the interface the agent wrote. The workflow (five stream gauges fetched, analyzed, and combined) was built from one chat prompt, and the chat transcript on the right is the agent explaining the fix that made this run succeed after an earlier failure. Node colors track live scheduler state (succeeded, running, pending, failed, held).

Figure 8: The help card. After a failed workflow has been re-run and the rerun has finished, Studio asks one question at the point where the answer is meaningful: did the assistant’s suggestion fix it? Here the EEG workflow of Section 8.5 succeeded on its fourth run after the assistant diagnosed the earlier failure. papers.abstract: We studied domain shift in adult elbow fracture classification from radiographs when training on a large public dataset and deploying on a small, institution-specific dataset (UofL). We implemented a domain-adversarial neural network (DANN) to align feature distributions across source (MURA) and target (UofL) domains while optimizing fracture classification. A pretrained convolutional backbone was adapted to grayscale inputs; the task head predicts fracture presence, and a gradient-reversal-based domain head encourages domain-invariant features via adversarial learning. We compared four settings: (1) Source-only, (2) Target-only (limited labels), (3) Naive merge (pooled training), and (4) DANN (MURA to UofL). Evaluation on UofL test data uses AUC-ROC, and accuracy. DANN outperformed Source-only and Naive merge baselines by reducing domain bias without overfitting to the small target set. Ablations showed that progressive adversarial weight, dataset-size-aware domain loss, and domain-balanced sampling improved stability and target performance. Results demonstrated that domain alignment is a practical path to robust clinical generalization from public to local data.
authors: M. Bolhassani, W. Furtado, D. Duvall, MJ Negahdar, J. Joshi, S. Contractor, A. Amini

papers.abstract: Transmitting LoRA adapters to rollout workers can bottleneck distributed on-policy post-training over bandwidth-constrained networks. Lowering the training rank may limit the capacity a workload needs, while adaptive optimizer updates are difficult to compress. Rollout workers can instead reconstruct updates from gradients by maintaining replicated optimizer states. We introduce HiLo, a compressor-agnostic framework that replaces parameter transmission with compressed gradient dissemination and local optimizer replay. By applying the same decoded gradients, the learner and workers maintain consistent policy states at the same version under reproducible execution. We further develop Spar, a budget-aware gradient compressor that combines spectral truncation, adaptive rank allocation and error feedback to decouple training rank from communication cost. Experiments across on-policy distillation and reward-guided post-training show that HiLo with Spar maintains learning quality close to full synchronization while transmitting as little as 1.6% of the adapter bytes, and accelerates end-to-end updates by up to $2.2\times$ under bandwidth constraints.
authors: Shenghui Li, Li Ju, Thiemo Voigt

figures.caption: Figure 3: Optimizer robustness on Countdown-4 at k = 1. HiLo + Spar is the only compressed method that stays within 3 pass@4 points of Full Sync across all four optimizers, while competing methods suffer substantial degradation under certain optimizers.

Figure 4: Per-update communication payload and pass@4 on Countdown-4. HiLo + Spar (k = 1) sends 62× fewer bytes than full adapter synchronization and 17× fewer than the strongest lossless delta codec, at comparable accuracy. Payload ratios are relative to HiLo; the lossless methods reproduce Full Sync exactly and share its accuracy.

Figure 1: HiLo with the Spar compression backend. (a) The learner compresses error-corrected LoRA-factor gradients and broadcasts zt. The learner and rollout workers decode the same gradient and apply the same optimizer transition, maintaining matching parameters and optimizer states under the conditions in §3.1. (b) Spar extracts spectra through small Gram eigendecompositions, greedily allocates communication ranks under a global factor-payload budget, and packs low-rank factors for transmission. Spectra and ranks are illustrative; the Gram construction shown is for aj ≥ bj , with the other case symmetric.

Figure 5: Left: lockstep seconds per update as the number of rollout workers N grows behind one learner GPU whose 1 Gbps uplink is shared by unicast, with the global batch fixed at 16 prompts × 8 rollouts. Figure 6: Fraction of the error-corrected gradient energy ∥ht∥2 that each compressor ships per step, averaged over updates 1–300 of the Qwen3-1.7B KK runs; bars are means over three seeds with sample standard deviations, labels in percent. All compressors send the same number of bytes at each rank.

Figure 7: Countdown-4 pass@4 at update 200 against bytes per update for Full Sync every K updates and HiLo + Spar at every update (k=1, 2, 4), with the recipe of Table 1 and one seed. Between full synchronizations, actors keep sampling from the last shipped adapter. The dotted line marks the HiLo rank-1 payload, which Full Sync matches at K=62.

Table 1: Held-out accuracy (%) on KK (update 300) and Countdown-4 (update 200), mean ± s.d. over three seeds. Payload is relative to fully synchronizing the rank-64 adapter. Low-rank LoRA reduces the training rank to k, whereas all HiLo variants keep rank 64 and compress only the communicated gradients; a fractional k denotes a global byte budget. Delta uses error feedback to compress post-optimizer changes at the same payload; the learner adopts the compressed weights, so workers keep no optimizer state.

A rank-one truncation that loses nothing on the gradient discards 60–80% of the update’s energy.
Table 2: Spar ablation on Countdown-4 at matched payload (AdamW; 5 seeds at k=1, 3 at k=2). c/n: c of n seeds collapsed and are excluded. Bold marks the best compressed variant per column.

All compressors run as shadows on the same Full Sync gradients, and only steps containing every listed diagnostic are retained (200 paired steps). Spar allocates its budget by raw gradient energy; the AdamW-metric variants allocate by the moment-normalized update instead. Bold marks the lowest error per rank.

Each step sketches every factor gradient along its long side with a fresh seeded random sign matrix, keeps RowAdam state and applies the low-rank update; the sketch rank matches the payload (17 for a 1024×64 factor). Predicted-KL step control is not used, so the learning rate is swept. Energy is the mean fraction of the gradient energy each update retains, in the random sketch for LoGRA and in the shipped directions of the error-corrected gradient for Spar. c/n: c of n seeds collapsed and are excluded.

papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of foundation models has transformed computer vision, yet their adaptation to medical imaging, particularly purpose built foundation models for spatio temporal echocardiography videos, remains limited. In this work, we explore the feasibility of fine tuning a pretrained foundation model for video (TimeSformer) for automated diagnosis of reduced ejection fraction heart failure (HFrEF) from apical four chamber videos. The model is finetuned on the publicly available RVENet A4C dataset with a phase aware clip generation strategy that captures complementary systolic and diastolic dynamics. We employ divided space time attention, layer wise learning rate decay, and multi clip inference to enhance robustness under limited data. Experimental results show that full fine tuning of the proposed model outperforms classifier only tuning and a 3D CNN baseline. These findings highlight the potential of leveraging foundation video models for echocardiography based heart failure diagnosis and motivates further domain adaptation studies in medical imaging.
authors: Mahyar Bolhassani, Tijana Geroski, Narayana S. Singam, Amir Amini

papers.abstract: Serving large language models at high concurrency with long contexts requires KV-cache capacity and attention bandwidth that grow with the decode pool. Existing parallelization strategies trade one against the other: data parallelism replicates model weights, limiting KV capacity; tensor parallelism stops scaling attention at the model's KV-head count and pushes dense collectives across nodes; and decode context parallelism (DCP) recovers capacity by sharding the sequence but adds cross-node aggregation of partial attention results. We observe that during decode, dense layers and attention scale differently: dense layers amortize weight reads across the batch and run efficiently within a single NVLink domain, whereas attention cost grows with every active request's KV cache. We present Decode Token Parallelism (TKNP), a decode-pool architecture that decouples weight placement from attention ownership. TKNP distributes a single model copy across nodes in balanced layer blocks. The active node holding a block executes its projections and MLP for the full batch using intra-node tensor parallelism, while every node computes attention for its own requests against locally resident KV cache. This extends request-local attention across nodes without replicating weights: only current-token activations cross the network, dense all-reduces remain within NVLink, and attention requires no cross-node merging of partial results. Implemented in vLLM and evaluated on Llama 3.1 405B and Nemotron-4 340B on up to 64 H100 GPUs, TKNP improves completion throughput for long-context, high-concurrency workloads by up to 1.7$\times$ over DCP and by up to 2.06$\times$ over data parallelism at matched GPU count.
authors: Susav Shrestha, Brad Settlemyer, Narasimha Reddy

figures.caption: Figure 2. Token Parallel architecture within a layer block. TP partitions KV heads within each node; TKNP partitions requests across nodes. The active root executes QKV and output projections and the MLP for the full batch, while all nodes compute attention for their own requests using local KV cache. Scatter/gather exchanges current-token activations over Ethernet or InfiniBand; dense all-reduces remain within NVLink. Four GPUs per node are shown for illustration. Weight storage on attention workers is omitted; the active root changes with the block.

Figure 6. Balanced weight placement and changing execution roles. Each node stores one stationary layer block and becomes the active root when that block executes. Other nodes compute attention for their assigned requests. The schematic shows equal-sized blocks; actual boundaries balance weight bytes, including endpoint parameters and quantization differences, to leave similar KV-cache budgets.

Figure 3. Single-layer decode latency for Llama 3.1 405B on H100 GPUs. (a) TP8 sustains relatively stable MLP latency through batch 128, with larger increases at batches 256–512. (b) Attention grows with batch size; TP8, TP16, and TP64 nearly overlap. Both panels use a 0–2 ms latency range; TP1 values above this range are clipped.

Figure 9. Admission waiting, active-request ITL, and average completion latency for Llama 3.1 405B at 64K context on 32 H100 GPUs, with 1K OSL. The x-axis counts all submitted requests; only a capacity-limited subset may be active. (a) Release to first scheduling. (b) Token intervals after the first token, excluding initial queue wait. Figure 12. TKNP sustains its throughput advantage under mixed input lengths. Llama 3.1 405B on 32 H100 GPUs. (a) SLO: arrival-to-completion time per output token ≤100 ms. (b,c) Completion throughput and p95 request completion time under Poisson arrivals and synchronized bursts.

papers.abstract: AI agents can write code, use scientific software, and revise computational workflows, opening new possibilities for MRI research. Effective assistance requires connecting acquisition physics, data conventions, specialized tools, and scientific validation. We present MRFoundry, an open-source, extensible package that connects MRI knowledge to agent actions and output checks. Project-local memory preserves decisions and evidence, while reviewed contributions allow researchers to improve shared guidance. Researcher-supervised examples demonstrate skill-guided sequence auditing and acquired-data reconstruction, connecting tool use, output checks, and documented decisions. Alongside MRFoundry, we introduce MRI Agent Bench to compare agents with and without the package across models and MRI task domains. Across 240 paired Core evaluations spanning 24 task types and ten models, all-checks-passed completion increased from 67.5% without MRFoundry to 78.3% with it. Across 134 Hard pairs, completion increased from 36.6% to 44.8%. MRFoundry makes MRI workflow expertise available as reusable guidance that researchers can inspect, adapt, and extend within existing agent and scientific software environments. MRFoundry is openly available at https://github.com/KeWang0622/MRFoundry.
authors: Ke Wang, Atakan Topcu, Hossein Momeni, Molin Zhang

papers.abstract: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipelines struggle with severely underexposed images, producing unstable colors, floating artifacts, and incomplete reconstructions in dark regions. To better account for noise in these low-light observations, RAW images offer a natural basis for noise-aware reconstruction by preserving linear sensor measurements and providing access to noise metadata. We present RetinexGS, a RAW-domain 3DGS framework that combines Retinex-inspired appearance modeling with sensor-informed optimization for low-light novel-view synthesis. We factorize each Gaussian's color into a view-independent base color and a shared, position- and view-dependent modulation field, regularizing the two components separately to constrain appearance learning from noisy observations. We use DNG noise metadata to weight the reconstruction loss for signal-dependent noise, while distortion-aware rendering avoids spatially resampling RAW targets. To address sparse geometry in dark regions, we introduce depth-guided initialization. We evaluate RetinexGS on three public RawNeRF scenes and two custom-captured low-light RAW scenes. With all methods trained on the same RAW inputs for each scene, RetinexGS outperforms LE3D and RawNeRF in mean sRGB PSNR by 2.18 dB and 2.71 dB respectively, across the five scenes, while supporting real-time novel-view rendering.
authors: Yulang Fei, Huaiyuan Weng, Chul Min Yeum

figures.caption: Figure 2: RetinexGS overview. Given noisy low-light RAW images and their DNG metadata, RetinexGS optimizes a Gaussian scene representation through three components. (2) Distortion-aware rasterization renders these colors directly onto the packed RAW grid, where training combines DNG-informed noise weighting, a log-domain reconstruction loss, and appearance regularization. (3) A frozen monocular depth prior supplies additional initialization points through dark-region sampling and distortion-aware unprojection. papers.abstract: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar provides weather-robust sensing and direct Doppler measurements, yet automotive perception pipelines often reduce its output to sparse point clouds or two-dimensional projections, leaving raw range-azimuth-Doppler (RAD) cubes underutilized. Ego motion induces Doppler responses from world-static structures, while Doppler wrapping aliases radial velocities, complicating moving-object detection and velocity estimation. We present RaMOD (Radar-based Moving-Object Detection), a real-time framework for moving-object detection and velocity estimation from raw RAD cubes acquired by a vehicle-mounted single-chip radar. RaMOD explicitly estimates frame-wise ego motion and uses the estimated radar translational velocity to predict the Doppler region of world-static structures and suppress returns within it. It temporally encodes the suppressed cubes into multi-scale features to predict RAD-space boxes with class labels. For each detected object, it predicts radial and forward velocities under raw-Doppler and Doppler-unwrapped hypotheses, together with Doppler-wrapping probabilities. On our BRIDGE-Liv dataset, RaMOD outperforms all compared raw-radar methods across RAD-cube, RA, and RD detection settings, achieving 80.8% cube mAP at IoU 0.30, 15.7 percentage points above the strongest RAD-cube baseline. Velocity MAE is 1.128 m/s, with 99.87% Doppler-wrapping accuracy.
authors: Yuan Fang, Long Zhuang, Lingzi Xing, Xijia Wei, Jingqi Jiang, Fangzhan Shi, Simon Julier, Kevin Chetty

papers.abstract: Recent work has identified a set of emergent symbolic mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in large language models, but it remains unclear what factors drive the emergence of these mechanisms. To address this question, we trained neural networks from scratch on abstract sequence tasks, varying both architectural and data distributional factors, and investigated the effects of these factors on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms. Using representational, attentional, and causal mediation analyses, we first confirmed that transformer-based language models trained from scratch on our task developed symbolic mechanisms. We then found that, across multiple axes of data diversity, greater diversity produced stronger symbolic signatures. Surprisingly, the same signatures emerged in modified transformer architectures and even multilayer perceptrons, indicating that architectural inductive biases are not necessary for the development of symbolic mechanisms. We also observed consistent patterns in an entity-attribute binding task. Together, these findings identify data diversity, not architecture, as the primary driver of emergent symbolic computation in neural networks.
authors: Melody Zixuan Li, Taylor Webb

papers.abstract: Temporal action segmentation (TAS) is commonly trained on large banks of pre-extracted frame features, but storing and replaying those features becomes a practical bottleneck for long-form video, especially in incremental TAS where past-task data must remain available to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. Recent TAS replay and condensation methods reduce this burden, but they rely on dense frame-wise annotations and allocate storage through fixed segment-level structures, limiting their flexibility for long procedural videos whose frame complexity varies substantially over time. We introduce Adaptive Residual-Quantized Variational AutoEncoder (ARQ-VAE), a compact and label-free memory representation for TAS features that learns a discrete residual quantization of frame-level video features and then adaptively truncates the residual chain on a per-frame basis, retaining only the residual prefix that best reconstructs each frame feature. This yields a practical compact feature memory that does not depend on frame-wise labels and can therefore support multiple TAS settings with the same stored representation, while a lightweight fine-tuning stage further improves reconstruction quality for the truncated codes that are actually retained. Across standard TAS benchmarks, ARQ-VAE achieves a substantially improved storage-performance trade-off over prior replay and condensation baselines. On Breakfast, our final representation reduces training-set storage from 28 GB for the original I3D feature bank to 10 MB while retaining strong downstream segmentation performance; with ASFormer, it achieves 71.5 Edit and 51.2 F1@50 in the supervised setting. We further show that the same label-free memory remains effective for incremental and unsupervised TAS. We position ARQ-VAE as a practical memory representation for TAS and a promising direction for broader dataset condensation applications.
authors: Gerard Donahue, Guven Gergerli, Ayush Gupta, Reza Ghoddoosian, Enna Sachdeva, Faizan Siddiqui
bullets: Addresses the storage and replay bottleneck of large frame-feature banks, especially for incremental TAS and long procedural videos.

Requires no frame-wise labels, enabling one shared memory representation across multiple TAS settings.
A lightweight fine-tuning stage improves reconstruction of the truncated codes that are actually stored.
On Breakfast, storage drops from 28 GB to 10 MB while ASFormer achieves 71.5 Edit and 51.2 F1@50 in supervised TAS; the abstract reports improved storage-performance trade-offs over prior baselines.

papers.tldr: ARQ-VAE compresses temporal action segmentation features into adaptive, label-free residual codes, dramatically reducing storage while preserving downstream performance across supervised, incremental, and unsupervised settings.

papers.abstract: A person running a bench experiment works from a printed instruction sheet, tells identical containers apart by the labels written on them, and looks at the bench again before each step. Lab automation usually works the other way around: the procedure is written as a script, and containers stand at fixed positions or carry fiducial markers. We present Curie's Jarvis, a system that lets a robot arm carry out a chemistry experiment on a bench set up for people. It reads the steps from a photo of the printed sheet, finds containers on an ordinary bench with no fixed positions or markers, tells identical-looking containers apart by reading their labels in four camera views, locates its target again before every step, and sets how each step is carried out, including its speed, from what is being handled. On a Franka Panda arm, Curie's Jarvis completed 5 of 5 runs of one protocol from a children's chemistry kit and 4 of 5 runs of another, with no human intervention, and in 160 locates on printed and handwritten labels it identified every container correctly. This brings robots a step closer to doing bench chemistry the way people do.
authors: Rumi Loghmani, Bozhang Song, Victor Alvarado, Aliyah Redding, Amir Barati Farimani

papers.abstract: In remote inference, edge devices transmit high-resolution images over wireless links to a receiver, where an artificial intelligence (AI) model answers task-specific questions about these images to enable reliable decisions. These answers are often determined by a small set of task-causal pixels, such as those of text, whose corruption changes the answer, so these pixels must be delivered with high fidelity. Conventional transmission protects every pixel equally, so it either consumes many resource elements (REs) or corrupts these regions at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). To overcome these limitations, in this paper, a zero-shot, domain-agnostic framework, termed semantic-criticality tiered allocation of resources (STAR), is proposed. In particular, a per-pixel semantic-criticality indicator (SCI) is derived from the attention of a frozen vision-language model, so new tasks and domains are handled by changing only the prompt, without retraining. The resulting task causality-aware resource allocation problem over protection tiers is solved exactly by a threshold rule on the SCI, realized by a coded tier for the task-causal pixels and an uncoded, downsampled base layer for the full image. Simulations over a 5G New Radio link demonstrate that STAR attains a semantic accuracy of at least 0.98 for $E_s/N_0 \geq -4$ dB and, at comparable semantic reliability, reduces the REs of robust coded transmission by 59.5% and 91.5% on factory- and vehicle-monitoring datasets, respectively, the latter without any change to the models. Although a deep joint source-channel coding baseline uses fewer REs at comparable semantic accuracy, it must be retrained with labeled data for every new task or domain.
authors: Albert Shaju, Christo Kurisummoottil Thomas, Mingzhe Chen
bullets: Targets remote image inference where only a small set of task-causal pixels determines the AI answer.
Derives a per-pixel semantic-criticality indicator from a frozen vision-language model, adapting to new tasks or domains through prompts rather than retraining.
Solves tiered resource allocation with an SCI threshold: coded transmission protects critical pixels, while an uncoded downsampled layer carries the full image.
Over a 5G New Radio link, STAR reaches at least 0.98 semantic accuracy for $E_s/N_0 \geq -4$ dB.

At comparable reliability, it reduces resource elements by 59.5% and 91.5% on factory- and vehicle-monitoring datasets, respectively; unlike the joint source-channel baseline, it requires no per-task labeled retraining.

papers.abstract: In this work, we develop an efficient Gauss-Newton optimization approach for finite basis physics-informed neural networks (FBPINNs). The key ingredient is the overlapping domain decomposition architecture of FBPINNs, which localizes the influence of each subnetwork and induces block sparsity in both the residual Jacobian and the corresponding Gauss-Newton matrix. We characterize this structure and exploit it through sparse automatic differentiation, using graph coloring to partition structurally orthogonal Jacobian columns or rows. This reduces differentiation costs and memory requirements while preserving all structurally nonzero derivative information. The resulting compressed Jacobian representations allow us to assemble the Gauss-Newton system directly in block-sparse form, enabling the use of sparse direct solvers and preconditioned iterative methods. In this way, the otherwise expensive second-order optimization problem is reduced to scalable sparse linear algebra. We demonstrate the approach on multiscale PDEs, where accurate approximation requires rich neural network parametrizations and large numbers of collocation points. Numerical experiments show that our block-sparse Gauss-Newton method attains high accuracy and substantially accelerates optimization relative to first-order baselines while remaining computationally tractable for large problem sizes.
authors: Denis Korolev, Adrian Hill, Jeeeun Lee

papers.abstract: Efficient robotic 3D reconstruction requires selecting views that contribute new surface measurements with few physical captures. Pretrained world models can guide this choice, but a predicted surface may not produce valid depth measurements under the operating conditions of the deployed sensor. We present a deployment adaptation methodology for next-best-view selection that learns a sensor-return adapter from limited local calibration data while keeping the pretrained predictor fixed. The adapter estimates measurement dropout over each predicted surface, allowing the selection method to favor views likely to fill gaps in the measured reconstruction. In a real-robot experiment with a structured-light sensor, the adapted method achieves higher measured surface coverage with 60% fewer captures than nominal selection. The adapted method recovers a surface region that the nominal method repeatedly targets but fails to measure. These results suggest that robots can reuse pretrained predictive models while adapting their decisions to local operating conditions in data-scarce environments.
authors: Nikita Sarawgi, Omey M. Manyar, Satyandra K. Gupta

papers.abstract: We introduce Latent Barrier Steering (LBS), a hierarchical semantic-to-path framework for safe flow-matching-based generative planning. Existing control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filters for diffusion and flow-matching planners act locally on generated samples, either during sampling or after prediction. Such repair is effective for small violations, but can struggle when a new constraint blocks the whole selected behavior mode rather than merely perturbing it locally. LBS decouples behavior selection from path certification through two coordinated interventions: it first steers the generator's behavior latent toward rollouts with larger safety margin, then decodes the steered latent and applies a path-space CBF quadratic program (QP) only for residual violations. We show that latent steering increases the margin available to the path-space corrector, yielding finite-time recovery guarantees and reduced correction burden. Experiments across navigation and robot end-effector planning tasks show that LBS preserves safety while improving goal reaching and reducing correction burden compared with path-level safety filters.
authors: Renhao Zhang, Mingzhe Li, Bruno Castro da Silva

figures.caption: Figure 2: Experimental domains and test-time safety constraints. Each row shows one planning domain: 2D point-navigation, Maze2D, and Franka 3D end-effector planning. The first column visualizes the original scene and multimodal demonstration dataset, where multiple behaviors can reach the same goal. The remaining columns show three test-time safety constraints imposed on the same pretrained planner. Green circles denote starts, orange stars denote goals, and red shaded regions denote unsafe sets. These constraints test whether a method can preserve safety and goal reaching when certification requires more than local path repair.

Figure 3: Latent steering provides the warm start needed for path-space repair. Stage I performs behavior-level selection by steering the latent and changing the decoded rollout before certification; Stage II then applies path-level CBF repair to remove residual violations. The second row removes Stage I and applies the same path-space correction directly, corresponding to SAFEFLOWMATCHER. Without the latent-steered warm start, the local corrector remains tied to the original rollout and fails to produce a goal-reaching safe path. With Stage I, the corrected trajectory starts from a better behavior and Stage II only needs to repair the remaining local violation.

Figure 1: Latent Barrier Steering separates behavior selection from path repair. A vanilla flow-matching planner may generate a goal-reaching but unsafe rollout under a new constraint. A path-space CBF corrector such as SAFEFLOWMATCHER can enforce safety locally, but may produce a trajectory that is safe while no longer reaching the goal when the selected behavior mode is blocked. LBS first steers the behavior latent from z0 to z+ toward a safer rollout, then applies path-level CBF repair only for residual violations, yielding a trajectory that is both safe and goal-reaching.

papers.abstract: Children's earliest years are a period of intense social learning, during which meaning is built through gaze, gesture, and physical contact. Yet, this critical aspect of social interaction remains under-evaluated in multimodal video understanding, as existing benchmarks prioritize the conversation-driven interactions of adults. We address this gap with \bench ($\textbf{N}$aturalistic $\textbf{E}$arly-childhood $\textbf{S}$ocial in$\textbf{T}$eractions), the first child-centric benchmark for nonverbal social reasoning. \bench comprises \totalvids manually annotated clips ($\sim$12s) curated for diversity across naturalistic settings, cultural contexts, and developmental stages. Beyond a lack of data, targeted model improvement in this domain is hindered by coarse evaluation schemas that conflate basic perception with higher-order reasoning. To resolve this, \bench introduces a compositional schema that builds atomic interaction cues into progressive levels of social reasoning: contextual, behavioral, interpersonal, and open-ended descriptions. Extensive analysis of state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs) reveals a stark performance collapse: despite strong contextual recognition, models exhibit substantial gaps in decoding precise behavioral and interpersonal cues. We trace these failures to specific biases, including poor consequence grounding and temporal sensitivity. Finally, we ground \bench in real-world applications by evaluating VLMs using domain adaptation strategies. Ultimately, \bench provides a rigorous testbed for advancing socially grounded artificial intelligence in early childhood. Project page: https://laubravo.github.io/nest_website/.

papers.abstract: Accurate and timely identification of road closures is critical for large-scale navigation and logistics systems, yet remains challenging due to the need to jointly reason over visual evidence, spatial context, and road network topology. Existing approaches either rely on manual map updates or focus on detecting closure-related objects without resolving which road segment is affected. In this work, we introduce a unified multimodal and multitask framework that jointly performs road closure classification (no, partial, complete) and road segment association within a single learning architecture. Our model integrates graph-structured map data, satellite imagery augmented with projected street-level detections, and street-view images using modality-specific encoders and cross-modal transformer attention, enabling explicit reasoning over visual cues and network topology. Evaluated on nearly 20K real-world scenarios collected from a large-scale commercial vehicle fleet, our approach achieves 72.7% closure classification accuracy and 60% road segment association accuracy, outperforming frontier vision-language models by over 28 percentage points on closure classification while being over 4,000x smaller and 100x faster at inference. Extensive ablations demonstrate the importance of cross-modal attention, edge-aware pooling, and graph message passing for accurate geospatial reasoning. This work establishes the first benchmark for joint road closure classification and segment-level attribution, and shows that task-specific architectural inductive biases substantially outperform general-purpose multimodal models for structured geospatial understanding.

papers.abstract: Expert parallelism (EP) shards the experts of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer across GPUs, so every MoE layer requires two all-to-all communications, namely dispatch and combine. Compared with training, inference processes relatively few tokens per GPU at a time, and at small batch sizes fixed costs that do not grow with the number of tokens, rather than data movement, dominate the latency. We present NVLinkOneSided, a one-sided EP all-to-all for GPUs within a single NVLink domain. Each source rank pushes its tokens, without first exchanging metadata, into rank-major buffers on the target GPUs, and the grouped GEMMs read them in place instead of from a per-expert copy. We provide two protocols for the synchronization that the communication requires, namely Fence and Sentinel, for high-throughput and low-latency scenarios respectively. On Blackwell GPUs, NVLinkOneSided completes dispatch and combine 1.2-3.0$\times$ faster than DeepEP, with the largest speedups at small batch sizes. The resulting MoE layer is up to 2.4$\times$ faster than DeepEP with DeepGEMM. It even outperforms the fused DeepGEMM MegaMoE at up to 128 tokens per GPU, making it still competitive for decoding. We expose NVLinkOneSided through a modular interface, so that it is agnostic to the activation quantization format, decoupled from the MoE compute backend and easy to integrate into inference frameworks.
authors: Bo Li, Chulian Zhang, Or Biri, Anthony Chang, Anton Korzh, Noam Duvdevani, XingFei Xi, Daniel Stokes, Zhenhuan Chen, Ludwig Schneider, Artem Y. Polyakov, Julien Demouth, Chandler Zhou

Sources push tokens directly into rank-major buffers on target GPUs, which grouped GEMMs read in place.
Provides Fence and Sentinel synchronization protocols for high-throughput and low-latency use cases.
On Blackwell GPUs, dispatch and combine are 1.2–3.0× faster than DeepEP, while the MoE layer is up to 2.4× faster with DeepGEMM.
A modular interface supports different quantization formats, compute backends, and inference frameworks.

Dispatch: each source rank stores its tokens into its own region of the dispatch workspaces of the target ranks and records the target rank and slot of each selection; T1 selects E0 and E1, both on R0, so it takes one slot there and its second selection records no slot (−1). MoE compute turns the tokens from each source rank into partial results at the same slots of the combine workspace. Combine: each source rank loads the partial results from the target ranks and slots recorded in dispatch and adds them. White slots are empty.

The indexing kernel turns the expert ids of the received slots into per-expert lists of slot indices (empty slots 3, 6 and 7 carry invalid ids); FC1 gathers tokens through these lists and multiplies them by the expert weights, FC2 multiplies the FC1 output by its own weights, and finalize adds the outputs of each token into its slot of the combine workspace.

papers.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) grounding maps a screenshot and a natural-language instruction to the screen location where an agent should act. Zoomed views can reveal small targets but may lose the context needed to identify them. We introduce GroundCascade, a training-free controller that uses agreement between a grounder's full-screen and zoomed predictions to decide when to consult a complementary model. It selects between zoomed predictions while preserving corroborated full-screen locations. An optional Finalizer predicts from an unmarked joint crop when disagreement remains (Full); omitting it yields the two-stage Selective variant. GroundCascade reaches 85.33% on ScreenSpot-Pro with Indeed-UI-32B/8B/32B and 88.43% on the visible-target OSWorld-G-Refined subset with Qwen3.6-27B/3.8-27B/3.8-27B, gains of 2.66 and 2.35 percentage points over the stronger standalone two-pass grounder. On UI-Vision, GroundCascade reaches 72.20% category-balanced accuracy, with Selective slightly higher at 72.28%. Across these three evaluations, GroundCascade in Full mode uses 2.42-2.73 calls per request, 31-39% fewer than unconditionally acquiring both models' two-pass predictions. At matched second-model call budgets, selective acquisition gains 1.52-2.56 points over standalone Two-pass, compared with 0.22-0.69 points from stratified random acquisition. GroundCascade leads the official ScreenSpot-Pro leaderboard and exceeds reported GUI-specialist comparisons on OSWorld-G-Refined and UI-Vision, subject to differences in external evaluation protocols.
authors: Adrian Phoulady, Hady Ahmady Phoulady

papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models can render a photorealistic analog clock but cannot control the time it displays. Across four pretrained models, fewer than 1% of generated clocks place both hands within 6 degrees of the requested time; the models instead collapse onto visually dominant configurations such as the canonical 10:10 pose. The same failure appears when a specific fraction of a circular object is requested, where models return complete or conventionally sliced objects. We observe that these two failures share a geometric structure: both target quantities can be parameterized by angular variables. We introduce a geometric token encoding framework that conditions generation directly on these angles. Each angular component is encoded as a periodic sine-cosine feature and projected into a role-specific token embedding that is injected into the prompt before a frozen text encoder. To spatially ground these tokens without requiring localization input at inference, we introduce Stochastic Localization Relaxation (SLR), which stochastically relaxes attention supervision from component-level to object-level to unconstrained localization during training. For clocks, we additionally introduce a hand-swap preference objective that discourages assigning the correct angles to the wrong hand roles. On analog clocks our method reaches 63-78% Acc@6 degrees across evaluation methods, compared with below 1% for the baselines. On circular-fraction generation, it achieves 89.5% Acc@0.10, while maintaining 88.8% on unseen object categories and 84.9% on unseen target values, compared with roughly 20% for pretrained baselines.
authors: Furkan G\"uzelant, Basavaraj Sunagad, Aysegul Dundar, Adam Kortylewski

figures.caption: Figure 2. Left: Overview of our geometric token encoding framework, illustrated for clock-time control. The target clock time (h,m) or fraction-sector boundaries are encoded as sinusoidal pairs and mapped through the projection network P to produce role-specific geometric tokens eh, em (or es, ee) injected into the prompt before the frozen text encoder. Both tasks share the same MLP architecture and condition a LoRA-adapted SD 2.1 denoising U-Net. Right: Stochastic Localization Relaxation (SLR). Training samples one of three localization regimes (55/30/15%): component-level CALL using component boxes, object-level CALL using a shared object box, and unconstrained standard cross-attention. No localization input is required at inference.

Figure 5. Fraction generation. Base models frequently produce complete objects or conventional slices, whereas our model accurately follows the requested fraction for both pizza and pie across five target values.
Figure 4. Clock generation. Under the same random seeds, baseline models often produce common clock configurations instead of the requested time, whereas our model accurately follows the target time.

Figure 7. Distribution of generated analog-clock times for pretrained text-to-image models. Several models exhibit strong modes near canonical configurations, particularly 10:10, despite variation in the requested target time.

Figure 9. In-scene generation with no bounding-box supervision at inference. (a) Clock time control across diverse room scenes. (b) Food-fraction control in top-down food settings. In both domains the model accurately tracks the requested geometric quantity (time / fraction) while maintaining scene coherence and object placement.

Figure 8. Qualitative comparison of the original periodic encoding and the augmented encoding with the scalar fraction f near the angular boundaries. The periodic encoding produces small sectors near 0◦ but may generate narrow slices even for complete-sector targets (360◦), reflecting its endpoint ambiguity. Adding f distinguishes the endpoints and enables complete-object generation, but can produce oversized sectors for small target angles (1◦–5◦). Results are shown for pizza, pie, and cake.

Figure 6. Generalization to unseen fraction objects. Our model follows the requested arc fraction across four object categories not seen during training (rows) and four target fractions (columns), without additional fine-tuning.

Figure 3. Dataset construction for the two domains. Top: Procedurally rendered clocks are restyled using ControlNet conditioned on Canny edges while preserving exact hand angles. Bottom: Complete circular objects generated by Flux.1 are segmented and arc-masked according to the target fraction.

papers.abstract: Effective search and rescue (SAR) operations require autonomous systems capable of coordinating multiple heterogeneous agents, adapting to dynamic hazards, and aligning with human mission intent. Existing language-guided reinforcement learning (RL) methods primarily focus on single-agent instruction following and lack mechanisms for team-level coordination in complex, partially observable environments. This paper presents a Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework based on Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LG-HRL) that integrates natural-language understanding, hierarchical policy decomposition, and a shared cognitive workspace to achieve cohesive multi-agent behavior in SAR scenarios. Human instructions are interpreted by a large language model (LLM) and transformed into structured semantic cues that guide high-level strategy selection and role assignment across UAV and UGV agents. A formal Language-Grounded Multi-Agent Hierarchical Decision Process (LG-MAHDP) is introduced to model the interplay between semantic grounding, hierarchical control, and distributed coordination. Comprehensive experiments in a simulated disaster environment show that LG-HRL improves learning speed by 2.3 times, increases coordination coherence by 37%, and enhances subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance by 46% and 31%, respectively. The system achieves 20-30% higher victim rescue rates, demonstrates emergent role specialization, and adapts immediately to human verbal updates. Ablation studies confirm that both the shared cognitive workspace and language grounding are critical to overall system performance. Overall, this work establishes a new paradigm for language-guided multi-agent SAR robotics, demonstrating that semantic grounding combined with hierarchical reasoning enables safer, more efficient, and more interpretable autonomous rescue operations.
authors: Sepideh Ravanbakhsh, Hamidreza Moradi
bullets: Addresses the lack of team-level coordination in language-guided RL for partially observable search-and-rescue environments.
Uses an LLM to convert human instructions into semantic cues for strategy selection and agent role assignment.
Introduces the LG-MAHDP formalism to model language grounding, hierarchical decisions, and distributed coordination.
In simulated disaster scenarios, the system reports faster learning, stronger coordination, improved subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance, and 20–30% higher victim rescue rates.
Ablations identify language grounding and the shared cognitive workspace as critical components; results are limited to simulated SAR settings.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework for Language-Grounded Hierarchical Decision-Making. Left: Verbal input 𝑣from the human operator is processed by the LLM-driven Context Extractor to produce contextual features 𝐶. These features, together with observations 𝑠from the Environment and information priorities 𝑀from the Information Space, are integrated within the Strategic Decision Engine (SDE). The Attention Space refines strategy selection by mapping semantic cues and priority information via Ψ(𝐶,𝑀). The SDE outputs high-level strategies 𝜔, which the Worker modules translate into low-level actions 𝛼executed within the Environment. The resulting observations are fed back into the shared workspace, enabling continuous learning and adaptation. Right: Comparison of LLM outputs with and without retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in simulated SAR operations, showing that RAG enhances contextual precision, hazard annotation, and task-specific semantic structure in generated outputs.

Fig. 5. Coverage-efficiency comparison across models. Grouped bar chart showing (from left to right) coverage ratio, revisit index, and dead-zone ratio for Flat RL, HRL, and LG-HRL. LG-HRL attains the highest coverage and lowest dead-zone ratio while also reducing redundant revisits, demonstrating the most efficient spatial exploration among all methods.

Fig. 7. Ablation results for core components. Normalized system performance under removal of key architectural elements. Removing any component reduces performance, with language grounding and the shared cognitive workspace contributing most strongly to mission success.

Fig. 8. Agent Trajectories Under LG-HRL Control. The plot above shows how UAV and UGV agents behave when guided by the proposed Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LGHRL) system. UAV trajectories (blue) exhibit broad-area scouting patterns characteristic of airborne reconnaissance, while UGV trajectories (green) remain grounded and focus on directed paths suitable for close-range navigation and victim retrieval. Hazard zones are denoted by red “X” markers, and both agents demonstrate safe, deliberate navigation around these areas.

Fig. 3. Coordination Entropy Reduction Across Training. Coordination entropy trajectories for Flat RL, HRL, and LG-HRL across 2000 training episodes. LG-HRL exhibits the fastest decline in entropy and stabilizes at the lowest value, indicating efficient division of labor and emergent cooperative behavior. HRL shows moderate improvements, while Flat RL continues to exhibit high entropy due to the absence of semantic grounding and hierarchical structure.

Fig. 6. Victim rescue performance across models. Comparison of rescue success rates for Flat RL, HRL, and LG-HRL across five disaster scenarios. LG-HRL consistently achieves the highest rescue rates (88–92%), surpassing HRL and Flat RL by a substantial margin.

Fig. 4. Impact of language grounding on strategic accuracy. Comparison of HRL without language grounding (yellow bars) and LG-HRL with language grounding (blue bars) across three metrics: subgoal-selection accuracy, hazard-avoidance success, and responsiveness to natural-language mission updates. Language grounding yields substantial gains in all three dimensions, highlighting the value of LLM-based semantic guidance for safe and aligned multi-agent decision-making.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models now exceed 95% success on the LIBERO simulation benchmark, yet it remains unclear how much of this performance requires generalization beyond the training demonstrations. In this work, we show that retrieving nearby demonstrations and reusing their action chunks achieves a success rate of 91.7 % on LIBERO without policy training. Under LIBERO-Plus perturbations, retrieval shows the smallest drop of all evaluated policies. Across nine publicly available VLAs, fine-tuning mostly makes the vision-language backbone a better retrieval key, and the actions of the VLAs remain close to the demonstrations. In addition, we introduce Local Action Consistency (LAC), an offline metric that measures whether nearby observations in representation space are also associated with similar future actions. We show that LAC tracks the success rate of retrieval and can guide the training of a retrieval key. Our evaluation and source code are available at https://github.com/sereact/lerobot_knn.
authors: Denis Grachev, Damien LaRocque, Omar Moured
bullets: Retrieving nearby demonstrations and reusing their action chunks performs strongly without policy training.
Retrieval experiences the smallest performance drop among evaluated policies under LIBERO-Plus perturbations.
Across nine public VLAs, fine-tuning mainly improves the vision-language backbone as a retrieval key; predicted actions remain close to demonstrations.
The proposed Local Action Consistency (LAC) metric correlates with retrieval success and can guide retrieval-key training.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are typically evaluated by whether they produce correct answers, but correctness alone does not reveal whether their outputs are supported by the right visual evidence. We introduce VIGOR, a benchmark for evaluating VIsually GrOunded Rationales in MLLMs. VIGOR represents visual rationales as explicit concepts paired with pixel-level groundings, covering multiple abstraction levels including low-level visual properties, intermediate structures, objects, parts and high-level motion, relations. To construct VIGOR at scale, we develop an automatic annotation framework that reuses existing dense supervision when available and generates missing concept groundings through proposal-based annotation followed by conservative multimodal verification. Using VIGOR, we evaluate whether MLLMs "look at what they say" by comparing model-derived visual evidence for each expressed concept against annotated ground-truth rationales. Our results show that current MLLMs exhibit limited visual rationale correctness and reveal distinct grounding failures across concept levels. VIGOR provides a benchmark and scalable data construction pipeline for studying whether MLLM outputs are supported by appropriate visual evidence. Code is available at https://github.com/deep-real/VIGOR
authors: Yanlin Chen, Tang Li, Xi Peng

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the VIGOR annotation pipeline. VIGOR builds a hierarchical concept vocabulary from heterogeneous source data, proposes masks with multiple annotation tools when source masks are unavailable, verifies candidate masks through MLLM voting, and combines verified masks with reusable source annotations to produce pixel-level visual rationales.

Figure 8: Qualitative examples of rationale failures on VIGOR. Models can attend to incorrect regions, cover only part of the ground-truth evidence, or produce diffuse attention maps, showing that generated concepts are often not fully grounded in the appropriate visual rationale.

Figure 4: Human evaluation of VIGOR annotation quality across concept levels. Most annotations are rated as Agree or Strongly Agree, indicating consistently high reliability of the propose-thenverify pipeline across different concept levels.

Figure 1: Illustration of the double correctness problem. Although the model produces a correct description by mentioning “traffic lights,” its visual rationale is misaligned with the actual traffic light regions, showing the gap between output correctness and rationale correctness.
Figure 5: AP and Recall distributions across concept levels on VIGOR. The large recall gap, especially for scene concepts, shows that model rationales often cover only partial supporting evidence.

Figure 7: Relationship between rationale correctness and hallucination benchmark performance across 16 MLLMs. The positive correlation indicates that models with better visual rationale grounding also tend to achieve stronger hallucination robustness. Hallucination performances are sourced from [51].
Figure 6: Layer-wise overall AP on VIGOR by normalized layer depth, averaged across all models.
Figure 3: Various distribution of selected annotation sources across concept levels. No single annotation tool is sufficient for all concepts, motivating the use of a heterogeneous proposal toolset.

papers.abstract: Attention, the core of language models, is a digital calculation over tokens: an exponential selects them, a division normalizes and a positional code sets the order. We show that attention can instead emerge from the synchronization of a receiver with its context tokens. Each past token is an oscillator whose state carries its content and whose frequency drifts with its age. The present token selects them by content, aligning an antenna with its query, and by position, setting the frequency of a receiver with its dial. Solving Kuramoto's problem for this receiver yields an attention layer in closed form with two phases: above a critical coupling set by the context, the receiver locks and its weights normalize; below it, it stays silent and its weights sum to less than one. Trained networks use both phases to select, abstain and count, fail where the theory predicts and keep reading far beyond the training length. Each part of attention finds its place in one device, a radio head: it tunes in to what to hear and when, and stays silent when nothing relevant is on air.
authors: Llu\'is Arola-Fern\'andez, Aissam Khadraoui, Alex Arenas
bullets: Models past tokens as oscillators whose content and age determine their state and frequency.
Uses Kuramoto synchronization to derive a closed-form attention layer with normalized weights above a critical coupling threshold.
Below the threshold, the receiver abstains, producing weights that sum to less than one.
Trained networks exploit both phases to select, abstain, and count, and continue reading beyond their training length.
The theory predicts observed failure cases, though the abstract does not specify quantitative results or evaluation settings.

papers.abstract: Learning-based decentralized collision avoidance must remain reliable under state-estimation uncertainty and heterogeneous agent dynamics. Existing methods typically address these factors through training-domain variation or by exposing uncertainty and capability estimates to the policy at runtime. However, both leave the policy to infer how these quantities should alter the physical separation required for safe interaction, which can couple collision-avoidance behavior to relationships learned from the training distribution. We introduce the Dynamic Oriented Bounding Box (DOBB), an online geometric representation that maps the current state estimate, uncertainty, and agent-specific response characteristics into a dynamic, direction-dependent safety margin. We derive geometric features that jointly characterize the relative configuration and severity of interactions between agents' DOBBs, along with a reward function that preserves the physical interpretation of those interactions. Across four evaluation environments, DOBB achieves the lowest mean total failure rate of 2.6%. This performance persists under out-of-distribution shifts in actuation dynamics and state-estimation uncertainty, with collision-based failure remaining at or below 2.3% in every tested condition. We attribute this robustness to the geometric abstraction of the safety margin, which is less coupled to the specific uncertainty and actuation regimes encountered during training.
authors: Pedro Antonio Alarcon Granadeno, Jane Cleland-Huang
bullets: Addresses collision avoidance under state-estimation uncertainty and heterogeneous agent dynamics.
Represents each agent with an online Dynamic Oriented Bounding Box whose safety margin depends on state, uncertainty, and response characteristics.
Uses geometric interaction features and a physically interpretable reward to guide learning-based policies.
Across four environments, reports a 2.6% mean total failure rate and collision-based failure of at most 2.3% under tested distribution shifts.
Scope: robustness is demonstrated for the evaluated environments and out-of-distribution actuation and uncertainty conditions.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented language model systems generally select context by query-conditioned relevance. We argue that long-lived AI systems require a second operator: activation-conditioned memory availability. We specify an architecture in which request and goal cues seed an authorized memory graph, activation and fan attenuation allocate a bounded traversal frontier, retrieved entities recursively emit cues, and a typed evidence graph is reconstructed before generation. The specification yields five architectural consequences about candidate selection, traversal control, graph regularization, evidence reconstruction, and reinforcement. We derive implementation-level cost estimates and define ablations, failure conditions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if a simpler graph reranker matches full traversal on causal and temporal recovery under equal budgets. This architecture-and-analysis preprint reports no benchmark measurements. If the claim holds, retrieval returns the evidence path that makes a memory available, not only a ranked list.
authors: Marvin Danig (Achiral Research)
bullets: Motivation: Query relevance alone may be insufficient for long-lived AI systems that must recover causally and temporally linked memories.
Method: Request and goal cues seed a memory graph; activation and fan attenuation bound traversal, while retrieved entities recursively emit cues.
Output: A typed evidence graph is reconstructed before language-model generation.
Analysis: The work specifies architectural consequences, cost estimates, ablations, failure conditions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol.
Scope: This is a preprint with no benchmark measurements; the claim is testable against a simpler graph reranker under equal budgets.

papers.abstract: In the absence of extrinsic rewards or task supervision, human behavior is guided by intrinsic motivation---neural signals that drive curiosity, creativity, play, and other essential facets of intelligence. Intrinsic motivation plays an important developmental role in building robust world models that enable generalization and adaptation. Yet existing studies leave open how a broad range of intrinsic motivations interacts with world-model representation learning to support downstream control. This limits our understanding of which intrinsically collected experiences build reusable models. To address these gaps, we integrate 24 intrinsic objectives, including established methods and explicit variants spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency, into a common model-based reinforcement learning framework. We evaluate the world models they build through zero-shot, few-shot, and multi-task control in locomotion, manipulation, and open-ended gaming environments, using three representation-learning strategies: observation reconstruction, latent prediction, and redundancy reduction. Curiosity-driven exploration with observation reconstruction yields the strongest aggregate family profile, although the best individual pairing depends on the experiment. In compositional vision-based tasks, intrinsic motivation derived from both episodic and lifelong novelty---providing a complementary memory to the world model's generic recurrent state---achieves the best zero-shot transfer and few-shot adaptation. These findings motivate designing intrinsic motivation and representation learning jointly. Our results demonstrate world models as a powerful tool for measuring the quality of intrinsically motivated experience, and positions intrinsic motivation as a key ingredient for building world models autonomously.
authors: Reece Keller, Declan Kutscher, Xaq Pitkow, Aran Nayebi
bullets: Integrates 24 intrinsic objectives spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency into a common model-based reinforcement-learning framework.
Evaluates learned world models on zero-shot, few-shot, and multi-task control across locomotion, manipulation, and open-ended gaming.
Compares observation reconstruction, latent prediction, and redundancy-reduction representation learning.
Curiosity with observation reconstruction performs best overall, while episodic plus lifelong novelty achieves the strongest transfer and adaptation in compositional vision tasks.
Results suggest intrinsic motivation and representation learning should be designed jointly.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trusted with mathematical, scientific and engineering work, yet their mistakes are often confidently written and hard to spot. A single wrong step tends to propagate, making the model waste inference tokens following a false premise. Existing safeguards either check only the final answer and restart from scratch, or rely on a verifier LLM that competes for GPU capacity and slows down response time. We propose online, deterministic verification: many kinds of reasoning steps can be validated by code, so a step can be verified in real time, as it is written, without any model call or GPU use. Whenever a check fails, we point out the mistake and let the model continue from the same spot. We demonstrate this approach on symbolic mathematics, where derivations already contain explicit expressions that a computer algebra system can check in milliseconds. Tested on the ASyMoB benchmark with three open-weights models, our online validation improves accuracy by 1.4-5.6 percentage points, corresponding to a 1.8-14.9% net reduction in incorrect answers, while increasing token usage by only 6-7%. Because the verifier is independent of the model, the approach complements progress in LLMs rather than competing with it: every new model can benefit immediately, and the benefit grows as deterministic checkers extend to more kinds of reasoning steps.
authors: Rotem Elimelech, Michael Shalyt, Ido Kaminer

(C) The three stages of the method, corresponding to the numbered annotations in panel B. Extraction and verification require no additional model calls.
