papers.abstract: Berglund and van der Merwe formalized byte-pair encoding and bounded how far an appended string can change a tokenization, leaving the converse open: how far can a string prepended on the left change it, which dictionaries make that ripple infinite, and can it be computed efficiently when finite? We answer all three for every dictionary. The origin radius, how far a prepend can change covering spans, is decided with radius certificates by a product of two runs of the automaton that guesses the final tokens, in time polynomial in the dictionary written out, and it is infinite exactly when one periodic word has two canonical tilings with no common boundary. Under their ordering condition it is infinite exactly when some rule (t, t) finds its two copies adjacent at its own stage, and such a rule makes any dictionary infinite. A finite radius makes every window of a width read off the radii have a cut, and the radius is finite exactly when such cuts are dense. The token machine completes for every dictionary, and the tokenization is subsequential, extending what Berglund, Martens and van der Merwe proved for proper ones under one pass per rule. A streaming tokenizer emits after every symbol exactly the tokens that no continuation changes, in polynomial time, answering a question of Dalirrooyfard and Ye. Boundedness of the label measure, the edit distance of the token sequences, is decided for every dictionary in polynomial time as well, and under the ordering condition the largest distance one edit causes over dictionaries of m rules lies asymptotically between m^2/10 and m^2/2. GPT-2's merge table carries 244 effective self-pairs, so its origin radius is infinite from the forty-second merge on, and that of cl100k, o200k and Llama 3 from their first. Every measured number is its program's output, and what is not executed is named.

papers.abstract: Reliable medical laboratory automation requires robots to complete entire workflows in protocol order while handling changes during execution. A robot may execute each motion correctly yet fail the workflow by confusing visually similar stages or stalling after human intervention. We present Robo-MLT, a dual-system framework that couples explicit workflow monitoring with learned action generation. A vision--language planner composes an ordered atomic-skill sequence from the protocol and the initial workspace observation. A multiframe execution monitor detects when the active skill has completed or become infeasible, then advances the workflow or triggers replanning. A skill-conditioned vision--language--action policy generates the manipulation trajectories, and an asynchronous runtime coordinates it with the monitor. We evaluate Robo-MLT against four policy baselines and a VLM-based monitor baseline on blood gas analysis and blood sample tube sorting, with 50 nominal configurations per method and 20 sample-removal configurations. Robo-MLT achieves task success rates of 82\% and 70\%, exceeding $\pi_{0.5}$ by 30 and 22 percentage points, respectively. After an operator removes the sample being handled, the system revises the remaining plan and continues processing the other samples. These results indicate that, under the evaluated conditions, explicit workflow monitoring makes long-horizon laboratory manipulation more reliable and recoverable.
authors: Zequan Zeng, Kai Wang, Delvin Ce Zhang, Huaping Liu, Zhipeng Yuan, Junqin Yang, YunLong Zhang

papers.abstract: Robot agents can improve reusable skills, planning procedures, and recovery strategies from execution feedback, yet a fixed practice source leaves the search for new weaknesses unchanged. Useful practice depends on the agent's current capabilities, so the procedure that chooses practice must also be revisable. We present RoboACE (Robot Adversarial Co-Evolution), a framework that jointly evolves curriculum and execution harnesses around frozen foundation models. The curriculum harness uses accumulated capability evidence to propose informative challenges, while the execution harness responds with reusable revisions that expand execution capabilities. Alternating updates hold one side fixed as the other changes, and admitted challenges form fixed snapshots for comparing execution revisions. Starting from a compact set of LIBERO practice conditions, the resulting frozen deployment outperforms the evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family panels. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 74.0% success, exceeding the initial deployment by 15.0 percentage points and direct execution by its VLA controller by 13.5 points. Case studies document changes to evidence-guided practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention.
authors: Delin Zhao, Zhengrong Yue, Junlin He, Yali Wang

figures.caption: Figure 3 The final deployment improves across all four evaluation panels. Bar labels give success counts on a 200-episode scale. Model baselines use checkpoints fine-tuned on original LIBERO and evaluated without further training on LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-PRO, and LIBERO-X.

(b) In RoboACE, the curriculum exposes current execution weaknesses, while execution expands its capabilities through reusable harness revisions. As capabilities grow, the curriculum targets new weaknesses, sustaining adversarial coevolution. The blue and orange robots represent the execution and curriculum harnesses, respectively.

Figure 2 Alternating revisions connect challenge production and execution. The curriculum side uses prior capability evidence to probe a fixed execution deployment. Admitted conditions form a fixed snapshot for comparing execution revisions, whose outcomes inform the next round. Independent agents run the harnesses, external optimizers revise them, and the Strategic Advisor periodically reviews the longer history.

Figure 4 Reusable revisions address concrete gaps in both harnesses. Each row follows a case from its starting point to a reusable revision and the recorded follow-up. papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have demonstrated strong generalization in robotic manipulation, yet processing dense visual tokens often incurs high inference latency. Visual token pruning offers a practical way to reduce this cost, but identifying a compact set of tokens that preserves reliable action generation remains challenging. Existing methods largely rely on static or immediate heuristic cues to estimate token importance. We introduce APS-VLA, a framework that learns visual token selection from robot demonstrations while keeping the pretrained VLA backbone frozen. A lightweight Decision Influence Estimator scores tokens conditioned on current visual observations, language instructions, and robot proprioception. Its training combines two complementary signals: action supervision matches both the full-input policy predictions and demonstrated actions, while an auxiliary visual transition objective uses demonstrated actions to predict subsequent visual features from the selected representation. At deployment, the estimator performs a single hard selection and packing step before the policy's native action-generation procedure; the auxiliary predictor is removed. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO and with $\pi_{0.5}$ and XR-1 on RoboCasa365 demonstrate inference acceleration with modest changes in task success. Across five real-world tasks on two dual-arm platforms, APS-VLA reduces mean policy inference latency from 137.25 to 93.25 ms, achieving a $1.47\times$ speedup with an average success rate of 61%, compared with 60% for the unpruned baseline. Together, these results support APS-VLA as a modular, plug-in framework for efficient robotic control across VLA architectures, preserving the underlying policy parameters and native action-generation procedure.

Across five real-world tasks, reduces mean latency from 137.25 ms to 93.25 ms (1.47× speedup) while achieving 61% average success versus 60% unpruned.

papers.abstract: AAA games offer a rich testbed for evaluating agent perception, reasoning, and control. However, evaluating whether agents can complete tasks in AAA games is challenging and often human-annotated because task outcomes are often difficult to verify automatically, let alone applying it for Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce GTAGym, an environment and framework for evaluation and RL on GTA V tasks. Its evaluation benchmark, GTAVBench, derived from GTA V main-story missions, contains 103 online tasks reconstructed across nine task families, alongside 47 image-based shooting and sniping tasks using GTA V imagery. A web server provides access to the online environment and evaluation interface, supporting parallel testing through screenshots and keyboard-mouse actions with automatic engine-state outcome checks. We evaluate six frontier LLMs on GTAVBench with textual task instructions and on its GTAVBench-AGI branch, where instructions appear only in the first screenshot and a harness automatically compresses interaction history. The best configuration achieves 70.9% overall accuracy in GTAVBench-AGI, yet aerial navigation, evasion and interception remain difficult. GTAGym also provides a scalable generator that samples task parameters within user-specified ranges and option sets under fixed templates, creating batches of 3D and image-based shooting environments for RL with automatic reward and termination signals. LoRA RL of Qwen3.8-27B on generated on-foot navigation tasks improves the in-domain performance and transfers to out-of-domain task categories, and native GTA V tasks from 15% to 23%.

A task generator creates parameterized 3D and image-based environments with automatic rewards and termination signals for RL.
LoRA RL on generated navigation tasks improves in-domain and cross-category performance, raising native GTA V task performance from 15% to 23%.

papers.abstract: Coding agents increasingly receive UI screenshots as part of bug reports, yet degraded image quality - caused by low resolution, compression artifacts, or small rendered text - can prevent them from identifying the relevant UI elements and source files. Vision-language models become less reliable as image quality deteriorates, while OCR-assisted approaches may propagate recognition errors from degraded inputs. Both approaches are limited when the visual evidence required for localization is no longer clearly observable in the query screenshot. We propose augmenting coding agents with repository-rendered reference images: crisp screenshots generated from the same codebase that the agent is tasked with modifying. These references provide readable visual evidence of the application's UI while preserving the current, potentially bug-containing implementation state. Because they are generated from the available repository rather than requiring a known bug-free version, they can be produced automatically for reproducible application states without manual image annotation. We evaluate the approach on a controlled benchmark derived from SWE-bench Multimodal by injecting visual UI bugs into a real web application. We vary screenshot degradation and reference-image provision and measure whether the coding agent identifies the correct source file. The results show that reference images improve file localization especially for degraded image quality, increasing the gold file match rate under fourfold downsampling with JPEG compression. We confirmed with further analysis that the proposed approach recognizes text approximately 12 percentage points better than language biased OCR under the same degradation.
authors: Fumiki Yohena, Toshiaki Sota, Shota Suzuki, Tomoko Okamoto, Michiaki Tatsubori
bullets: Problem: Low-resolution, compressed, or text-heavy UI screenshots can prevent agents from identifying relevant interface elements and code files.
Method: Generate crisp UI reference images directly from the target repository, preserving its current implementation state and avoiding manual annotation or a known bug-free version.
Evaluation: A controlled benchmark based on SWE-bench Multimodal injects visual UI bugs and varies screenshot degradation and reference-image availability.

Results: Reference images improve source-file localization, particularly under fourfold downsampling with JPEG compression; text recognition improves by approximately 12 percentage points over language-biased OCR under the same degradation.
Scope: The approach is evaluated on controlled web-application UI bugs and focuses on identifying the correct source file.

papers.abstract: Block drafters such as DFlash draft a block of future tokens in one forward pass, and draft trees such as DDTree verify the prefixes ranked highest by the product of the drafter's per-position distributions. Under tree verification, the expected number of accepted tokens is the probability mass the tree covers. We show that a product misallocates it: when the continuation can follow several futures, it splices them into chimeras, prefixes stitched together from different futures that the target never produces, and gives them as much budget as the futures themselves. Barring ties, no product-ranked tree can hold two futures that disagree in $m$ positions without $2^{m-1}-1$ chimeras, however well the drafter is trained, and in practice chimeras make up 27-33% of a 64-node tree. We propose Multi-Future Drafting (MFD), which restores the coupling with a latent variable instead of the chain rule: $K$ learned mode embeddings at the drafter's input draft $K$ coherent blocks in the same pass, and a mixture DDTree lets the verifier pick the future the target takes, losslessly and with $K+1$ extra vectors. On four Qwen targets from 4B to 27B parameters, at batch size 1, MFD reaches up to 7.8$\times$ speedup, 5-8% faster than the best single-mode tree trained identically and, on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, 9-16% faster than the released DARTree trained on the same prompts.
authors: Haoyu Huang, Jialiang Kang, Linlin Yang, Xiao Yang, Baochang Zhang
bullets: Product-ranked draft trees can waste 27–33% of a 64-node tree on chimeric prefixes that combine incompatible futures.
MFD uses K learned mode embeddings to draft K coherent future blocks in one forward pass.
A mixture DDTree lets verification select the future matching the target, with only K+1 extra vectors.
Across four Qwen targets from 4B to 27B parameters, MFD is 5–8% faster than an identically trained single-mode tree.
It is 9–16% faster than released DARTree on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B under the reported setup.

papers.selection_reason: Speculative decoding with mixture block drafters reduces LLM inference latency, a clear efficiency contribution.
papers.title: Multi-Future Drafting: Mixture Block Drafters for Tree-Verified Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: Multi-Future Drafting improves tree-verified speculative decoding by drafting multiple coherent futures instead of probability-product chimeras, achieving up to 7.8× speedup on Qwen targets.

papers.abstract: Synthetic data augmentation promises to scale offline reinforcement learning beyond fixed logged datasets, but leading diffusion-based generators model the transition tuple (state, action, next state, reward, terminal) as a monolith: no single factor can be natively redrawn in isolation. We present FaST (Factored Synthesis of Transitions), which factors transitions via the chain rule into state, action, dynamics, reward, and terminal stages, fitting each with an estimator matched to its statistical properties. Across twelve D4RL locomotion and maze benchmarks, TD3+BC and IQL agents trained on FaST transitions match the SynthER diffusion baseline while generating transitions over 90x faster. The explicit action-given-state conditional can also be re-queried for a fixed state, enabling targeted action synthesis: drawing N candidate actions per generated state and keeping the highest-advantage one under a value function fit to the same data, thereby synthesizing improved behavior during generation rather than filtering for it post-hoc. Best-of-10 synthesis beats training on real data on 11 of 12 medium and medium-replay settings (+8.9 D4RL points on average, up to +28.4), and is competitive with advantage-filtered SynthER at a fraction of its generation cost. On expert mixtures both mechanisms degrade identically, tracing the failure to the advantage estimate itself rather than to either targeting mechanism.
authors: Daniel Campa, Spandan Das, Srinjoy Das

figures.caption: Figure 4: Next-state marginals (top) against delta marginals δj = s′j − sj (bottom) for dimensions 0, 1, 4, 7, 10 of hopper-medium-replay-v2, on a set of non-terminal transitions. Raw next-state marginals are broad and multimodal with mass piled at joint and velocity limits (dim 4), while the corresponding deltas are unimodal and concentrated at zero. papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) often report a finding because the question names it; standard benchmarks miss this. From public segmentation datasets we build counterfactual views without manual annotation: the lesion erased by inpainting, a same-shape control edit elsewhere, and unedited lesion-free images. The evidence sensitivity gap (ESG) is the rate of absent-or-refer answers after erasure minus the rate after the control edit; it is zero for a model that ignores the image or reacts to both edits alike. MedScope-4B (Qwen3.5-4B, LoRA, image tools) was trained on label-derived trajectories, selected by a pre-registered rule and tested once against nine frontier and six open VLMs; four pre-registered checks then probed the mechanism. On 507 internal cases across five imaging types, MedScope-4B reached ESG 0.758 and claimed an erased lesion in 9.6% of cases, against 0.27-0.47 and 41-62% for the frontier models (all p<0.001), without significant loss of accuracy on real lesions. Without counterfactual views ESG fell to 0.279+-0.107 (three seeds); the effect replicated on MedGemma 1.5 4B and two unseen inpainting tools. At four external centres the advantage held but frontier models detected more real lesions; on a fresh external test MedScope-4B detected 0 of 48 pneumothorax films, with net utility below gemini-4-argon's (-0.36 [-0.50, -0.23]). Matching the control edit was not shown to matter; over three seeds no fresh-external ESG advantage over removal-based DPO was established; a paired-view consistency objective did not beat a matched-compute control, while that continuation alone cut erased-lesion claims on unseen tools at every seed, at a cost in sensitivity at one. Training on erased and edited images gives a small model an evidence-gated disposition that prompting does not give frontier models; it does not improve perception, and rare critical findings need coverage.
authors: Bhaskar Gurram
bullets: Standard VLM benchmarks may reward models for repeating findings named in questions rather than verifying image evidence.
MedScope-4B was trained with lesion-erased views, control edits, and label-derived trajectories to promote evidence-sensitive reporting.
On 507 internal cases, it achieved an evidence sensitivity gap of 0.758 and claimed erased lesions in 9.6% of cases, with no significant loss of real-lesion accuracy.
The effect replicated across another model and unseen inpainting tools, while prompting alone was insufficient.
External testing revealed scope limits: frontier models detected more real lesions, and MedScope-4B detected 0 of 48 pneumothorax films on a fresh test.

papers.selection_reason: Counterfactual training for medical VLM to reduce hallucination.
papers.title: Seeing Is Not Believing: Counterfactual Lesion Erasure Teaches a Small Medical Vision-Language Agent to Report Only What the Image Shows
papers.tldr: Training on counterfactual lesion-erased images helps a small medical VLM report findings only when they remain visible, but it does not improve perception and can miss rare critical findings.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning agents are often deployed with policies that cannot be retrained or modified. In digital environments whose states can be copied and resumed, an operator has another option: sample several continuations from the current state, evaluate them, and continue from the endpoint of the selected branch. We call this procedure branch-and-commit. We study when it improves return, what produces the improvement, and where its computational budget should be spent. Across four environments, two frozen policies, five continuation verifiers, and a model-free selection rule, we find that the benefit of branching depends on dispersion: the difference between the best candidate return and the mean candidate return. Branching provides no benefit in low-dispersion settings, while increasing return by 12.8% in our main Craftax-Medium setting. Most of this gain comes not from selecting better actions, but from selecting among different stochastic realizations of the same action. Several competent verifiers achieve similar episode returns, suggesting that verifier quality is not the main constraint at our operating budget. Instead, computation is better allocated to states where useful dispersion is likely. On held-out seeds, gating branching using predicted dispersion retains 69% of the improvement from uniform branching while using 48% as many branching calls. These results characterize when branch-and-commit is useful and clarify what its gains represent.
authors: Sahar Admoni, Assaf Hallak, Yftah Ziser, Ofra Amir

figures.caption: Figure 1: Branch-and-commit with a frozen policy. At a selected state, the operator forks the simulator, samples 𝐾 candidate continuations from the unchanged policy, scores the complete continuations, and resumes execution from the endpoint of the selected branch. Gains can arise from action selection, when branches begin with different actions, or from realization selection, when they begin with the same action but encounter different stochastic outcomes.

Figure 2: Candidate dispersion predicts episode-level lift. Predicted lift ℓ̂𝑐 = ˆ𝛽𝑣Δ𝑐 versus observed lift ℓ𝑐 across 103 conditions. Colors indicate verifier classes and markers indicate environments. The dashed line shows equality between predicted and observed lift. Slopes are fitted separately for each verifier through the origin.

Mean signed gap 𝛿pick = 𝑅(𝜏LLM-pick)−𝑅(𝜏VF-pick) on decisions where the LLM and the value head disagree, by within-decision dispersion tertile (cutoffs 0.20 and 0.91 in 𝐻 -step reward units). Bars are pooledmeans ± standard error over 𝑛=6,886 disagreements, the raw rows of Table 21. GPT-4o-mini is on the MLP policy, the other panels on GTrXL.

Figure 6: Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds for Table 23 on Craftax-Medium. Per-condition seed-level mean returns are aggregated by 10,000-iteration bootstrap; ×marks individual seeds. The 𝜏=0.30 row is a further over-branching threshold, below the 𝜏=1.0 stress test of this appendix, whose return collapses to 17.5. The no-branching marker is the canonical 32.09 pool of Appendix B.3. DoorKey-8x8 is omitted because its policy is at the reward ceiling (Table 5).

Table 15: Most measured dispersion is the environment’s realization, not the policy’s action. Sharing the environment’s random draws across branches removes 69% of mean dispersion and roughly doubles the share of decisions with no dispersion at all. The direction holds in every seed. papers.abstract: Embodied Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are backbones for robotic planning and manipulation. However, for coordinate prediction in grounding tasks, existing architectures suffer from two distinct bottlenecks: discrete tokenization disrupts spatial continuity with high decoding latency, while standard point regression fails on multi-contact affordances and irregularly shaped targets. To resolve these challenges, we propose PhysMoE, introducing three core contributions: (1) sharing lower layers for multimodal context while routing upper layers to specialized spatial (pixel) and linguistic (text) experts by physical modality, eliminating gradient interference; (2) encoding each coordinate as a single token by reusing the visual encoder's learned positional embeddings, injecting 2D spatial priors to natively align coordinates with visual features and ease training; and (3) differentiable Signed Distance Field (SDF) supervision on pointing, accommodating affordances and irregular geometries without costly mask decoders. Compared to the base model, PhysMoE achieves a 15.7% average gain and an 8.31x throughput speedup across 9 coordinate-based grounding benchmarks (trajectory, affordance, and localization), while preserving multimodal understanding and reasoning across 11 text-based embodied benchmarks.
authors: Ruimeng Liu, Denan Liang, Ruofei Bai, Fuming Zhang, Kuan Xu, Shenghai Yuan, Lihua Xie
bullets: Targets slow, discontinuous discrete coordinate decoding and inadequate point regression for multi-contact or irregular affordances.
Shares lower multimodal layers while routing upper layers to specialized spatial and linguistic experts to reduce gradient interference.
Represents each coordinate as one token using visual positional embeddings, aligning coordinates with image features.
Uses differentiable Signed Distance Field supervision without requiring costly mask decoders.
Reports a 15.7% average gain and 8.31× throughput speedup across 9 coordinate-grounding benchmarks, while preserving performance across 11 text-based embodied benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Multimodal (e.g. vision-language, in this work) attribution aims to interpret the models without access to ground-truth explanatory supervision. Existing multimodal attribution methods typically rely on paired modalities as proxy supervision, implicitly assuming that image-text pairs are semantically aligned. Information bottleneck (IB)-based attribution methods follow this general paradigm and instantiate it through a global sufficiency-compression objective. In realistic multimodal datasets, however, this assumption is frequently violated due to partial semantic misalignment and unreliable cross-modal correspondences. Through theoretical analysis, we show that, under such misalignment, information-bottleneck-based attribution objectives exhibit a structural limitation: by assuming equal reliability across all proxy supervision signals, they induce posterior over-contraction and forced explanations. To address this issue, we propose TIB, a sample-wise Tempered Information Bottleneck framework that adaptively modulates attribution strength according to cross-modal reliability, without assuming semantic alignment. Extensive experiments on controlled benchmarks and large-scale datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed approach, while also validating the identified failure mode.
authors: Qiming Huang, Peixi Liu, Jianbo Jiao
bullets: Existing information-bottleneck attribution methods can produce forced explanations when paired modalities are partially misaligned.
Theoretical analysis identifies posterior over-contraction as a structural failure caused by treating all proxy supervision signals as equally reliable.
TIB uses a sample-wise tempered information bottleneck to modulate attribution strength based on cross-modal reliability.
Experiments on controlled benchmarks and large-scale datasets demonstrate TIB’s effectiveness and validate the identified failure mode.

papers.abstract: Knowledge editing has emerged as a promising approach for efficiently updating embedded knowledge in large language models (LLMs). It first computes an ideal target hidden state that steers the LLM toward the new output, and then edits the model parameters so that the original hidden state is mapped to this target. While most existing methods focus on the second stage of parameter editing in preserving other knowledge, we find that the upstream construction of the target hidden state also plays an important role in allocating the model's limited capacity space. We first establish a theoretical connection between interference in the parameter space and interference between target hidden states, showing that the two are positively correlated. Building on this insight, we propose a simple yet effective $\ell_1$ regularization method that prunes away unnecessary ``tentacles'' of each knowledge vector, retaining only the essential components. With fewer extraneous tentacles, each edit affects less other knowledge, enabling better coexistence. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmark datasets verify the effectiveness of our method. Code: https://github.com/wintersdragon-c/STO.
authors: Dongyao Chen, Jiayun Lei, Zhiyuan Ji, Zhiying Deng, Wei Liu, Xiaobo Sun

papers.abstract: Multimodal attributed graphs (MAGs), in which nodes carry text, images, and other modalities while edges encode relations among entities, underlie e-commerce, social media, content platforms, and creative applications. Learning on MAGs has developed along two complementary lines: graph-centric methods redesign how modalities are fused, propagated, and connected within message passing, while foundation-model-centric methods pretrain transferable multimodal graph encoders or bring graph context into multimodal large language models for prediction and generation. In parallel, several benchmarks have appeared with different datasets and evaluation protocols. This survey takes an algorithm-centric and evaluation-grounded view of the field and makes three contributions. Modeling: we introduce a unified message-passing formulation and organize methods into five integration levels (feature, propagation, topology, learning, and foundation model), covering discriminative and graph-conditioned generative models; within this formulation we derive representative methods as special cases, compare their assumptions, expressiveness, and cost, and identify cross-modal sensitivity as a property that separates otherwise similar architectures. Datasets and evaluation: we review recent benchmarks, summarize their datasets and metrics, define model-independent descriptors (label homophily, average degree, clustering, and edge provenance), and map each evaluation protocol to the baselines it uses. Frontiers: we connect multimodal graph learning to AI agents, covering the multimodal graphs that agents perceive and remember and graph engineering, the practice of organizing agent workflows as explicit graphs; we then discuss open problems, concrete efforts for the community, and research directions, including when graph structure helps in the presence of strong multimodal foundation models.
authors: Rui Xue, Tianfu Wu

papers.abstract: Does a useful self-update remain useful after the model updates again? Third Eye separates immediate performance from the outcome of a further native update. We evaluate five 3-8B backbones on math and code: 64 fresh runs, three candidates per run, and three continuations per candidate. Selection and final scoring use disjoint items. In the balanced Qwen3-4B/Llama-3.2-3B comparison, immediate-selected utility is near zero, but continuation reduces it by 1.78 percentage points (simultaneous 95% interval [0.68, 2.88]). Candidate-averaged immediate utility is already negative: selection partly accounts for the apparently neutral first step. Continuation also lowers utility for SmolLM3-3B and Llama-3.1-8B; Qwen3-8B remains inconclusive. Target and out-of-distribution losses dominate retention changes. Matched recipe and recipient-donor controls identify neither a reliable mitigation nor a single mechanism. The results support evaluating persistent self-updates as adaptation transitions, with independent scoring and a no-update baseline, rather than interpreting immediate performance as their full value.
authors: Sujato Dutta, Padala Indira Sneha, Kypu Mahitha, Shashank Vanga, Neeraj Choudhary
bullets: Third Eye separates immediate utility from the utility of a subsequent native update.

papers.abstract: Spike cameras encode dynamic scenes into high-temporal-resolution binary spike streams for efficient high-speed vision. Although spiking neural networks (SNNs) can process such signals with sparse and accumulate-only computation, existing SNN-based reconstruction methods are typically shallow and still lag behind ANN-based models in reconstruction fidelity. This paper proposes MADSNet, a Multi-scale Axial-attentive Dense Spiking Network for spike camera image reconstruction. MADSNet adopts a hierarchical spiking encoder--decoder, where a multi-scale spike stem extracts early features, axial spike attention captures long-range dependencies, a dense spiking bottleneck enhances feature reuse, and a spike-to-continuous decoder reconstructs continuous intensity images from spike-domain representations. Experiments on gray-scale and color spike reconstruction show that MADSNet outperforms SSIR by 4.3 dB PSNR and Spk2ImgNet by 1.94 dB on SREDS. Compared with Spk2ImgNet, it achieves about 15$\times$ lower latency and uses only about 1/40 of the estimated energy, demonstrating that carefully designed SNN architectures can improve reconstruction quality while preserving computational efficiency.

papers.abstract: Distilling flow matching models for one-step generation generally follows two paradigms. Trajectory alignment supervises the student with the teacher's probability flow ODE, but its performance degrades under very small sampling budgets. Distribution matching directly optimizes the generated distribution, but estimating its reverse Kullback-Leibler gradient typically requires a separate network to track the evolving student score. We propose trajectory-regularized distribution distillation (TRD), which combines distribution-level and trajectory-level supervision through a momentum-mixture policy predicted in a single student forward pass. This policy serves simultaneously as a one-step generator, an estimator of the student's marginal velocity that removes the need for a second trainable network in distribution matching, and a closed-form time-dependent velocity field supervised along the teacher ODE trajectory. Experiments on SANA-1.6B and Stable Diffusion 3.5 show that TRD outperforms representative consistency and distribution matching baselines in generation quality and training efficiency for both one-step and few-step generation, with a trade-off in sample diversity.
authors: An Zhao, Yixiang Zhou, Zejian Li, Yi Guo, Pei Chen, Lingyun Sun
bullets: Addresses the weaknesses of trajectory alignment at very small sampling budgets and distribution matching’s need for an extra score-estimation network.
Uses a momentum-mixture policy predicted in one student forward pass.
The policy acts as the one-step generator, estimates the student’s marginal velocity, and provides a closed-form velocity field for trajectory supervision.
Outperforms representative consistency and distribution-matching baselines on SANA-1.6B and Stable Diffusion 3.5 in generation quality and training efficiency.
Improved quality and efficiency come with a trade-off in sample diversity.

papers.abstract: Time-series forecasting has recently seen a paradigm shift with the introduction of foundation-style models that adapt large pretrained language architectures to sequential data. However, effectively exposing fundamental temporal structures, such as trend, scale, and temporal dependence, to these models remains an open challenge, particularly when the available observations are limited. In this paper, we conduct an exploratory empirical study across different generations of forecasting architectures and propose StatPrompt-LLM, a lightweight statistical refinement of Time-LLM. StatPrompt-LLM augments the existing Time-LLM prompting mechanism with dataset-level statistical information and introduces a zero-initialised autoregressive bypass as a complementary linear forecasting pathway. We evaluate our framework on electricity and meteorological time-series benchmarks, including ETTh1, ETTh2, and Weather, under full-prefix and reduced-prefix configurations. Under the 10% reduced-prefix configuration, StatPrompt-LLM achieved lower in-sample prediction errors than Time-LLM, with unweighted average relative reductions across datasets of 40.2% in MSE and 21.4% in MAE. Full-prefix results were more dataset-dependent. Ablation analyses revealed relatively modest and dataset-dependent changes when selected additional statistical descriptor groups were masked within the combined architecture. Computational profiling indicated additional model parameters and runtime overhead relative to Time-LLM.
authors: Aniket Sinha, Veronica W. Tsou

papers.abstract: Federated fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces communication and computational overhead by training and exchanging compact trainable LoRA factors. Clients may use different LoRA ranks to meet adapter communication budgets and accommodate different local adaptation needs. The server must process these differences during aggregation and construct adapters at each client's rank for local training. We distinguish pre-aggregation alignment, which handles factor dimensions and scaling conventions before aggregation and rank-specific LoRA adapter extraction, which constructs client-sized pairs from the aggregated global model. Two common approaches to rank-specific extraction are direct rank truncation and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of the dense update. Direct prefix truncation keeps the leading columns of one aggregated factor and the corresponding rows of the other. It is cheap but can increase reconstruction error. The dense SVD approach first forms the product of aggregated LoRA factors. It then decomposes this matrix and retains the leading singular components to construct adapters at the target rank. This gives the optimal rank-constrained approximation in Frobenius norm but incurs significant computational overhead. To address this trade-off, we propose RBLA+ as an extension of RBLA. It uses established compact QR/core-SVD decomposition to minimize Frobenius error for the extracted LoRA update without forming the dense update. It also accounts for client and server scaling conventions during upload and broadcast. Across vision and language tasks, RBLA+ improves accuracy over RBLA in multiple heterogeneous settings. In CPU benchmarks with synthetic adapters, RBLA+ has lower extraction time than the dense partial-SVD baseline. RBLA+ preserves each client's prescribed adapter size and per-round communication payload.
authors: Shuaijun Chen, Omid Tavallaie, Xin Chen, Wentao Gao, Nguyen Tran, Albert Y. Zomaya
bullets: Addresses federated fine-tuning where clients use different LoRA ranks and scaling conventions.
Uses compact QR/core-SVD decomposition to minimize Frobenius reconstruction error without forming the dense update.
Improves accuracy over RBLA across vision and language tasks in multiple heterogeneous settings.
Runs faster than dense partial-SVD extraction in CPU benchmarks with synthetic adapters.
Preserves each client’s prescribed adapter size and per-round communication payload.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large models have accelerated AI for Science toward agentic science, where AI agents autonomously conduct scientific discovery. Realising this vision requires closing the loop between computational reasoning and physical experimentation, positioning self-driving laboratories (SDLs) as critical enablers. However, existing SDLs exhibit a fundamental paradox: foundation model integration has increased linguistic sophistication while severing physical grounding. By treating models as disembodied planners that output symbolic workflows for separate robotic systems, current architectures inherently block the development of embodied experimental intuition. We argue that overcoming this paradox requires embedding \emph{learnability} along three interdependent axes: cognitive learnability (learning what to investigate), experimental learnability (learning where to search), and embodied learnability (learning how to act). Building on this view, we introduce the Embodied Science Agent (ESA), which unifies digital intelligence with physical embodiment through three synergistic components: a Digital Agent that provides cognitive and experimental learnability via memory-based reasoning and Bayesian optimisation, an Embodied Agent that provides embodied learnability via generalisable instrument control, and an Embodied Unified Interface for seamless coordination. We validated ESA in autonomous wastewater treatment experiments, navigating over 200 million possible conditions. Through 15 continuous rounds, ESA raised the final solution transmittance from 82\% to 99.7\%, corresponding to a 98.5\% reduction in residual dye concentration and near-complete decolourisation, while its learned visuomotor policies generalised across varying instrument placements, a promising step toward next-generation SDLs for autonomous scientific discovery.
authors: Yihang Che, Zhongwei Yu, Yang Li, Xingyu Lu, Hongxia Yu, Jun Wang
bullets: Current self-driving laboratories often separate language-based planning from robotic execution, limiting physical grounding and embodied intuition.
ESA combines a memory-based reasoning and Bayesian-optimisation Digital Agent, a generalisable instrument-controlling Embodied Agent, and a unified coordination interface.
In autonomous wastewater-treatment experiments, ESA explored more than 200 million possible conditions over 15 continuous rounds.
Solution transmittance improved from 82% to 99.7%, with a reported 98.5% reduction in residual dye concentration and near-complete decolourisation.
Learned visuomotor policies generalised across varying instrument placements, supporting broader autonomous laboratory operation.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Illustration of the Bayesian Optimisation framework as a central component of the ESA architecture. BO receives initial experimental configurations and objectives from the Principal Investigator (PI) Agent. As experiments are conducted by the Embodied Agent, the outcomes are relayed back to BO, providing essential data for refining its surrogate model. BO utilises this feedback to update its predictions and identify the next optimal configuration for experimentation. The Scheduler facilitates the execution of these configurations by coordinating between BO and the Embodied Agent. Ultimately, the best decision obtained during BO is recommended to the Reporter.

Figure 1: The Evolution of Self-Driving Laboratories. This timeline traces the development of autonomous experimentation systems from initial concepts in the 1940s to foundation model integration in recent years, spanning three eras: Early Era (1940s–2009, bottom) establishing foundational principles from design of experiments to closed-loop robot scientist; Modern Era (2009–2022, middle) deploying specialised robotic platforms across scientific domains; and LLMs Era (2022–present, top) integrating foundation models for high-level reasoning.

Figure 2: The architecture of the Embodied Science Agent (ESA), a hybrid cognitive–embodied paradigm for self-driving laboratories with three components. The Digital Agent, the cognitive core and central novelty of ESA, evolves open-endedly by integrating online knowledge, embodied experimentation, and past experience for reasoning, planning, and decision-making. The Embodied Agent orchestrates diverse robots and scientific instruments through multiple control modules for generalised, reliable, and adaptive operation. The Embodied Unified Interface connects digital intelligence with heterogeneous laboratory devices via standardised, low-latency, and safe protocols. Together, they close the loop between perception, reasoning, and embodied execution for autonomous scientific discovery.

Figure 3: Overview of the robotic platform. The dual-arm robot comprises two 6-DoF robotic arms equipped with 1-DoF grippers, a 2-DoF articulated head, an omnidirectional AMR base offering 2 planar DoFs for holonomic motion, and a 1-DoF lift for vertical adjustment. These degrees of freedom are highlighted in the blue box. The platform also integrates a synchronised multi-camera sensing suite consisting of one RGB and one depth camera mounted on the head, two RGB cameras on each wrist, and one RGB camera on the chest, as indicated in the orange box. Together, these components provide rich proprioceptive and multi-view visual feedback to support both global perception and fine-grained manipulation.
Figure 4: Transmittance results across 15 experimental rounds.

Figure 6: Performances of the robot in the generalisation case study of Section 4.4. The three rows correspond to three different initial placements of the electrode holder, circled with red boxes in the first column. Across all three trials, the robot’s left arm reliably approaches and grasps the edge of the electrode rack with a reasonable grasping posture, while the right arm inserts the electrode into the beaker, demonstrating spatial generalisation of the learned visuomotor policies.

papers.abstract: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) reduces the computational cost of attention through token-level selection. However, its indexer still scores the entire causal prefix for each query, making indexing a dominant source of latency in long-context inference. Notably, the indexer alone can account for more than 50% of total prefill GPU time at long context lengths. To address this bottleneck, we propose ADIndex, an Adaptive and Distillation-driven Indexing method for token-level sparse attention. ADIndex integrates three key components: (i) a layer-wise calibration strategy that adaptively accommodates cross-query retrieval overlap, motivated by our observation of pronounced inter-layer heterogeneity; (ii) a group-level distillation scheme that leverages this heterogeneity to efficiently train adaptive layer-wise group indexers, capturing salient retrieval signals from individual queries; and (iii) a low-latency inference strategy that reduces repeated full-prefix scans through token bank sharing within query groups while retaining query-specific refinement. Experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1 demonstrate that ADIndex preserves near-lossless task performance on LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER while delivering substantial efficiency gains over standard DSA, including prefill and decoding kernel speedups of up to 6.22x and 3.40x, respectively, at a context length of 256K across the layer-wise reuse configurations, as well as an end-to-end serving speedup of 1.54x at a context length of 128K.
authors: Jin-Fei Qi, Yiduo Li, Jiang-Xin Shi, Kan Liu, Tao Lan, Hanlin Tang, Yu-Feng Li
bullets: Targets the indexer bottleneck, which can exceed half of prefill GPU time at long context lengths.
Uses layer-wise calibration to handle heterogeneous cross-query retrieval overlap across layers.
Trains adaptive layer-wise group indexers through group-level distillation while retaining query-specific refinement.
Reduces repeated full-prefix scans via token-bank sharing within query groups.
On DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1, reports up to 6.22× prefill, 3.40× decoding-kernel, and 1.54× end-to-end serving speedups while maintaining near-lossless LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER performance.

papers.abstract: We study when and how multimodal input improves knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) in large vision--language models. Using a controlled evaluation over 1,500 WebQSP and CWQ questions and six VLMs within a fixed KGQA pipeline, we compare text-only prompting against text-plus-graph visualization at the per-question level and analyze performance changes as a function of reasoning complexity, model size, and image layout. Adding a graph image yields an average gain of 1.85 F1 points, driven by strong precision improvements on low-complexity questions (+4.65 F1). Mixed-effects and regression analyses show that these multimodal gains do not depend strongly on model scale, but are highly sensitive to graph layout: image-only settings sharply degrade performance, hierarchical Graphviz layouts outperform less organized renderings, and decomposing large subgraphs into separated paths yields the largest improvements. Taken together, the results indicate that visual prompting primarily aids KGQA by enhancing prediction precision in low-complexity contexts, provided that visual design respects cognitive and perceptual constraints. To optimize both accuracy and inference efficiency, we argue for adaptive visual prompting policies that selectively append diagrams to small, visually sparse subgraphs with well-structured layouts, avoiding unnecessary visual clutter and token overhead on complex queries. We conclude by relating these findings to a visual notation design theory, outlining how principled diagram encoding can guide future multimodal VLM prompting.
authors: Luiz do Valle Miranda, Andreas L. Opdahl, Grzegorz J. Nalepa
bullets: Evaluates text-only versus text-plus-graph prompts across 1,500 WebQSP/CWQ questions and six VLMs.
Graph images improve average F1 by 1.85 points, mainly through a +4.65 F1 precision gain on low-complexity questions.
Benefits are largely independent of model scale but highly dependent on visualization layout.
Hierarchical Graphviz layouts and separated paths perform best; image-only prompts and cluttered graphs can hurt performance.
The findings support adaptive prompting that adds diagrams selectively to small, visually sparse subgraphs to limit clutter and token overhead.

papers.abstract: Intelligent landslide detection is essential for disaster prevention. However, existing models primarily focus on isolated visual tasks, require extensive labeled data, and lack deep analytical and scene-understanding capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose LandslideFM, the first unified foundation model that connects visual perception tasks with contextual interpretation of landslides. Specifically, LandslideFM adapts to multiple visual tasks via a Source-Agreement Graduated Trust semi-supervised learning framework that leverages limited labeled data alongside abundant unlabeled data. Furthermore, predicted landslide regions provide explicit spatial guidance to a Vision-Language Model adapted through parameter-efficient fine-tuning, enabling comprehensive landslide reasoning. To support training and evaluation in this domain, we also present LandslideVL, the first benchmark for intelligent landslide analysis, combining visual imagery and newly introduced textual prompts. Comprehensive experiments across public datasets and LandslideVL demonstrate that LandslideFM achieves superior quantitative and qualitative performance. Most importantly, LandslideFM surpasses general-purpose VLMs in specialized landslide reasoning and scene analysis. Our code is released at https://github.com/wangshanwen001/LandslideFM.
authors: Shanwen Wang, Sirui Wang, Xin Sun, Jungong Han
bullets: Addresses the limited labeled data and weak scene-understanding capabilities of existing landslide detection models.

Introduces LandslideVL, a benchmark combining landslide imagery with textual prompts for intelligent landslide analysis.
Experiments on public datasets and LandslideVL report strong quantitative and qualitative performance, including better specialized reasoning than general-purpose VLMs.

papers.abstract: While multimodal agents now carry out complex data analysis with tools, their ability to turn decades of satellite imagery into reliable land-change analysis, crucial for Earth observation science, remains unmeasured. Existing benchmarks fall short: they pose questions on curated images or give agents preprocessed inputs, leaving out the raw multi-sensor archives where such analysis begins. We introduce EarthRecord, a benchmark built on the raw record of 56 sites: four decades of Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 data, with cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization left to the agent. It poses 238 land-change questions across ten analysis tasks, scored against withheld references from global products, agreement among methods, and visual interpretation. Two controls test what answers rest on: the closed book removes the record, and instrument pairs alter one satellite's data while nothing changes on the ground. Evaluations of twelve multimodal agents reveal that leading agents complete most analyses end to end but falter when an answer requires mapping from imagery. Further analysis shows that the record moves answers from prior knowledge to the pixels but not yet to the real change on the ground: when one satellite's data are altered, half of the right answers follow the alteration. EarthRecord thus provides a principled platform for measuring and advancing agents from pixels to land change.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing high-fidelity LiDAR simulation scenes from real-world driving logs is essential for cost-effective safety validation of autonomous driving systems. While simulators based on Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) achieve realistic scene reconstruction, their large-scale adoption is limited by slow rendering speeds. Recent 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) approaches have improved rendering efficiency through explicit primitive representation and differentiable rasterization. However, existing 3DGS-based methods remain largely restricted to rigid vehicles and produce redundant primitives through unconstrained densification. To address these limitations, we propose URL-Sim, a unified and regulated dynamic LiDAR simulation framework. URL-Sim constructs a dynamic Gaussian scene graph that decouples the modeling of traffic participants, including vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists, enabling accurate reconstruction of heterogeneous dynamic objects within a single framework. It further introduces a regulated Gaussian densification strategy that ranks primitives with multi-dimensional importance scores and allocates Gaussians to the most critical regions while keeping the total primitive count bounded. Experiments on the Waymo and KITTI-360 datasets demonstrate that URL-Sim achieves higher quantitative accuracy and visual quality than existing baselines under comparable primitive budgets, and accurately recovers the geometry and poses of diverse dynamic traffic participants.

papers.abstract: Assisted history matching remains non-unique because many geological realisations can reproduce equivalent production responses with substantial differences between individual well matches. This ambiguity increases when a field comprises several depositional settings and modelling strategies. The paper applied a graph autoencoder approach to history matching of a benchmark Brugge field that comprises different depositional zones. Each stratigraphic zone is modelled with its dedicated generative model that comprises a joint latent space for optimisation history matching loops. Graph-based generators operate directly on the active cells of the corner-point grid, so its irregular geometry is handled without conversion to a regular lattice. The optimisation search in the 160-dimensional joint latent space is done with the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy. The multi-component objective function includes static well data mismatch, dynamic production mismatch, and a geological realism penalty based on the Decoder induced latent metric. Latent space diagnostics with topological data analysis are applied prior to history matching to test whether one generator is sufficient or whether a multiple generator formulation is required. The results show that the zone-based formulation gives coherent latent spaces, preserves the main porosity and permeability relations that vary from one zone to another, and supports history matching while keeping the solutions within the learned geological manifold. The matched models reproduce field oil and water production within the prior uncertainty range and provide a comparable well-level match to previously published Brugge studies based on Ensemble Kalman Filter, Particle Swarm Optimisation with principal component analysis of parameterisation, and Multiple Kernel Learning with Particle Swarm Optimisation.
authors: Gleb Shishaev, Anton Shirokov, Shadfar Davoodi, Mohammed Al-Shargabi, Vasily Demyanov, Daniel Arnold

papers.abstract: Multimodal humor detection requires interpreting language, vocal delivery, and visual behavior jointly. Expressive fusion must also regulate how interactions of different orders enter the final judgment. We propose M\"obius Interaction Filtering (MoIF), which learns a modality-subset prediction function and imposes order-selective spectral regularization through its aggregation structure. Private temporal encoders and balanced reciprocal interaction construct supervised unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal predictors. Their uniform aggregate is exactly a M\"obius-domain filter with a geometrically decreasing interaction-order response. This formulation retains higher-order representations while regulating their contribution to prediction. Controlled UR-FUNNY perturbations reveal a pronounced decline in label-aligned signal-to-noise ratio across interaction orders. The induced filter improves the final ratio by 1.62-2.79 times relative to the co-trained trimodal predictor while preserving its own clean class-aligned signal under perturbation. Five-seed experiments achieve 70.6% accuracy and weighted F1 on UR-FUNNY, exceeding thirteen reproduced methods on these detection metrics. CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI evaluations establish applicability to sentiment prediction, and cross-seed analyses show more stable estimates on all three datasets. MoIF connects the organization of multimodal interactions to their statistical reliability through an executable spectral constraint. Code is available at https://github.com/D-ST-Sword/MoIF.
authors: Jiahao Qin, Yiwen Wang

papers.abstract: Context compression is now routine for language models with long inputs, but a compressed context is useful only if it keeps the evidence for the answer. Existing checks compare the reader model's answer or its most likely words, and thus miss a frequent failure, silent evidence loss: key evidence is removed while the answer stays the same, leaving the answer unsupported and risky for other models that reuse the context. To address this challenge, we propose SELD (Silent Evidence Loss Detector), which needs no training and no labels. Its principle is that when evidence is lost, a reader model's preferences among the answers it leaves unsaid shift even if its answer does not, so comparing these preferences before and after compression reveals losses that answer checks cannot see. We also build SEL-Pairs, a benchmark of length-matched evidence and control deletions from three question-answering datasets. Quantitative and qualitative experiments with five reader models on it show that SELD consistently outperforms strong and recent baselines across compressors, compression rates and models, identifying the evidence-removing edit in 83% of matched pairs with unchanged answers, against 70% for the strongest baseline. These results show that evidence loss in compressed contexts can be detected even when the answer is unchanged.
authors: Wentao Lei, Li Liu
bullets: Silent evidence loss can make compressed contexts unsafe for reuse because answers may remain correct but unsupported.
SELD compares shifts in a reader model’s preferences among unchosen answers before and after compression, requiring no training or labels.
The authors introduce SEL-Pairs, a benchmark of matched evidence-removal and control deletions from three QA datasets.
Across five reader models, compressors, and compression rates, SELD identified the evidence-removing edit in 83% of unchanged-answer pairs, versus 70% for the strongest baseline.
The method targets evidence loss beyond answer-preservation checks; its evaluation scope is the benchmark’s datasets, models, and compression settings.

(a) How often each check scores the keysentence deletion above its equal-length control, among pairs whose answer did not change (50% is chance; LUMINA-ECU is post hoc). (b) The two main tests (pooled over reader models) and eight per-reader tests. Figure 1: Silent evidence loss and how SELD detects it (illustrative; bars: gray for the original context, blue for the compressed one). (1) Compression removes the only sentence that states the answer. (2) With the full guide, both reader models answer the right. After compression, reader model A still answers the right from its default, so an answer check passes; reader model B, reading the same compressed context downstream, falls back on a different default and answers the left. The loss was silent for A, so nothing stopped the context from reaching B. (3) Checks that look at the top answer (answer agreement, JS divergence, answer-likelihood drop) see almost no change; in our tests they change less than when an equally long, harmless sentence is deleted. SELD compares the reader model’s preferences among all the answers it leaves unsaid, which shift when the evidence is gone. A real case with measured scores is given in Section I.

Figure 2: SEL-Pairs and SELD (schematic). (1) For each input, an evidence edit (red) removes evidence and a control edit (gray, dashed) removes other text of exactly the same token length: single-sentence deletion from the original context on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA (denoted S and C in the text); swaps inside LLMLingua-2 outputs at 25, 50 and 75% and inside Provence outputs (B and C, with the output as input A; LLMLingua-2 swaps are refilled to equal length); and MuSiQue’s official unanswerable context against a control that keeps the key paragraphs (U and T ). (2) SELD (step 1) reads the reader model’s scores for every possible next word under O and X , so that the answers left unsaid count; (2) centers them and ignores their scale, so that a mere change in confidence does not count; and (3) measures the angle between the two patterns. A check passes a pair when it scores the evidence edit above its equal-length control.

papers.abstract: Recent advancements in multimodal diffusion language models (MDLMs) have exhibited strong global modeling capabilities through iterative refinement. We observe that mask uncertainty follows an overall downward trend during iterative denoising, while a few denoising steps exhibit localized entropy spikes closely associated with hallucinations. We argue that anomalous steps can be identified by measuring the entropy deviation of each denoising step from its neighboring temporal window. We hypothesize that discrete token commitment discards the distributional information at masked positions, limiting the continued interaction between candidate semantics and the context during entropy spikes. With this goal, we present StepRefine, a plug-and-play decoding strategy that leverages semantic context to achieve reliable denoising. The core of our method lies in a step-aware switch between discrete denoising and latent refinement. The model employs probability-weighted embeddings at entropy spike steps to preserve diverse reasoning hypotheses and performs multiple rounds of continuous refinement. Meanwhile, a refinement controller monitors distributional stability to reduce unnecessary loops and switch the model back to standard discrete denoising. Through extensive experiments, StepRefine demonstrates significant hallucination mitigation across different MDLMs on multimodal benchmarks.
authors: Zhongxing Xu, Zhonghua Wang, Zhe Qian, Shiyan Su, Ming Hu, Xiaocheng Zou, Wei Feng, Mingquan Lin, Yuyin Zhou, Yifan Peng, Hamid Rezatofighi, Zongyuan Ge
bullets: MDLM denoising uncertainty generally decreases, but localized entropy spikes are linked to hallucinations.
The method identifies anomalous steps by comparing step entropy with that of a neighboring temporal window.
At spike steps, probability-weighted embeddings preserve multiple semantic hypotheses instead of committing to discrete tokens.
A stability-aware controller performs repeated latent refinement only when needed, then returns to discrete denoising.
Experiments report significant hallucination mitigation across multiple MDLMs on multimodal benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Entropy spikes characterization across decoding steps. (a) Token-level scatter of stepwise entropy change on LLaDA-V (top) and Dream-VL (bottom). Roughly 80% of hallucinated tokens fall in the area above µ+ σ. (b) Distribution of entropy spikes across denoising steps on LLaDA-V (top) and Dream-VL (bottom). On both models, entropy spikes mostly occur in the early-to-middle decoding stage, when few tokens have been committed and the available context is still limited. (c) Effect of random remasking on performance using LLaDA-V. Top: replacing low-confidence remasking with random remasking at 10% of randomly selected steps causes a substantial drop on three datasets. Bottom: applying the same random remasking only at entropy spike steps yields negligible change. At entropy spike steps, confidence signals may become less discriminative, making discrete commitment decisions less reliably grounded in the current contextual information.

Figure 1: Entropy spikes in denoising dynamics. (a) A representative example illustrating the correlation between entropy spikes and hallucinations. Tokens committed at steps with an entropy spike closely correspond to hallucinated content in the response. (b) Mean mask entropy decreases steadily across denoising, while a few steps show sharp rises that break the local trend, which we refer to as entropy spikes. (c) A step is flagged as an entropy spike when its stepwise entropy change exceeds the µ+ σ bound from the calibration window.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved promising performance for generalized robotic manipulation, yet their reliance on expensive real-robot data remains a fundamental bottleneck. A scalable alternative is to transfer knowledge from off-the-shelf human-centric videos. However, existing methods extract latent action representations that are entangled with scene-specific noise, diluting the transferred knowledge. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Action-Intent Transfer (AIT), a two-stage method that transfers knowledge through a clean action representation shared across humans and robots. In the first stage, AIT extracts explicit action intents and disentangles the implicit action intent from manipulation videos. In the second stage, AIT aligns the human and robot domains within this shared intent space and decodes the intent into executable robot actions. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world environments demonstrate that AIT transfers human knowledge more effectively and consistently outperforms prior baselines.

(c) Our method also learns from easy-to-acquire raw videos, yet extracts a clean Action Intent shared across humans and robots, enabling noise-free knowledge transfer to the robot.

papers.abstract: Learning robust manipulation policies for diverse everyday objects remains challenging because objects with different materials exhibit distinct deformation and contact dynamics. While diffusion policies provide a powerful framework for modeling multimodal manipulation behaviors, they typically lack explicit physical reasoning and may produce averaged actions when facing heterogeneous objects. We present a physics-aware diffusion policy that augments visual imitation learning with object physical understanding. Our framework recovers material properties from visual demonstrations by coupling 3D Gaussian Splatting with differentiable Material Point Method simulation, where video guidance and particle-level constraints enable accurate physical parameter estimation. The estimated physics conditions are further integrated into a material-aware Mixture-of-Experts diffusion policy, allowing adaptive behavior generation across different physical regimes. For practical deployment, we introduce a physics memory bank that provides efficient physical retrieval without requiring online simulation optimization. Experiments on a wide range of simulated and real-world objects demonstrate improved manipulation success and generalization over existing diffusion-based approaches. These results show that incorporating physical knowledge is critical for scalable robot manipulation in diverse environments.
authors: Can Wang

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed training framework. Given multi-view images, we first estimate the physical properties of the manipulated object by combining feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF-3DGS) with MPM via a differentiable physical simulation. The simulator is coupled with a differentiable rasterizer and optimized under video guidance, where gradients are back-propagated through the simulation. Physics-based constraints, including Dirichlet boundary conditions for manipulation events and geometric consistency via temporal Chamfer distance, further regularize the estimated physical parameters by aligning simulated particle dynamics with demonstration videos. The learned physical parameters are then injected into a physical-aware diffusion policy as physics conditions, together with language instructions and visual observations, enabling the policy to predict physics-consistent robot actions and gripper states.

Fig. 3. Object preservation results on fragile objects. Among successful pick-and-place trials, the methods differ in their ability to preserve object integrity. We evaluate object preservation by measuring grape rupture and irreversible deformation of paper cups over 30 successful pick-andplace trials. A trial is considered successful only if the object remains intact, exhibiting neither grape rupture nor irreversible deformation. Our method achieves the highest object preservation success rate on both object categories.

Fig. 4. Visualization of learned material-aware routing weights in our MoE policy. Each row represents an object and each column corresponds to a physical-property expert. The bubble size and color indicate the routing weight assigned to each expert. The learned router discovers clear expert specialization, where objects with different physical characteristics are preferentially routed to their corresponding experts while maintaining adaptive soft assignments across experts.

papers.abstract: Human-level dexterity remains a central open problem in robotics, yet few simulation frameworks cover the full workflow of dexterous manipulation, from setting up a robot to collecting dexterous demonstrations and evaluating policies. We present DexSuite, an all-in-one simulation framework for dexterous manipulation built on the Genesis simulator. DexSuite provides 30 tasks and assembles its 10 arms and 12 end-effectors, from parallel-jaw grippers to dexterous hands, into more than 100 single-arm robots and thousands of bimanual pairs. It also ships a standardized environment API, integrated teleoperation, and simulated tactile sensing. Moreover, we define a benchmark of 16 task-embodiment pairs spanning diverse contact complexities and horizons, and release a dataset of 4,700 successful episodes in simulation from human teleoperation, scripted experts, and learned policies. We release DexSuite as open source and hope others will build on it. Videos and datasets are available at https://dexsuiteorg.github.io

papers.abstract: User-facing LLM agents must identify which behavioral policies apply at each turn, but evaluating every policy with an LLM is costly. We introduce Signals and Queries (S&Q), a lightweight first-stage relevance filter developed for Parlant 4.0 that removes at least 30% of candidate policies before downstream evaluation while preserving high recall. For each policy, an LLM generates activating examples and hard negatives offline. An independent logistic classifier trained on their embeddings then predicts relevance using embeddings and vector dot products, with no per-turn LLM calls. This shifts expensive relevance evaluation to a smaller candidate set, while allowing each policy's classifier to be updated independently. Evaluated against 9,144 LLM-judge relevance labels covering 254 $τ^2$-bench conversation prefixes and 36 airline policies, S&Q achieves higher precision than top-K and cosine-threshold retrieval at every evaluated recall level, with consistent results across two embedding providers. These findings support inexpensive, per-policy classification as a practical first stage for reducing downstream evaluation workload in customer-facing agents.
authors: Yam Marcovitz

papers.abstract: Preference labels align model training, but the judgments behind them are difficult to inspect or verify. In this paper, we examine how preference construction can be checked when intermediate decisions are recorded, and which of them remain uncertain. We present Symbolic Preference Labeling, a method in which a pretrained language model classifies predefined attributes of prompts and responses. Explicit rules assign response verdicts, and a fixed verdict ranking determines the preference label. Each preference label has a recorded derivation: the response verdicts and preference label can be recomputed from the stored attribute assignments, rules, and verdict ranking without rerunning the language model. On 200 prompts annotated by human raters, the language model produces valid structured outputs for 192 prompts. All eight parsing failures occur in the subset of self-harm prompts marked as harmful. Using 465 preference pairs, we train one policy model with direct preference optimization across five training seeds. Mean measured benign refusal is 40.82 percent on 1,319 benign prompts that resemble unsafe ones, and mean measured toxic refusal is 84.98 percent on 655 toxic prompts. This study distinguishes the reproducibility of preference labels from attribute correctness. The recorded derivations make preference construction open to inspection, while attribute correctness and semantic safety require separate validation.

papers.abstract: The demand for personalized LLMs is shifting from style imitation toward content quality. We investigate whether self-distillation can bridge this gap in existing fine-tuning paradigm. To address this limitation, we introduce MIRROR(Meta- personalization by Internalizing Reference-Revealed On-policy Reflections), a novel self-distillation framework that shifts LLM personalization from imitation toward preference internalization. First, we replace reference-token imitation with reference-revealed on-policy self-distillation, aligning the model's next-token distributions along its own generation trajectories with those of its reference-conditioned self, thereby internalizing user preferences rather than reproducing reference wording.Second, we introduce MIRROR-F, a focal plug-in that augments on-policy distributional alignment with selective supervision over informative reference tokens, thereby strengthening content generation while preserving user-specific expression. Across three personalized generation benchmarks, two model scales, and complementary reference-based and LLM-based evaluations, MIRROR and MIRROR-F achieve leading overall personalization performance and superior text quality, while exhibiting less catastrophic forgetting than SFT-based baselines on three unseen personalized generation tasks. The gains are consistent across model scales and application scenarios, translating to improved performance in LLM personalization tasks.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon urban navigation requires sequential local decisions whose errors can compound over time. Imitation learning (IL) rarely learns from failures, while physical trial-and-error reinforcement learning (RL) is costly. Action-conditioned world models can provide imagined feedback by predicting visual consequences for candidate actions. However, a frozen world model may become less reliable as the policy evolves. In this paper, we introduce RIWANAV, a post-training framework that casts the coupled adaptation of a world model and an action model (policy) as task-specific recursive self-improvement (RSI). Each cycle alternates two updates. The world model evaluates policy actions through imagined outcomes, providing comparative feedback for group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). The improved policy then constructs a grounded self-curriculum, selecting expert-consistent action-video pairs by behavioral novelty and prediction error. The refined world model supplies feedback for the next policy update, closing the recursive self-improvement loop. Experiments show that RIWANAV outperforms training baselines and prior methods, validating the proposed recursive self-improvement loop between the policy and world model. Real-world trials further demonstrate its practical applicability.
